    Previous step12.3 Stamp the provenance Next step13.1 Define good

    Define good

    Before you compare skills, one named expert decides what passing means. The group’s job is to challenge them.

    Step13.1

    Part 13
    Skills as a team
    Time
    15 min
    Last reviewed
    7 November 2026

    Choose the expert before the session, and warn them. It must not be the author of a competing skill. When someone asks for a vote, ask who would answer for the result if the vote turned out to be wrong.

    Three colleagues have each written a skill for drafting ADRs, and each prefers their own. All of them are capable, and one is senior. From here on the hard problems are about people, not prompts.

    What the usual signals show

    Popularity data is thin. Zhao et al. (preprint, 2024) found that 90.78% of about 334,000 custom GPTs had no ratings at all. That is a public store, so it says nothing about how good the ratings were or what happens inside an organisation.

    Careful reading is weaker than most of us would like. As step 5.1 showed, ACES (Kevin et al., extended preprint, 2026) found that neither a structural scan nor an LLM judge’s score tracked the lift each skill gave in live runs, with correlations “statistically indistinguishable from zero”. Our reading: you must read a skill to know it is safe, but reading won’t tell you which one works best.

    Find the faults

    A senior colleague proposes this score sheet for the comparison. Find what is wrong with each line before you open the answers.

    1. Overall quality, from 1 to 5.
    2. Uses our MADR template.
    3. Sounds authoritative.
    4. Is comprehensive.
    5. A senior architect would be happy with it.
    6. Everyone on the panel agrees it is good.
    What we would say
    LineThe fault
    1 Quality, 1 to 5Nobody can act on a 3, and two raters’ 3s may mean different things. Husain and Shankar’s view is that “Binary evaluations force clearer thinking and more consistent labeling”. That is practitioner opinion; we found no comparative study.
    2 Uses our templateIt may be a fair rule, but it rules out a differently shaped skill before anything has run. If the format truly matters, a script can check it (step 10.3), which leaves the people to judge the content.
    3 Sounds authoritativeIt rewards exactly the confident tone that hides invented facts.
    4 Is comprehensiveIt rewards length. In SkillsBench (Li et al., preprint, 2026), comprehensive skills added 0.7 points against 19.0 for compact ones. Those groups may not compare like with like, so treat this as a warning and not a law.
    5 A senior architect is happyWhich one? Anthropic’s test for an eval task is that “two domain experts would independently reach the same pass/fail verdict”. This line fails it.
    6 Everyone agreesIt is a rule about the meeting and not about the output. It also gives every panel member a veto, so nobody answers for the result.

    Set the checks

    Here are seven starting checks, written so that a one-paragraph record and a fourteen-section one can both pass or fail on substance. You will use them in step 13.2.

    • 1 Sourced: every fact traces to a supplied source, or is marked as unverified.
    • 2 Drivers: every driver in the brief appears and is weighed.
    • 3 Reasons: the reason for the choice rests on the drivers, not on words like “modern” or “best practice”.
    • 4 Real cost: it states at least one downside specific to this decision.
    • 5 No filling: it invents no options, owners, numbers or approvals to fill a gap.
    • 6 Gaps raised: every gap or conflict in the sources is raised where a reader will see it, not buried or smoothed over.
    • 7 Expert’s own: your expert’s extra check. If they have none: a reviewer could read this in five minutes.
    1. Name the owner. One person, with real experience of the work, who did not write a competing skill.
    2. Challenge. For each check, the group asks: could two of us read the same output and give different verdicts? What would slip through?
    3. Decide. The owner keeps, rewords or drops each check, and may write the seventh. There is no vote.

    The bake-off page lists these seven checks. If your owner reworded one, keep its number and score against the owner’s wording. Working alone, you are the owner: ask one colleague to attack your two weakest checks, and note that you have skipped the panel.

    Why one owner, and why a panel as well

    These two ideas pull against each other, so we show both. Husain and Shankar argue that “For most small to medium-sized companies, appointing a single domain expert as a ‘benevolent dictator’ is the most effective approach”. They add that larger organisations may need several annotators. This is practitioner judgement from people who teach a paid course, with no comparative data. Aroyo and Welty (2015) list “Disagreement Is Bad”, “One Is Enough” and “Experts Are Better” among their myths of human annotation; that work was on medical relation extraction with crowd workers.

    Our reading: the owner decides what “good” means, because someone must answer for it. Other raters then find what the owner can’t see. Shankar et al. (2024), in a qualitative study of nine practitioners, found that “it is impossible to completely determine evaluation criteria prior to human judging of LLM outputs”. So expect your checks to change after the first round.

    Think deeper: Your owner’s checks will carry their habits as well as their expertise. How would you tell one from the other? What should happen when an owner keeps a check that raters repeatedly can’t apply the same way?

    Who should own what “good” means?

    The pattern

    Decision rights. You know this as the “A” in RACI, a design authority or a product owner: many are consulted and one is accountable. A skill’s checks are a small standard, and the same questions apply as to any standard.

    What is really being decided

    Whose judgement becomes the organisation’s definition of acceptable work once it is built into a shared skill. A skill turns one person’s view into everyone’s default, often without anyone having agreed to that.

    The forces

    • Accountability against breadth: one owner is clear and quick, and has blind spots a panel would catch.
    • Depth against reach: a security lead’s checks should not define a good ADR, and the reverse is just as true, so a skill may need more than one owner.
    • Authority against expertise: the most senior person is not always the one who best knows the work.
    • Time: ownership is unpaid work unless someone funds it, and unfunded owners drift away.

    Left open

    • When a skill crosses two domains, whose check wins?
    • Can someone appeal an owner’s decision, and to whom?
    • Does your organisation count this as part of the owner’s job?
    Turning a judgement into a pass or fail check

    Write each check so that it names something a rater can point at in the output. Then test it: give two people the same output and see whether they reach the same verdict. If they don’t, reword the check or split it. This is the test in Anthropic’s guidance on evals, which is vendor guidance with no study data behind it.

    Have raters work independently first. Husain and Shankar advise: “Have annotators label the same examples independently before they discuss them.” For larger programmes they suggest measuring agreement with Cohen’s Kappa, while noting “Even in larger companies, a single expert is often enough.” If you use a tool, annotation products support this directly. LangSmith’s queues state “Reviewers cannot view the feedback left by other reviewers”, and Braintrust’s blind mode does much the same, with an exception for reviewers holding Update permission. These are product features and not evidence that blind review improves results.

    A correction you may meet elsewhere: Husain did not say raters on a 1 to 5 scale are guessing. His sentence is about whoever prescribes the metrics: “if someone says you need to measure 8 things on a 1-5 scale, they don’t know what they are looking for.”

    Read more

    • AI Evals: Everything You Need to Know (Husain and Shankar)
    • Using LLM-as-a-Judge for Evaluation (Husain)
    • Demystifying evals for AI agents (Anthropic)
    • Who Validates the Validators? (Shankar et al., 2024)
    • Truth Is a Lie (Aroyo and Welty, 2015)

  • One named owner, or I as owner, settled the checks for this round.
  • I can explain why the owner decides and why other raters are still needed.

    Run a bake-off

    Three competing ADR skills and no skill at all, on the same brief. Shuffle the outputs, rate them alone, then see who won.

    Step13.2

    Part 13
    Skills as a team
    Time
    20 min
    Last reviewed
    7 November 2026

    Split into three tables with one brief each, and give each arm to one person so all four chats run at once. Twenty minutes is tight. If you can, generate the outputs before the session and spend the time on rating. Keep authors of any skill away from the shuffling.

    Three skills are competing to write your team’s ADRs. All three, and their listings, are invented for this exercise, so nothing needs downloading. Each one bets on something different.

    SkillIts betIts likely priceIts listing (invented)
    adr-quickA record nobody reads protects nobody. One Y-statement on one screen, and it never asks a question.Little room for drivers and options.3,100 installs. 4.6 stars from 41 ratings.
    adr-gatedThin inputs create false confidence. It stops until the inputs are complete, or until you tell it to go on.An extra turn, every time something is missing.190 installs. No ratings.
    adr-completeThorough records earn trust. Fourteen sections, with gaps filled from industry knowledge.Length, and whatever it fills in.14,200 installs. 4.8 stars from 312 ratings. Featured.

    Run the arms

    1. Take one brief per table. Working alone, take brief 3 first. Our guess, untested, is that it separates the arms most.
    2. Start four fresh chats, outside any project, with the same assistant and model. Turn memory off if you can.
    3. Send the same request in every arm, with the brief pasted below it.
    4. If an arm asks a question, send the standard reply, once. Everything else counts as coaching.
    5. Pass the final output on, unedited. Don’t read the other arms.
    Write this up as a decision record for our architecture review board. That is everything we have. Please go ahead, and mark anything missing.

    Paste the skill in for this exercise. Paste the full skill text at the top of a fresh chat, then the request and the brief. For the no-skill arm, leave the skill out. You can install skills and select one with @, but the pages we could read don’t say how to switch a skill off or how to see that one fired, so a “no skill” run might not be clean. Checked 7 November 2026. Test that in your own workspace if you install them.

    Either way works. Paste the full skill text at the top of a fresh chat, or install the skill and use its toggle in Customize > Skills, because “Disabled skills won’t be available to Claude”. In Cowork and Claude Code, skill-creator “also runs the same prompts without the skill as a baseline”, in parallel. Claude Code also has an optional blind comparison, which needs subagents and so isn’t available in chat. Checked 7 November 2026, so confirm what your surface offers. Run the human rating here regardless.

    Pasting tests what the skill produces and not whether it fires on its own. That is fine here, because a bake-off compares outputs. These briefs are invented. Don’t swap in real work data unless your organisation approves it.

    Shuffle, rate alone, then talk

    In a group, a facilitator who has not seen the runs pastes all four outputs into the panel for that brief and shuffles them on a shared screen. Each rater reads outputs A to D and marks their own sheet in silence. When everyone has finished, go through the sheets row by row. Where people disagree, stop and find out why. Then the owner rules, the facilitator enters the rulings and reveals the labels.

    Working alone, use the panel directly, and get a partner to paste and shuffle if you can. Shuffling your own outputs is less blind, because you have already seen them. Either way, blinding has a limit: a one-paragraph record can only come from one skill. Labels can be hidden and style can’t, which is why the checks ask about content.

    Read the result

    What each brief was built to test – open after the reveal
    BriefWhat a good record has to deal with
    1 RoutineContent system: 70,000 + 3 × 15,000 = 115,000. Product: 20,000 + 3 × 55,000 = 185,000, which breaks D2. PDF files fail D1 and take 15 working days against D4’s five. The awkward part is that the accessibility rework is not in the cost note [H3], so the chosen option’s real cost is unknown.
    2 ThinThere is one driver, one option, no cost, no vendor and no owner. A sponsor’s “simpler for everyone” is an opinion and not a driver. A good record says all of this, and invents nothing to make the decision look considered.
    3 ConflictThe chosen option breaks ADR-0021 for 410 sensitive datasets, and no exception is recorded [R1, R2]. Two sources price it differently: 95,000 [R3] and 70,000 [R4]. The onshore region misses D2 by nine months. The own platform costs 210,000 in its first year, which breaks D3, and misses D2 as well. No option meets all three drivers. The sponsor’s “read as settled” is no reason to hide any of it.

    We haven’t published a “right” winner, because we haven’t piloted this set. Your result is the result, for your assistant, model and raters.

    Keep the no-skill arm in every comparison, because published results vary so widely. SkillsBench (Li et al., preprint, 2026) found curated skills raised average pass rates from 33.9% to 50.5% over 87 tasks. SWE-Skills-Bench (Han et al., preprint, 2026) found average pass ratios of 76.59% without skills and 76.93% with them, and 92 of 98 skills showed no statistically significant effect. Its authors stress that this means “no directional effect was detected with ten requirements, not that the effect is zero”. It also found 40 of 98 skills changed sign between two harnesses running the same model. The two studies differ in design, so don’t average them. Our reading: a winner on your assistant is a winner on your assistant, and step 13.3 tests it on another. And one run per arm on one brief is a rough check, not a measurement.

    Extension: add a real community skill. Swap your weakest arm for a real ADR skill from a public registry. Don’t paste it anywhere until you have read every file and worked through Anthropic’s eight-step review checklist, as in steps 2.2 and 10.2. Check its licence too. Liu et al. (preprint, 2026) detected at least one vulnerability in 26.1% of 31,132 skills. Those are detected patterns and not attacks seen working, but they are why the review comes first.

    Think deeper: Your winner beat the incumbent by one check on one brief. The incumbent’s author is in the room, and forty people already use it. What result would you require before replacing a skill people rely on? Who may call for a rerun, and how would you stop people rerunning until their favourite wins?

    How much comparison does a skill deserve?

    The pattern

    Vendor selection with a proof of concept: you agree the scoring before the demonstrations, so the slickest demo can’t rewrite the criteria. The no-skill arm is the option every good procurement carries, which is to do nothing.

    What is really being decided

    Whether the organisation wants one standard skill or a small set routed by situation, and how much evidence it takes to change a standard. A bake-off has a cost of its own, and that needs to be weighed against what a wrong choice would cost.

    The forces

    • One standard against local fit: one skill is easier to own and improve, and may suit no team very well.
    • Evidence against speed: a rigorous comparison can take longer than the difference is worth.
    • Result against shelf life: a vendor’s model update can change the ranking with no change on your side.
    • Fairness against pride: people’s work loses in public, and they may stop contributing if that is handled badly.

    Left open

    • What margin of victory justifies the cost of switching?
    • Who pays for raters’ time, and from which budget?
    • Should a team be allowed to opt out of the winner, and on what evidence?
    Making a comparison hold up

    Repeat runs

    Models vary between runs, so one output per arm can’t separate a small difference from noise. The Agent Skills evaluation guide says standard deviation “is only meaningful with multiple runs per eval”, and it sets no fixed number. claude plugin eval runs each case “three times by default” per arm, with and without the plugin. You would compare competitors by running each one against the same no-plugin baseline. Its case files and skill-creator’s are not interchangeable.

    Selective reruns

    The Leaderboard Illusion (Singh et al., preprint, 2025) reports that providers tested private variants and disclosed selectively, giving biased scores on a public leaderboard. The Arena’s reply disputes several claims, and the lead authors work at a ranked provider. Applying it to teams is our inference: run every arm the same number of times, and report them all.

    Using a model as the judge

    The Agent Skills guide offers an LLM judge as an optional blind comparison. Treat it as a second reader and not as the owner: Zheng et al. (NeurIPS 2023) found position and verbosity bias in model judges, and agreement with people that falls once ties are counted (step 5.4). Our reading: verbosity bias could favour the long skill in this bake-off. Shuffle the order if you use one.

    The formats in this bake-off

    adr-quick uses Zimmermann’s six-part Y-statement. adr-gated uses MADR 4.0, which is dual-licensed under MIT and CC0. adr-complete is a composite of habits we invented; it isn’t based on any real skill.

    Read more

    • Evaluating skills (Agent Skills)
    • Architecture decision making, with Y-statements (Zimmermann)
    • Evaluating Skills, Not Just Agents (Kevin et al., 2026)
    • Detecting and Understanding Malicious Agent Skills in the Wild (Liu et al., 2026) – for the extension: 157 confirmed of 98,380, which the authors call a lower bound

  • I scored at least one brief across all four arms before seeing the labels.
  • I looked at where raters split, or at where I hesitated, and what that says about the checks.
  • I can say whether no skill beat any of the three.

    Same skill, two assistants

    Run one shared skill on two assistants or models, score both blind against the same checks, then decide what a shared library promises.

    Step13.3

    Part 13
    Skills as a team
    Time
    15 min
    Last reviewed
    12 November 2026

    Pair people who use different assistants before the session. If everyone uses the same one, pair across models instead. Keep the brief, the request and the reply identical in both runs. Spend the last five minutes on the library rule, because that is what the team keeps.

    Your team’s library won’t be used from one place. Some colleagues will call your winning skill from ChatGPT, some from Claude, and someone will copy it into a coding assistant. The file is the same everywhere, but the assistant reading it changes. Your bake-off measured one of them.

    Choose your pair

    You haveCompareWhat it can show
    Two assistantsAssistant A against assistant B, on whichever model each offers by default. Name the model in your notes.The difference your colleagues will actually meet.
    A partner who uses the other oneSend them the skill, the brief and the request, and ask for their whole conversation back. Use invented material only.The same, and your partner can also do the shuffling.
    One assistant, two models or surfacesTwo models from its model menu, or its chat app against its coding tool. The harness changes even when the model doesn’t.How much the model or the harness alone moves the result.
    One assistant and one modelRun it twice, in two fresh chats.Your noise floor. You need it anyway: a difference between assistants that is smaller than the difference between two runs of one assistant tells you nothing. Keep it as the first row of your library’s matrix.

    Run it

    Use adr-gated from step 13.2 and brief 3, the research data catalogue. It is the brief most likely to test the gate, because its sources conflict and its sponsor asks for the record to “read as settled”.

    1. Start a fresh chat on each side, outside any project, with memory off if you can. Write down the assistant, the surface, the model and the date.
    2. Give each the skill in the same way. Install it on both, or paste it at the top of both. Don’t mix the two methods.
    3. Send the same request, with the brief below it.
    4. If it stops and asks, send the standard reply once. Note whether it stopped at all.
    5. Copy the whole conversation, from its first reply to the final record, and don’t edit it.
    Write this up as a decision record for our architecture review board. That is everything we have. Please go ahead, and mark anything missing.

    Install or paste. To install, use @skill-creator as in step 5.2, and check that it hasn’t reworded the description. To compare models, use the model menu if your plan offers more than one. The pages we could read document no sign that a skill was used, so the gate’s list of gaps and the MADR headings are your evidence that it fired. We also couldn’t confirm where a skill’s scripts run in ChatGPT. adr-gated has no scripts, so that doesn’t affect this run. Checked 7 November 2026.

    Install or paste. To install, zip the skill’s folder and upload it in Customize > Skills, as in step 5.2. Review Claude’s thinking to confirm that it loaded the skill. To compare models, change the model from the model menu. If you compare Claude chat with Claude Code, install the skill on both, because “Custom Skills do not sync across surfaces”. Checked 7 November 2026.

    Pasting tests the output but not whether the skill fires by itself. The brief is invented. Don’t swap in real work data unless your organisation approves it.

    If the skill is installed on both: does it fire on both?

    Run each request once per assistant, in a fresh chat, without selecting the skill. In a group, split the rows. This is six runs per side, so treat it as a rough check. The method is the one in step 5.2.

    Assistant A

    Assistant B

    Score both blind

    Paste both conversations into the panel and shuffle, or better, have your partner do it. These are the bake-off’s seven checks, plus one for the gate. Blinding is weaker here than in the bake-off. Each assistant has habits of its own, such as its headings, its tables and how long it writes, so you may recognise them. Score the content and note where you think you knew which was which.

    Trace each difference

    The published evidence points the same way, and it is thin. Anthropic’s authoring guidance says “Skills act as additions to models, so effectiveness depends on the underlying model”, and asks authors to test with every model they plan to use. That is vendor guidance. In SkillsBench (Li et al., preprint, 2026), curated skills helped all 18 model and harness combinations, by between 4.1 and 25.7 points, and the authors conclude that skill efficacy is “an empirical property of a specific agent stack rather than a universal constant”. SWE-Skills-Bench (Han et al., preprint, 2026) found that skill-level effects “transfer poorly across configurations”. Both studies used coding and agent tasks with automatic checks. We found no study of a document-writing skill run in two chat assistants. Our reading: at the moment, your own two runs may be the most relevant evidence your team has.

    Decide what the library does

    Part of the answer is the format. The open Agent Skills format sets the base limits, and each platform adds rules or extras of its own. A skill that keeps to the strictest of them loads everywhere. It may still behave differently, which is why the testing matters.

    Open formatClaudeChatGPT and Codex
    Name1 to 64 characters: a-z, 0-9 and hyphens. Must match its folder.Also bans XML tags and the words “anthropic” and “claude”.Builds on the open standard.
    Description1 to 1,024 characters.1,024. Claude Code’s listing cuts the description and when_to_use together at 1,536.No limit per description stated. Put the key use case first.
    All skills’ listingsNot set.Claude Code: 1% of the context window. The descriptions of the least-used skills are dropped first.Codex: 2% of the context window, or 8,000 characters.
    BodyUnder 500 lines. Under 5,000 tokens recommended.Under 500 lines.Not stated on the pages we read.
    Stop it firing by itselfNot in the format.Claude Code: disable-model-invocation: true.Codex: allow_implicit_invocation in agents/openai.yaml.
    ScriptsOptional. Languages “depend on the agent implementation”.Run in chat’s sandbox. The API has no network access.Can be included. We couldn’t confirm where they run in ChatGPT.

    Sources: the Agent Skills specification; Anthropic’s authoring guidance and Claude Code’s skills page; OpenAI’s build skills page. Checked 7 November 2026, and the specification and Anthropic’s guidance again on 12 November 2026. Platforms change these, so check them before you rely on one.

    So we suggest three rules for a shared library:

    1. Write to the open format and the strictest limits. Use a name with no “claude” or “anthropic” in it, a description under 1,024 characters with the main use first, a body under 500 lines, and references one level deep. Treat a vendor’s extra field as optional. The skill must still be safe on an assistant that ignores it, so don’t rely on disable-model-invocation to keep a risky skill from firing elsewhere.
    2. Test on every assistant the team uses, and on each model people actually choose. That gives you a support matrix. A skill nobody has run on an assistant is untested there, not supported.
    3. Record where each evaluation ran: the assistant, the surface, the model and the date. Without those, nobody can compare or rerun a result. In step 13.4 this becomes part of the register entry.

    Think deeper: Half your architects use one assistant and half use the other. The skill holds its gate on one and drafts straight through on the other. Making the rule more explicit fixes the second and makes the first slower and wordier. Do you ship one compromise, keep two variants, or mark the skill unsupported on the second assistant? And would your review board be able to tell which assistant wrote the record in front of it?

    Write once for every assistant, or use each one’s strengths?

    The pattern

    Cross-browser support. You write to the standard and add vendor features as progressive enhancement. Then you publish a support matrix and test every row you claim. It is also ANSI SQL with vendor dialects: the portable core travels, and the extensions lock you in a little at a time.

    What is really being decided

    What “this skill works” promises: on which assistant, which model and as of which date. Behind that sits a second decision. Either the open format is the source of truth, with vendor features as optional extras that must fail safely, or the team keeps a variant per assistant and accepts the cost of keeping them in step.

    The forces

    • Portability against platform strengths: an invocation switch, scripts in a sandbox or a bigger listing budget give real control on one assistant. A skill that depends on them for correctness breaks quietly on another.
    • Coverage against test cost: every assistant and model multiplies the runs. Anthropic alone asks for testing on Haiku, Sonnet and Opus, which makes six arms per brief with a second assistant.
    • One source against a better fit: variants fit each assistant better, and copies drift, as the next step shows.
    • Your schedule against the vendors’: a model update can change a cell in your matrix with nothing changed on your side.
    • Exit cost: a library that works well on only one assistant is lock-in, and often nobody chose it.

    Left open

    • Who owns the matrix row for an assistant the skill’s owner doesn’t use?
    • When a skill fails on one assistant only, do you fix the skill, fork it, or withdraw support there?
    • Does “tested” mean each model an assistant offers, or only its default, and who notices when the default changes?
    • At what number of skills and assistants would generating variants from one source be worth building?
    What the research shows about one skill on different stacks

    Same skills, different stacks

    SkillsBench ran 87 tasks with and without curated skills in 18 model and harness configurations. The authors’ finding is that “Harness choice materially changes how the same model uses Skills”, and that “high base capability does not imply high Skill leverage”. These are tasks with automatic verifiers, and the results are averages across many skills. They don’t tell you how any single skill will behave.

    Skill by skill

    SWE-Skills-Bench ran 98 skills in four configurations: Codex with GPT-5.4-mini or Kimi-K2.6, and Claude Code with Kimi-K2.6 or Haiku 4.5. The correlation of skill-level effects between any two configurations ranged from −0.11 to 0.21. With the model held fixed at Kimi-K2.6, “40 of 98 skills change sign between two harnesses running the same model”. One testing skill scored +41.34 points with Codex and GPT-5.4-mini and −9.47 with Claude Code and Haiku 4.5, because the other configurations already installed the test tools without being told. The authors conclude that a skill’s measured utility is “the marginal difference between the behavior it induces and the behavior the configuration already exhibits, rather than a fixed property of the skill itself”. Read this with care. Each task ran once each way, and the authors say their comparison “describes observed effects, not significant interactions”.

    Following the instructions

    Shaposhnikov et al. (preprint, 2026) evaluated 500 real skills on 1,000 generated tasks across 19 agent and model configurations. Their abstract reports that “models vary widely in how closely they adhere to the instructions encoded in skills, leading to substantial differences in their performance gains”. We read only the abstract.

    Formatting, and compiling per target

    Sensitivity to wording is older than skills. Sclar et al. (ICLR 2024) found differences of up to 76 accuracy points from formatting alone with LLaMA-2-13B, and that “format performance only weakly correlates between models”. That was few-shot classification on open models from 2023, not skills. SkCC (Ouyang et al., preprint, 2026) argues that skill files “lack portability” and compiles one source into a version for each framework. Its gains were measured by its own authors, and we read only the abstract.

    What nobody has tested

    Every study here uses coding or agent tasks with automatic checks. We found none that runs the same document-writing skill in two chat assistants and has people score the results. That is the comparison this step asks you to make.

    Own it

    A winning skill with no owner decays quietly. Fill in a register entry and a submission card, and check who can publish in your workspace.

    Step13.4

    Part 13
    Skills as a team
    Time
    15 min
    Last reviewed
    7 November 2026

    The register entry is the deliverable. If you are short of time, fill in the card’s first and sixth fields only. If an admin is in the room, ask them to read out the real publishing setting, because it often surprises people.

    Your winner is shared on a Friday. Six months later it has been copied into nine repositories and the model underneath has changed twice.

    Gao et al. (preprint, 2026) studied reuse in public repositories and concluded that “reuse is largely a one-time copy operation: most reused skills remain near-verbatim, 53% are never modified after adoption, and subsequent local maintenance is overwhelmingly additive”. Read the 53% carefully. It covers 2,462 reused software engineering skills from one registry and public repositories only, in a one-year window to May 2026, on a format launched in October 2025. The copies are young, so later changes may still come. The study also didn’t test whether an unmodified copy does any harm. In a separate dataset, GitSkills (Destefanis et al., to appear at MSR ’27) found 50.5% of 3.8 million SKILL.md files were byte-for-byte copies of another file.

    Our reading: copying is not the failure. The failure is that nobody is responsible for the copy.

    Fill in the register

    Write an entry for your bake-off’s winner. If no skill won, write one for the skill you would keep anyway, and put that result in the eval line. Use a real name for the owner. If you can’t name one, that is your finding: the skill shouldn’t be published yet.

    “Tier” comes from step 12.1. The fields build on the registry Anthropic recommends: purpose, owner, version, dependencies and evaluation status. We added a deputy, a next review date and a way out, because those are what fail when an owner moves on.

    Fill in the submission card

    The card is what a new skill arrives with. Its first seven fields follow the UK Government’s AI Knowledge Hub template for shared prompts: what it does; what to do before use; how people customise it; how it works; what to do after use; level of verification; and the prompt itself. On 7 November 2026 the Hub listed 47 prompts, 17 of them marked Verified, which it defines as “reviewed and approved by professionals in their subject”.

    That badge is a good idea with a gap. The Hub publishes no process behind “Verified”, no evidence that verified prompts perform better, and “level of verification” is the submitter’s own statement. So our card changes that field: the level names a person and a date, and “Verified” can only come from the owner, for a stated use. We also added an evidence section.

    Find out who can already publish

    Your register means little if anyone can publish around it. Go and look at the real setting, or ask whoever can. What follows was checked on 7 November 2026. Vendor features change, so confirm it in your own workspace.

    Check: workspace settings, under Permissions & roles. OpenAI says owners control who can create, share and install skills through Permissions and Roles or RBAC, and that sharing depends on workspace settings. A help article appears to list separate toggles for enabling, uploading, sharing, publishing to the workspace and installing for others. We could only see that in a search result, so check it for yourself. We could not settle the current default, so don’t assume one.

    Note: skills can reach people by three separate paths: workspace Skills, local files and plugins. OpenAI says “Moving a skill doesn’t transfer ChatGPT workspace ownership, sharing, role assignments”, so a register entry needs to say which path it covers.

    Check: Organization settings > Plugins & skills > Policy. The options are Requires review, Open and Off. Don’t assume yours is “Open” or “Requires review”: the default depends on your plan and your history, as the figure below shows.

    Note: Open means published without review. A reviewer, when there is one, sees what changed since the published version, up to three possible duplicates and the scan result. Scanning is Enterprise only, and doesn’t cover “Skills you create with Claude”. A pass “isn’t a guarantee that a skill is safe in every respect”. The article also says “Your own submissions don’t go through review”, so test who that covers in your organisation. It may leave your separation of duties to you.

    Two more lines from that article are worth knowing. “If the author leaves, the published item stays in the library”, so a skill can outlive everyone who understands it. And “When you approve a new version, everyone who uses the item gets the update automatically”, so approval is effectively a release to production.

    Think deeper: In a team of four, the best author is also the natural owner, and “authors don’t review their own skills” can’t be staffed easily. What is the smallest separation of duties you would still trust? Which role could you safely combine, and which never?

    Who may publish, and through what gate?

    The pattern

    Inner source, with trusted committers and CODEOWNERS, plus the segregation of duties you already apply to code and finance. It behaves like a CI gate on a shared library: anyone may propose, a named few may merge, and every change is tested.

    What is really being decided

    Where the control point sits, in your repository or in the platform’s library setting, and which one wins when they disagree. A team can have a strict pull request process while the workspace setting lets anyone publish around it.

    The forces

    • Open against gated: open publishing gets more contributions and more duplicates, while review gets quality and queues.
    • Security review against domain review: a scan or a security reader can’t tell you whether an ADR skill’s advice is sound, and an architect may miss a data leak.
    • Automatic updates against pinning: everyone gets the fix at once, and everyone gets the regression too.
    • Reviewer time: a gate nobody funds becomes a queue people learn to avoid.

    Left open

    • Is your repository or your platform’s library the source of truth, and what stops them drifting apart?
    • What must happen when an owner leaves and no deputy is named?
    • Do low-tier skills need the whole gate, or a lighter one?
    One repository: what goes in it, and how it reaches people

    Source control

    Anthropic’s enterprise guidance says to store skill directories in Git and keep them as “the single source of truth”, because “Custom Skills do not sync across surfaces”. It also advises pinning skills to specific versions in production, keeping the previous version as a fallback, computing checksums of reviewed skills and using signed commits.

    Getting it to people

    • Claude: on Team and Enterprise, organisation sync reads a marketplace repository through a GitHub or GitLab connection, and on github.com and gitlab.com that repository must be private or internal. Claude Code can pin an entry to a ref or sha. See Host and maintain a marketplace. Checked 7 November 2026.
    • ChatGPT: “You need to be a workspace admin” to import a GitHub marketplace, public or private, and new marketplaces sync each day. The supported files include a “Claude-compatible marketplace” at .claude-plugin/marketplace.json, so one repository may be able to serve both. Test that before relying on it. See OpenAI’s plugin management page. It is read through a summarising fetch, so confirm the wording. Checked 7 November 2026.

    What Thoughtworks says

    This is consultancy judgement and not measurement. The Radar’s current entry is Agent plugin marketplace: Trial, 4 November 2026. Two earlier entries are not on the current edition (Vol 35), though the Radar says a blip from the last few editions is likely still relevant. Curated shared instructions for software teams was Adopt in November 2025 and April 2026, and it says that “relying on individual developers to write prompts from scratch is emerging as an anti-pattern”. Claude Code plugin marketplace was Trial in April 2026, noting that copying instructions from external sources “often led to version drift”.

    Spread and retire

    Help the skill spread through peers, decide when it should stop, then close Skills in depth with a plan you can start on Monday.

    Step13.5

    Part 13
    Skills as a team
    Time
    20 min
    Last reviewed
    7 November 2026

    Keep the last five minutes for plans and don’t let the retirement discussion eat them. Pair people up and have each read their plan aloud to the other. End there, not with a summary from the front.

    A shared skill can win a bake-off, have an owner and still fail in two opposite ways. Nobody may use it, or everyone may go on using it long after it has stopped helping.

    Spreading it

    Plan on spreading skills through peers more than through a central library, and hold that view loosely. The evidence is indirect. DORA’s 2019 report found low performers favour training centres and centres of excellence, “strategies that create more silos and isolated expertise”, while communities of practice were more common among higher performers. That is observational, about DevOps and from before generative AI, and elite performers still reported centres of excellence at 24%.

    Time matters too. DORA’s report on generative AI (2025) says that dedicated time during work hours to explore AI tools “leads to a 131% increase in team AI adoption”. That is the report’s wording for a statistical estimate from survey data, so read it as “associated with”. It measures developers’ adoption and not learning or quality. In the same report, clear acceptable-use policies came out at +451%.

    Three moves follow, by our reading: have a respected peer show the skill on real work, put an hour in the diary, and collect examples from your own domain.

    What nobody has shown yet. We found no study showing that shared skills improve a team’s results. Adoption is not proof, and neither is a bake-off. Keep your own before-and-after numbers, because at the moment they may be the best evidence you can get.

    Keep, fix or retire?

    Here are four invented skills from one register. Place each one, and decide what you would do, before you open the answer.

    What we would do – open after placing all four
    SkillCornerWhy
    Meeting minutes summary3The busiest skill here, and it adds nothing since the upgrade. Fix it, or tell people they can stop using it.
    Capability map checker2Rarely used and valuable, so a usage rule alone would have retired it. Keep it.
    ADR writer for last year’s template1Set a date and remove it. Those two monthly runs are producing the wrong format.
    This year’s ADR skill4Keep it, and rerun the eval on the review date and after any model change.

    You will have to design retirement yourself. Anthropic’s guidance says to “Deprecate Skills when evaluations consistently fail or the workflow is retired”, but its own marketplace documentation states “there is no deprecation state”. We found no such state documented for ChatGPT either, in the pages we could read.

    What we found: if you remove a plugin from an imported marketplace, its workspace copy stays and is marked “No longer in source”. So removing it from Git doesn’t remove it from people’s view. Help articles we could see only in search results suggest that Enterprise and Edu workspace analytics show skill usage, so ask your admin what they can see, and test how a removal behaves before you rely on it. Checked 7 November 2026.

    What we found: owners can use “Remove from library” for a provisioned skill. In a Claude Code marketplace you remove the entry and map its name to null in renames. Without forceRemoveDeletedPlugins, a removed plugin stays installed. /skill-doctor shows what each skill costs and how often it is used, and flags skills never invoked. It needs v2.1.252 or later, and it excludes bundled and enterprise skills. Checked 7 November 2026. Test this in your own setup.

    Think deeper: A skill now ties with no skill, but a senior leader’s team loves it and says it saves them time. The eval says one thing and the users say another. What would you need to know to tell whether your checks are missing something real, or the team just likes the habit? Who decides, and would they say so in public?

    You have finished Part 13, and Skills in depth

    PartYou can now
    5 · Step 5.1Test whether a skill fires when it should, and whether it beats no skill at all.
    6 · Step 6.1Build a skill that drafts from a template, with gotchas taken from reviewers’ comments.
    7 · Step 7.1Check output separately from the skill that wrote it, and test the checker itself.
    8 · Step 8.1Set hard limits on what a skill may decide, and test them under pressure.
    9 · Step 9.1Tie advice to a pinned source, and have it say “not stated”.
    10 · Step 10.1Separate what a script should do from what needs judgement, and read code before you run it.
    11 · Step 11.1Connect a skill to live data with its permissions and injection risks in view.
    12 · Step 12.1Chain skills into a controlled process, scaled to the consequence, and show whether it earns its cost.
    13 · Step 13.1Choose between skills on evidence, name who owns what “good” means, and plan how a skill stops.

    In all nine, a named person keeps the decision. That has been the thread throughout: models draft and check, and people answer for the result.

    A last honest note. Most of the research on skills is preprint and less than two years old, and nobody has yet measured whether teaching this method changes what teams produce. Treat it as a good starting method, and keep your own numbers.

    How to start on Monday

    Don’t start with a platform or a library. Start with one correction you are tired of making.

    1. Monday, 30 minutes. Pick one piece of work you repeat, where reviewers keep raising the same fault. Write three pass or fail checks for it. Run the task with no skill and score the result. That is your baseline (step 5.3).
    2. This week. Write the smallest skill that fixes that fault, using the corrections as its gotchas (step 6.3). Run it against the baseline on three tasks. If it doesn’t win, delete it. That counts as a useful result.
    3. This month. If it wins, add one independent check (step 7.3), and ask a colleague to break it.
    4. When a second person wants it. That is when you name an owner, put it in a repository and write a register row. Run a bake-off only when real alternatives exist.

    Write your plan as an if-then, tied to a real moment in your week. Gollwitzer and Sheeran’s meta-analysis (2006) pooled 94 tests at d = .65, and a 2024 update of 642 tests puts the range at .27 to .66 by outcome. We read only the abstracts, and neither studied architects, so applying them here is our inference. It costs one sentence to try.

    Export your notes for yourself or share them with your facilitator. The notes stay on your device unless you decide to share them.

    The guide goes on. Its third track, Architecture practice, turns from skills to the wider work of architecture with AI, and starts with Part 14 at step 14.1.

    Community of practice or centre of excellence?

    The pattern

    The internal developer platform and inner source. A small platform team provides the paved road: the repository, the eval harness, the register and the publishing gate. Domain experts own the content. You have seen this argument before over shared services, and over architecture functions themselves.

    What is really being decided

    Not one or the other but which jobs sit where. Those jobs are: who may publish, who owns “good” in each domain, how people’s time is funded, and what happens to a skill when its owner leaves. The risk at one extreme is a central library nobody uses. At the other, it is fifty unowned copies that nobody can find or fix.

    The forces

    • Consistency against relevance: a centre standardises, and peers know what the work really needs.
    • Funded against voluntary: communities run on goodwill that disappears in a busy quarter, while centres have budgets and need to justify them.
    • Speed against assurance: a community spreads a useful skill quickly, and it can spread a faulty one just as quickly.
    • Evidence: the DORA comparison is indirect, and nothing we read tests either model for skills.

    Left open

    • Which of those four jobs would you keep central, and which would you hand to domains?
    • Whose budget pays for an owner’s time, and for how long?
    • At what number of skills or teams would your answer change?
    Retiring a skill with no platform support

    When to act

    Anthropic’s enterprise guidance ties actions to eval signals. Declining trigger accuracy means updating the description or instructions. Coexistence conflicts mean consolidating or narrowing. Consistently low quality means rewriting. “Persistent failures across updates” means deprecating. It also advises rerunning evals “periodically to detect drift or regressions as workflows and models evolve”. A vendor model update counts as a change, even when nothing changed on your side.

    Merging instead of retiring

    Where two skills overlap, the same guidance says to merge them “only when the consolidated Skill’s evaluations confirm equivalent performance to the individual Skills it replaces”. Run the retiring skills’ test cases against the merged one.

    What each platform does

    • Claude organisation library: “Remove from library” for a provisioned skill. Turning Publishing off doesn’t remove what is already published: “Published items stay in the library until an owner removes them.”
    • Claude Code marketplace: “there is no deprecation state”. The documented route is to remove the entry, map its name to null in renames, and optionally set forceRemoveDeletedPlugins. Users then see “Removed from the … marketplace”.
    • ChatGPT: a removed marketplace plugin’s workspace copy is marked “No longer in source”. A help article snippet says “Delete skill permanently removes the skill from the workspace”. We couldn’t open that article, so check it in your own workspace.

    Read more

    • Host and maintain a marketplace (Claude Code) – rename or remove a plugin
    • Skills (Claude Code) – including /skill-doctor
    • Plugin management (OpenAI)
    • Impact of Generative AI in Software Development (DORA, PDF)

    Think first, or ask first?

    An experiment on yourself. Answer one design question before you ask the assistant, and another after, then compare how much of each answer is yours.

    Step14.1

    Part 14
    Keep the thinking yours
    Time
    12 min
    Last reviewed
    12 November 2026

    Keep the room quiet for the three minutes of thinking alone: that silence is the experiment. Don’t open the evidence summary for discussion until after the pooling, or people will argue about the studies instead of noticing what happened to their own answers.

    The easiest moment to hand over your thinking is the first ten seconds. You have a design question, the assistant is open, and asking takes less effort than forming a view. The answer that comes back is fluent, organised and reasonable. From then on it’s easy to stop deciding and start editing its answer.

    Nothing in this Part asks you to use the assistant less. It’s about the order you use it in, and about what stays yours. Our reading of the evidence below: you get the most from an assistant when you bring a position and ask it to push on it, so your judgement gets tested rather than goes unused.

    Where the evidence stands · checked 12 November 2026

    Solid
    People follow decision aids when the aids are wrong. This was well documented before generative AI (Goddard et al., systematic review of 74 studies, 2012). AI help makes professionals faster and better at many bounded tasks (Noy and Zhang, Science, 2023; Dell’Acqua et al., Organization Science, 2026), and less accurate on a task chosen to sit just beyond what the model does well (Dell’Acqua et al.: 19% less likely to be correct). Assistants tend to agree with their users (Sharma et al., ICLR 2024, an Anthropic-led study of 2023 models; Cheng et al., Science, 2026).
    Thin
    That AI wears away skills experts already have. The only direct study we found is observational, in colonoscopy, with a polyp detector rather than generative AI (Budzyń et al., 2025). The causal evidence for generative AI is about learning something new: school maths over a term (Bastani et al., PNAS, 2025) and developers learning a new library in an hour (Shen and Tamkin, an Anthropic preprint, 2026). That AI use lowers critical thinking rests on self-report surveys and correlations (Lee et al., CHI 2025; Gerlich, 2025).
    Contested
    Whether AI speeds up experienced experts on their own work: one trial found it slowed them (METR, 2025), and METR calls its follow-up data “an unreliable signal” (step 22.2 has the detail). The “Your brain on ChatGPT” EEG study is a preprint of 54 people, 18 in the session behind its best-known claims, and other researchers have posted a critique of its methods. Whether training prevents automation bias: one review says it doesn’t (Parasuraman and Manzey, 2010); another lists training among the things that reduce it (Goddard et al.).

    So the honest summary: there are good reasons to think the order matters, though nobody has tested it on design work; the effect on your own expertise is unproven; and the effect on what you learn has been measured, in two trials. Try it on yourself.

    1 Question 1: think first

    Spend three minutes on this alone, without the assistant. Write a position and your two strongest reasons. A rough answer is fine; a blank one isn’t.

    Westmere question 1. The student help chatbot and the staff policy assistant will both answer from the Policy Library: 412 documents, 38 of them for staff only. Should the two assistants share one search index, or have one each?

    Now ask. The prompt is neutral on purpose: it doesn’t hint at your answer. Everything here is invented; don’t use real work data unless your organisation has approved it.

    I'm an architect at a university. Two planned assistants, a student help chatbot and a staff policy assistant, will both answer from the same Policy Library of 412 documents, 38 of which are for staff only. Should they share one search index or have one each? Give a recommendation and your reasons in under 200 words.

    2 Question 2: ask first

    This time, ask before you think.

    Westmere question 2. The ICT service desk assistant could reset a student’s password itself, or draft the steps for a service desk analyst to carry out. Which should it do?

    I'm an architect at a university. A planned service desk assistant could either reset a student's password itself, or draft the steps for a service desk analyst to carry out. Which should it do? Give a recommendation and your reasons in under 200 words.

    Read its answer once, then close or scroll away from it, and write your own view.

    3 Compare

    Imagine you’re at the review board with the chat closed. Which of your two answers could you defend under questioning? Which one has reasons you could rebuild from scratch?

    In a group session, pool two numbers with a show of hands: on question 1, how many people changed their position after reading the answer; on question 2, how many ended up where the assistant started. Then ask the people who changed on question 1 why. A new consideration is a good reason to change. “It sounded right” isn’t.

    What this can’t show: it’s one person, two different questions and no control group, so it gives you the feel of anchoring, not a measurement. Question 2 may simply have been easier. Your assistant’s answers will differ from your neighbour’s.

    Think deeper: Your comparison is confounded: different questions, a fixed order, and you knew what was being tested. Design a fairer test you could run on your own team’s design reviews, one that would show whether “position first” improves the decisions, not just how people feel about them. What would you measure, who would judge, and how long would it take to know?

    Should your decision process make people commit before they see the assistant’s answer?

    The pattern

    Independent estimates before discussion. You already use it as planning poker and Wideband Delphi, where everyone commits a number before anyone speaks, as sealed bids, and in audit, where the preparer and the reviewer form their views separately. Buçinca et al. (2021) tested the same idea with AI advice and called it a cognitive forcing function: in their “update” design, people decided first, then saw the AI’s answer and could revise. Forcing designs “significantly reduced overreliance” compared with simply showing explanations, but didn’t remove it.

    What is really being decided

    Whether to build “position first” into the process, or leave it to habit. In a process it might be an ADR field for the author’s initial preference, completed before any AI drafting, or a review board rule that the presenter states a recommendation before showing an AI-assisted analysis. As habit, it costs nothing to introduce and nothing to ignore.

    The forces

    • Independence against speed: a written first position costs minutes. Buçinca et al. also found that people “assigned the least favorable subjective ratings to the designs that reduced the overreliance the most”. What works best is what people like least, which matters for adoption.
    • Real against performed: a field in a template can be filled in after the fact. Unless something records the order, you’re trusting people to have done it.
    • Information against recommendation: Goddard et al. (2012) list “the provision of information versus recommendation” among the things that reduced automation bias. An assistant that sets out options and evidence leaves more of the choice with the person than one that recommends.
    • Accountability: the same review lists user accountability as a mitigator. A named decider who must explain the reasons in their own words carries the same effect, with no new tooling.
    • How far the evidence travels: the forcing studies used crowdworkers, simulated AI and short tasks. Nobody has tested them on architecture decisions.

    Left open

    • Would you require an author’s first position before AI drafting for work that informs funding or governance, and only for that?
    • If the assistants you deploy should inform rather than recommend, who decides which is which for each one?
    • How would you know the first position was really written first?
    Automation bias and anchoring: what has been measured

    Before generative AI. Parasuraman and Manzey’s review (2010) describes automation bias as producing both omission and commission errors when decision aids are imperfect. It found the bias in novices and experts alike, in individuals and teams, and reported that training and instructions didn’t prevent it. Goddard, Roudsari and Wyatt’s systematic review (2012, 74 studies, mostly healthcare and aviation) put numbers on it. In prospective studies, decisions that were right before the advice and wrong after it “ranged from 6% to 11% of cases”. Pooling four healthcare studies, when the decision support was wrong it “increased the risk of an incorrect decision being made by 26%”. Workload, time pressure, task complexity and trust made it worse; training, accountability and giving information rather than recommendations made it better. The same review notes that most decision support systems improved performance overall. The bias is the cost of a tool that usually helps.

    With language models. The studies are newer and smaller, and the tasks are short:

    • Si et al. (NAACL 2024, 80 crowdworkers checking claims): an assistant’s explanations made people faster than search with similar accuracy, but people over-relied on it when its explanation was wrong. Showing the case for and against reduced that, without beating search.
    • Steyvers et al. (Nature Machine Intelligence, 2025): people overestimated answers’ accuracy given the default explanations, and “longer explanations increased user confidence, even when the extra length did not improve answer accuracy”.
    • Kim et al. (FAccT 2024, 404 people, preregistered): when the system said “I’m not sure, but…”, people agreed with it less and were more accurate, with over-reliance “reduced (but not fully eliminated)”.
    • Jakesch et al. (CHI 2023, 1,506 writers): an assistant built to favour one side of an issue shifted the opinions people wrote, and their answers on a later survey.

    The two reviews disagree on training. Parasuraman and Manzey found it didn’t prevent the bias; Goddard et al. list it among the mitigators. Both can be true: training may reduce the effect without removing it, which is why the rest of this Part looks at process and design as well as habits.

    Read more

    • Automation bias: a systematic review (Goddard, Roudsari and Wyatt, JAMIA, 2012)
    • Complacency and bias in human use of automation (Parasuraman and Manzey, Human Factors, 2010)
    • To Trust or to Think: cognitive forcing functions (Buçinca, Malaya and Gajos, 2021)
    • LLMs help humans verify truthfulness, except when they are convincingly wrong (Si et al., 2024)
    • What large language models know and what people think they know (Steyvers et al., 2025)
    • “I’m Not Sure, But…”: uncertainty expression and reliance (Kim et al., 2024)
    • Co-writing with opinionated language models affects users’ views (Jakesch et al., 2023)

    What to hand over

    Sort twelve architecture tasks by how much of your thinking they need. The traps are tasks that feel like drafting but are really deciding.

    Step14.2

    Part 14
    Keep the thinking yours
    Time
    12 min
    Last reviewed
    12 November 2026

    Three minutes of silent sorting, then go straight to the items that split the room. “Considered Options” and the vendor scores usually do. Let people argue for “It drafts, you decide” before you open the key: the disagreement is about where a draft stops and a decision starts, which is the point of the step.

    In step 3.10 you placed uses of AI by how bad a wrong answer would be and how easily it could be checked. Step 12.1 tiers work by what it will inform. This step asks a third question, about the same work: whose thinking does the result carry?

    Some tasks you can hand over and check. Some the assistant can draft while you make the calls. And some contain the decision itself, so its draft would be the decision unless you’ve formed your own view first.

    Sort these

    Place all twelve before you open our sorting. Assume the work is for Westmere, and that you’re the architect responsible for it.

    Saved in this browser and included in your exported notes.

    Our sorting – open it after you have placed all twelve
    TaskOursWhy
    Move an approved ADR into the new templateHand over, then checkThe decisions are already made. Check that nothing changed in meaning.
    Your own workshop notes into actions and ownersHand over, then checkYou were there, so you’ll spot a wrong owner straight away.
    A described design into diagram codeHand over, then checkYou made the design; it only translates. Step 18.2 shows what to check.
    Find Policy Library documents on retentionHand over, then checkA search, not a judgement. Check against the library, as Part 4 showed (step 4.5).
    Decline a vendor’s meeting requestIt drafts, you decideLow stakes. You decide the tone and whether to leave a door open.
    First-draft test questionsIt drafts, you decideA good use: it widens the set. You decide which questions count and what the right answers are.
    Summarise a white paper for yourselfIt drafts, you decideFor your own reading. It becomes a trap the moment the summary goes to a board instead of the paper (step 12.1).
    Trap: “Considered Options”Think first, then askChoosing which options appear, and how fairly each is put, frames the decision. Part 7’s planted ADR hid a straw man here (step 7.4). Ask the assistant for options you missed after you’ve listed yours.
    Trap: score vendor responsesThink first, then askThe scores are the decision, and a number looks more certain than the judgement behind it. Score first, then ask it to challenge your scores.
    Trap: top three concerns from interviewsThink first, then askPicking three from twelve is the judgement. Ask it what you missed, not what matters.
    Trap: the board’s feedback on a designThink first, then askFeedback is the board’s view. A fluent draft becomes the view unless the board has one first.
    Trap: learn a protocol before a reviewThink first, then askUse it, but ask questions about how the protocol works rather than for a verdict on the design. That’s the pattern that kept learning intact in Shen and Tamkin’s study (see Going deeper).

    The rule under the traps: if choosing what goes in is the decision, the draft is the decision. That’s true of options, scores, priorities and feedback, and it’s why they feel like drafting: they are written documents. The question to ask is whether a different, equally fluent draft would lead the reader somewhere else.

    Think deeper: If the assistant writes every first draft, a junior architect spends their first two years reviewing instead of composing. Yet in Shen and Tamkin’s study, some people used the assistant heavily and still learned. They asked it to explain, or asked only conceptual questions. Design a junior architect’s first year around that finding. What would you stop them handing over, for how long, and how would you tell when they were ready?

    Where must judgement stay with people, and how will the next architects learn it?

    The pattern

    Two patterns you already run. Decision rights: a delegation-of-authority schedule or RACI says which decisions belong to whom, and a task can be delegated without the accountability. Graduated responsibility: apprentices, registrars and junior engineers take on more as they show judgement, and code review doubles as teaching. AI drafting puts pressure on both. It does the work juniors used to learn from, and it makes the line between drafting and deciding easy to cross without noticing.

    What is really being decided

    Two things. Which decisions are reserved to people, written down rather than assumed. And how juniors get enough practice composing, not only reviewing, to become the people who can check the assistant later.

    The forces

    • Throughput against the pipeline: in Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond’s study of 5,172 support agents (2025), less experienced and lower-skilled agents gained most from AI help. They are also the people whose practice it replaces. The same study reports evidence that the assistance helped agents learn, so help and learning aren’t always opposed.
    • Review needs the skill it replaces: in Lee et al.’s survey (CHI 2025), 58 of 319 knowledge workers reported barriers to inspecting AI output, such as not knowing enough about the topic. In Shen and Tamkin’s trial, the biggest gap was in debugging, the skill you need to supervise the tool.
    • Practice costs time: a junior composing an ADR alone is slower, and the cost shows up this quarter while the benefit shows up in three years.
    • The evidence fits juniors best: the causal studies are about learning something new, which is exactly a junior’s situation. They say much less about experienced architects.

    Left open

    • Which decisions would you put on a published “reserved to people” list, and who maintains it?
    • Should juniors compose some work without AI, and how would you choose which?
    • Who on your team could review a design in an area where the assistant has drafted everything for two years?
    What the skill studies show, and what they don’t

    Learning a new library (Shen and Tamkin, 2026). A randomised trial by Anthropic researchers, published as a preprint. 52 developers with more than a year of Python, recruited through a crowdwork platform, learned an unfamiliar asynchronous library (Trio) in about an hour, half with a GPT-4o-based chat assistant. The AI group averaged 50% on the quiz against 67% for the group that coded by hand, a gap of 4.15 quiz points (Cohen’s d = 0.738, p = 0.010), with the largest gap in debugging, and wasn’t significantly faster on average. The authors identify six ways people used the assistant. Three kept learning intact: asking it to explain the code it wrote, asking for explanations along with code, or asking only conceptual questions. The authors list the limits: one task, one hour, one quiz, and some analyses not pre-registered.

    Learning school maths (Bastani et al., PNAS, 2025). Nearly 1,000 high school students. With GPT-4 access, practice grades rose (48% with a plain chat interface, 127% with a tutor version built to protect learning). When access was taken away, the plain-chat group did 17% worse than students who never had it, and the safeguards in the tutor version “largely mitigated” the harm. These are teenagers, not professionals. The finding is about design: the same model, set up differently, gave different learning.

    Critical thinking (Lee et al., CHI 2025). A survey of 319 knowledge workers about 936 tasks. Higher confidence in AI was associated with less critical thinking; higher self-confidence with more. Effort moved to verifying, integrating and stewarding. It’s self-report and cross-sectional, so it can’t show cause, and the authors note that people sometimes confused less effort using AI with less critical thinking. Gerlich (2025, 666 people) found a similar correlation, with the same limits.

    Two studies people cite, and their limits. “Your brain on ChatGPT” (Kosmyna et al., 2025) recorded EEG while 54 people wrote essays. It is a preprint; its claims about switching tools rest on 18 people; and a comment by other researchers (also a preprint) raises sample size, reproducibility and EEG methods. The colonoscopy study (Budzyń et al., Lancet Gastroenterology and Hepatology, 2025) found endoscopists’ adenoma detection rate without AI fell from 28.4% to 22.4% after AI was introduced. It is observational, over three months either side, and the AI was a polyp detector, not a language model. It’s the closest evidence we found to experts losing a skill they had, and it’s thin.

    Read more

    • How AI Impacts Skill Formation (Shen and Tamkin, preprint, 2026)
    • Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning (Bastani et al., PNAS, 2025)
    • The Impact of Generative AI on Critical Thinking (Lee et al., CHI 2025)
    • Generative AI at Work (Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond, QJE, 2025)
