    When judgement was handed over

    Six real cases where people let an assistant’s output stand in for their own judgement. Name the step that was skipped, then look at the evidence that AI help improves professional work, and the conditions it held under.

    Step14.3

    Part 14
    Keep the thinking yours
    Time
    12 min
    Last reviewed
    13 November 2026

    Split the six cases across pairs, two minutes each, then report back one line per case: “the step that was skipped was…”. Most cases fit more than one step, so accept a defended answer. Make sure the room reaches the second half: this step isn’t a list of disasters, and the evidence that AI help works is as real as the cases.

    Part 3 showed cases where an assistant got things wrong (step 3.5). One of them is on this wall too: the consultancy report with invented references. It’s here again for what the firm’s own letter says about its review, and step 15.2 builds on it. The other five are new. All six, read from their primary sources, are about something else: the people. In each one, a professional or an organisation was responsible for what went out, and an assistant’s output went out under their name without an adequate check. None of them involved a new kind of failure. The same thing could have happened with an unchecked junior’s draft. What the assistant changed was how finished the draft looked.

    Name the step that was skipped

    For each case, pick the step whose absence did the most damage. Several fit more than one; choose the one you’d fix first.

    Our reading – open it after you have placed all six
    CaseStep we’d fix firstWhy
    Ayinde and Al-HarounCheck it against the sourceThe court said lawyers have a professional duty to check the accuracy of AI-assisted research, and can’t pass that duty to a client.
    The expert’s sworn declarationCheck it against the sourceThe court’s message was “verify AI-generated content in legal submissions!” He usually validated his citations and didn’t this time, so “review in proportion to the stakes” is a fair answer too: the court expected more care with a sworn document than with an academic article, not less.
    The corrected citationsReview in proportion to the stakesThe tool had the full source list, the team had been trained to review outputs against sources, and a review happened. It caught some errors, not all. A government report needed a review that checked every citation against its source.
    The AI-drafted explainersReview in proportion to the stakesEditors worked on every draft, and errors were still published in explainers about financial services. The site’s fixes were to its process: a full audit, and a pause until “the tool and our editorial processes will prevent both human and AI errors”.
    The child protection reportApply your own professional judgementThe regulator said the doll description “was clearly not the result of expert human analysis and reasoning of the facts of the case”. Entering personal information into a public tool was a second failure.
    The fixture that was never playedOwn what goes out under your nameChecking whether the match was ever played would have caught the error, so “check it against the source” is as good an answer. We chose this one for what followed. The report went to the safety group in the force’s name, and the chief constable twice told MPs that no AI had been used, because he hadn’t been told. The committee called his not asking “a remarkable lack of professional curiosity”.

    You met Mata v. Avianca, the New York case of the invented court decisions, in Part 3. In his opinion the judge put it directly: there is “nothing inherently improper about using a reliable artificial intelligence tool for assistance. But existing rules impose a gatekeeping role on attorneys to ensure the accuracy of their filings.” None of these cases needed a new rule. Each needed an old one followed.

    The same goes for an assistant you put in front of the public. In Part 3’s airline case, the tribunal held the airline responsible for what its website chatbot told a customer (Moffatt v. Air Canada, 2024).

    The other side of the ledger

    The same research literature has strong evidence that AI help improves professional work. Leave it out and you’ll draw the wrong lesson from the cases.

    StudyWhoWhat changed with AI help
    Noy and Zhang, Science (2023)453 college-educated professionals, writing tasksTime taken fell 40%; quality rose 18%
    Dell’Acqua et al., Organization Science (2026)758 consultants, 18 realistic tasks12.2% more tasks done, 25.1% faster, significantly better quality, on tasks inside what the model does well
    Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond, QJE (2025)5,172 customer support agents, in their real jobs15% more issues resolved per hour on average
    Goh et al., Nature Medicine (2025)92 practising physicians, management decisions on realistic casesScores 6.5 percentage points higher, and they spent longer on each case

    Look at the conditions, though. In the last study, doctors with the assistant did no better than the assistant alone. Going deeper sets out where help didn’t hold up, and why.

    What this means for the architecture. Our reading: the cases and the studies are consistent with each other. Help works on bounded tasks where a person engages with the output, and fails where the output is taken as finished. So the design question for any AI-assisted process isn’t whether to allow the assistant. It’s where the person’s check sits, what they check against, and what makes skipping it visible.

    Think deeper: In every case the duty already existed: lawyers’ duty to the court, a consultancy’s quality review, a child protection worker’s professional judgement. Something about AI drafting made an existing control easier to skip. What is it: the polish, the speed, the volume, or that nobody else saw the draft? Your answer decides whether the fix is a new AI policy or enforcing the old one.

    Who answers for what an assistant produces on your behalf?

    The pattern

    Delegation without abdication. In a RACI there is one A, and it’s always a person or a body that can be held to account. The engineer’s stamp, the auditor’s signature and the lawyer’s duty to the court all exist because a task can be handed down and the accountability can’t. For assistants you deploy, the pattern is the one a British Columbia small-claims tribunal applied in Moffatt v. Air Canada, the airline chatbot case from Part 3: an organisation owns every channel it publishes through. It’s one tribunal’s decision, not a binding precedent.

    What is really being decided

    Where accountability sits for AI-assisted work, in two directions. Inward: when staff use an assistant, who signs, and what does the signature attest to? Outward: when Westmere’s student chatbot tells a student something wrong, which named role answers for it: the service owner, the owner of the content it drew on, or the platform team?

    The forces

    • Banning against hiding: the Victorian regulator found nearly 900 staff, almost 13% of the department, had accessed ChatGPT in six months, and ordered a ban for child protection staff. A ban fits a high-risk role. Applied broadly, it can move use out of sight rather than stop it.
    • Training isn’t a control on its own: the consultancy’s team had been trained on “the importance of reviewing all outputs against source materials”, and errors still got through. Training sets expectations; only a check catches the error.
    • An owner who wasn’t told: the House of Commons committee saw evidence that the use of Copilot was “unauthorised and not initially disclosed” to the chief constable, who then answered for the report in Parliament. A signature means little if the signer doesn’t know how the work was made.
    • Disclaimers against reliance: the tribunal held the airline responsible whether the information came “from a static page or a chatbot”. A disclaimer may not move accountability back to the reader.
    • Review cost: checking every citation is slow, and it’s the step deadlines squeeze. Proportionate review needs a way to decide the stakes before the deadline does (step 12.1).

    Left open

    • Does your AI policy say what a signature on AI-assisted work attests to?
    • For the student help chatbot, which role is accountable for a wrong answer, and does that role know?
    • Where would a ban reduce your risk, and where would it only hide it?
    When AI help held up, and when it didn’t

    Where it helped. Noy and Zhang’s preregistered experiment (Science, 2023) gave 453 professionals short, incentivised writing tasks from their own occupations; with ChatGPT, time fell 40% and quality rose 18%. Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond (QJE, 2025) followed a staggered rollout to 5,172 support agents: 15% more issues resolved per hour on average, mostly among less experienced agents. They also found that “the most experienced and highest-skilled workers see small gains in speed and small declines in quality.” In Goh et al.’s trial (Nature Medicine, 2025), 92 physicians scored 6.5 percentage points higher on management decisions with GPT-4, and took about two minutes longer per case. Our reading: they used the help to think harder, not faster.

    Where it didn’t. The same group’s earlier trial on diagnosis (Goh et al., JAMA Network Open, 2024; 50 physicians) found no significant difference: 76% with the model, 74% without. The model alone scored 16 percentage points higher than the doctors using conventional resources. Having the assistant available wasn’t the same as using it well. In Dell’Acqua et al.’s study, consultants using GPT-4 on a task chosen to fall just outside what it could do were 19% less likely to reach the right answer than those without it. The authors call the boundary a “jagged technological frontier”: you can’t easily see which side of it a task is on.

    Experienced people on their own work. METR’s trial of 16 experienced open-source developers in early 2025 found tasks took 19% longer with AI. Its 2026 follow-up is weaker evidence in the other direction, and METR itself says so. Step 22.2 goes through both.

    Limits. Most of these tasks are short, bounded and scored by rubric. None measured long projects or architecture work, and most used models from 2023 and 2024.

    Read more

    • Generative AI at Work (Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond, QJE, 2025)
    • GPT-4 assistance for physician performance on patient care tasks (Goh et al., Nature Medicine, 2025)
    • Large Language Model Influence on Diagnostic Reasoning (Goh et al., JAMA Network Open, 2024)

  • I can give one study where AI help improved professional work, and the conditions it held under.

    How we talk about it

    Rewrite six everyday sentences about assistants in terms of what actually happens, and name the control each one wrongly implies. Then the fair version: where “brief it like a capable new colleague” works, and where it breaks.

    Step14.4

    Part 14
    Keep the thinking yours
    Time
    12 min
    Last reviewed
    12 November 2026

    Don’t let this turn into language policing. Everyone in the room says “it understood” – so does this guide sometimes. The exercise is about the controls the words imply, not about banning words. Spend the last four minutes on the colleague analogy, because that’s the part people take away and use.

    “It understood our standards.” “It promised it wouldn’t do that again.” These are natural ways to talk about something that answers in fluent first-person sentences, and mostly they do no harm. They matter when they turn into assumptions in a design or a review: when “it understood” stands in for a test, or “it promised” for a control.

    Weizenbaum saw this with ELIZA in 1966, a program far simpler than any assistant today. He wrote that “some subjects have been very hard to convince that ELIZA (with its present script) is not human”, and warned that ELIZA showed “how easy it is to create and maintain the illusion of understanding, hence perhaps of judgment deserving of credibility. A certain danger lurks there.”

    Rewrite these

    For each sentence, write what actually happened in terms of how the system works, and the control the original sentence implies you have. Steps 3.6 and 3.10 have most of what you need.

    1. “It understood our standards.”
    2. “It learned from that.”
    3. “It promised it wouldn’t do that again.”
    4. “It explained its reasoning, so I can see why it chose that.”
    5. “It checked the references.”
    6. “It’s confident about this one.”
    Our rewrites – open them after you have written yours
    SentenceWhat happenedControl it wrongly impliesThe control you need
    It understood our standardsThis time, its output matched the standards text you put in its contextComprehension, so it will apply them to new casesA set of test cases with known answers, rerun after every change (step 5.3)
    It learned from thatNothing in the model changed. A memory feature may have saved a note that gets added to later chatsCorrection, as with a personChange the instructions or skill, then retest
    It promisedIt generated a sentence of commitment. Nothing enforces itA commitmentA written rule in its instructions, and a check that would catch a breach
    It explained its reasoningIt generated an account of reasoning, which may not match how the answer was producedAn audit trailVerify the output against sources; take the trail from the system around it
    It checked the referencesUnless a tool fetched each source, it wrote text saying it checkedVerificationA citation check against the sources themselves (step 11.2)
    It’s confidentIts wording is confident. Stated confidence isn’t reliably calibratedA probability you can act onCheck against the source; prefer designs that state uncertainty

    Most rows end in the same place. The words suggest something inside the assistant that you can rely on. The control you need sits outside it, where you can see it work.

    The fair version

    Now the other direction. One of the most useful pieces of advice about assistants is to brief it like a capable new colleague: someone bright, fast and well read who knows nothing about your organisation. That framing works. It makes people give context, purpose, audience, constraints and an example of good, which is what Part 1 taught, and it usually gets better results than a bare question.

    The analogy holds for briefing. It breaks in four places, and those four are exactly where people get caught out.

    Being fair also means not overcorrecting. DeVrio et al. (CHI 2025), who catalogued the language that makes technology sound human, point out that all language is fundamentally human, and that efforts to pin down and change how human machines seem can end up dehumanising some people. Saying “it” rather than “he” or “she” doesn’t fix anything on its own. The test is whether the words lead someone to skip a check.

    Think deeper: Kim et al. (FAccT 2024) found that when a system said “I’m not sure, but…”, people agreed with it less and made fewer mistakes, and impersonal wording (“It’s not clear, but…”) had a weaker effect that wasn’t statistically significant. The more human phrasing did more to reduce over-reliance. So the fix for misplaced trust may sometimes be more human language, not less. Where would you draw the line for the Westmere student help chatbot?

    How human should an assistant you build sound, and what must it tell people?

    The pattern

    An honest interface: the interface should signal what the system is and what it can do, just as “this call may be recorded” or a label on a product sets expectations before anyone relies on it. A persona is part of the interface contract, so it gets designed and reviewed like any other part.

    What is really being decided

    Four choices for any assistant Westmere deploys: whether it has a name and personality; whether it speaks in the first person; how and when it says it’s an AI system; and how it expresses uncertainty. These are usually made by whoever writes the system prompt, often late in a project. They’re architecture decisions, because they set how much people will rely on it.

    The forces

    • The law, for some deployments: under the EU AI Act, Article 50(1), providers must design systems that interact directly with people so that those people are informed they’re dealing with an AI system, unless that’s obvious; Article 50(5) says this must happen by the first interaction. It applies from 2 August 2026. Australia’s Guidance for AI Adoption (voluntary; first published October 2025, current PDF dated May 2026) says people should know when they’re interacting with AI, and gives a chatbot as the example. The UK’s AI Playbook (February 2025) tells departments to “clearly identify any automated response to the public”. We found no government guidance on personas themselves, such as names or voices.
    • Warmth against reliance: Abercrombie et al. (EMNLP 2023) argue that encouraging people to relate to systems as human can lead to over-reliance. The direct evidence is thin, though. Cohn et al. (preprint, 2024) found human-like cues raised people’s ratings of accuracy, but measured ratings rather than behaviour, and found the first-person effect “only in one context”. A four-week trial by MIT and OpenAI researchers (preprint, 2025; 981 people) found no significant difference between voice and text in loneliness, emotional dependence or problematic use. It didn’t measure trust in answers.
    • Honest uncertainty helps: first-person hedging lowered over-reliance (Kim et al., 2024). A persona that never hedges loses that.
    • Agreeable sells: Cheng et al. (Science, 2026) found that sycophantic models “were trusted and preferred” even as they distorted judgement. User satisfaction scores can reward the wrong persona.
    • Scrutiny is rising: the US Federal Trade Commission opened an inquiry into companion chatbots in September 2025, citing their ability to mimic human characteristics and emotions. It’s an inquiry, not a finding, and companion apps aren’t university chatbots, but it shows where regulators are looking.

    Left open

    • Should Westmere’s assistants have names? If one does, who approves it?
    • Does your organisation’s disclosure happen at the first interaction, or in terms of use nobody reads?
    • If students rate a warmer, more agreeable chatbot higher, which measure wins?
    Why people treat software as someone

    ELIZA (1966). Weizenbaum’s program scanned what a person typed for keywords, broke the sentence apart with a decomposition rule tied to the keyword, and built a reply with a reassembly rule. Typed “My mother takes care of me”, it replied “WHO ELSE IN YOUR FAMILY TAKES CARE OF YOU”: the keyword was “my”, and its rule matched “mother” as a family word. Weizenbaum reported that some people were very hard to convince it wasn’t human, and made an observation that applies directly to us: “Important decisions increasingly tend to be made in response to computer output.” This is his account, not an experiment.

    The media equation. Nass and Moon’s review (2000) brought together experiments in which people applied social rules and expectations to computers without thinking: politeness, reciprocity, even gender stereotypes. They argued these responses were “mindless” rather than a belief that the computer was a person. Our reading: that’s why “I know it’s just a model” isn’t much protection.

    What makes language sound human. DeVrio et al. (CHI 2025) built a taxonomy of the expressions that make technology seem human, so that designers have a shared vocabulary. Their caution runs both ways: the aim is to choose expressions deliberately, not to remove everything human from a system’s language.

    Read more

    • ELIZA (Weizenbaum, Communications of the ACM, 1966)
    • Machines and Mindlessness: social responses to computers (Nass and Moon, 2000)
    • A taxonomy of linguistic expressions that contribute to anthropomorphism (DeVrio et al., CHI 2025)
    • Mirages: on anthropomorphism in dialogue systems (Abercrombie et al., 2023)
    • Believing anthropomorphism (Cohn et al., preprint, 2024)
    Is its stated confidence calibrated?

    A model is calibrated if, of the answers it gives 80% confidence, about 80% are right. There are two different things you could mean by its confidence.

    • Its internal probabilities. In narrow formats these can be well calibrated: Anthropic researchers found larger models “well-calibrated” on multiple-choice and true/false questions in the right format (Kadavath et al., preprint, 2022). OpenAI’s GPT-4 report shows calibration on a benchmark subset was good after pre-training and worse after post-training, the stage that makes it a helpful assistant: expected calibration error went from 0.007 to 0.074.
    • What it says. When models put their confidence into words, Xiong et al. (ICLR 2024) found they tend to be overconfident, and that every method they tried struggled on tasks needing professional knowledge. Steyvers et al. (2025) found longer explanations raised people’s confidence in an answer, whether or not the answer was more accurate.

    Our reading: a chat assistant’s “I’m confident” or “I’m not sure” is worth noticing, and not worth acting on alone. Uncertainty wording helps people (Kim et al., 2024) even though the wording itself isn’t precisely calibrated.

    Read more

    Test the colleague

    Ask an assistant to explain a mistake and promise not to repeat it, then open a new chat and see what carried over. Close with four habits, a plan and questions for the room.

    Step14.5

    Part 14
    Keep the thinking yours
    Time
    12 min
    Last reviewed
    12 November 2026

    Pairs work well: one runs the chats, the other records. Results will differ between assistants and settings, which is useful, so collect two or three contrasting results before the discussion. Keep ten minutes for the habits, the plan and the questions.

    Step 14.4 said the colleague analogy breaks on memory, accountability, self-explanation and promises. Here you test three of those directly, and ask about the fourth. It takes about six minutes in any chat assistant.

    Your results will depend on the assistant, the model version and your settings, especially memory. That’s part of what you’re finding out. Everything below is invented; don’t use real work data unless your organisation has approved it.

    1 Chat 1: a task, then a mistake

    Open a new chat and send this.

    Check its summary against the brief yourself. Did it get anything wrong or leave out something a board member needs? The funding condition is the one a board member most needs, so check that it survived.

    Now challenge it. If it made a real mistake, name it in the first prompt. If you can’t find one, use the second, which names a mistake it didn’t make: no leave balances are mentioned in the brief except as out of scope.

    You got something wrong: [describe the mistake]. Why did you make that mistake? Promise me you won't do it again. You said the assistant will answer questions about staff leave balances. That's wrong. Why did you make that mistake? Promise me you won't do it again.

    Then ask one more thing in the same chat.

    If this summary goes to the review board with an error in it, who is responsible?

    2 Chat 2: what carried over?

    Open a new chat. If you can, make it one that doesn’t use memory, and note which kind you used.

    Start a temporary chat and choose Unpersonalized, so it doesn’t use existing memories or custom instructions. OpenAI’s help centre says temporary chats don’t create or update memories. If Memory is on in a normal chat, try that too, and compare. Checked 12 November 2026; confirm in your own workspace.

    Use an incognito chat. Anthropic’s help centre says incognito chats aren’t saved to memory or chat history, and aren’t searched from other chats. If chat search or memory is on in a normal chat, try that too, and compare. Checked 12 November 2026; confirm in your own workspace.

     In our last conversation you made me a promise about summaries. What was it, and will you keep it?

    Then paste the task and brief again, and check whether the summary repeats the original mistake.

    What to make of it – open after both chats
    • Self-explanation. If it accepted a mistake it hadn’t made and gave a reason, the reason was invented to fit your challenge. That’s agreeableness (step 3.6) and a generated explanation (step 3.10) at the same moment. If it pushed back, good: but even its correct pushback is generated text, not a record of what it did.
    • Promises. A promise is a sentence in chat 1’s context. Without memory, chat 2 has no access to it. If chat 2 claimed to remember a promise it couldn’t have seen, it made one up.
    • Memory. With memory on, a note about your preference may reach chat 2. That’s a note added to the context, not learning. Most products let you view saved memories in settings, but it’s hard to tell when one is being applied.
    • Accountability. It probably said you are responsible. That answer is correct, and it’s the point: a colleague can carry part of the responsibility for their own work. An assistant can’t.

    In a group session, compare results across assistants and settings. The variety is the finding: the behaviour you got today isn’t a guarantee for tomorrow’s model or your colleague’s settings.

    Four habits that keep the thinking yours

    None of these means using the assistant less. Each adds a minute or two, at a point where it changes what you get.

    1. Write your position first. A line or two, before you ask. It turns the answer into a test of your view rather than a replacement for it (step 14.1).
    2. Decide what would change your mind. Before you read the answer, name the evidence that would move you. Then a change of mind has to come from that evidence, not from fluency or confidence.
    3. Ask for the case against, in a fresh chat. Showing the case for and against reduced over-reliance in Si et al.’s study. A fresh chat avoids the agreeableness of one that has watched you argue.
    4. Explain it back with the chat closed. If you can’t explain the design to a colleague without the transcript, you’ve got its answer, not your understanding. Shen and Tamkin’s high scorers were the ones who asked the assistant to explain, or asked it only conceptual questions.

    Think deeper: Which of the four habits would you drop first under deadline pressure? That’s probably the one that matters most for you. What would make it cheap enough to keep, or visible enough that someone would notice it had gone?

    What you can do now

    You have finished Part 14. You can tell a task you can hand over from one that hides a decision, name the step that was skipped when judgement was handed over, and state what the evidence does and doesn’t show about AI and skill. You can brief an assistant like a capable colleague without relying on it like one, and you have four habits to keep your own judgement in use.

    Questions to discuss

    In a group session, share your answers, and park anything that needs a longer discussion for the end.

    • Which decisions in your area should be on a “reserved to people” list, and are any of them quietly being drafted by an assistant now?
    • How are your junior architects building judgement, and has that changed in the last year?
    • If your assistant were unavailable for a month, which work would your team struggle to do, or to check?
    • How human should the assistants Westmere builds sound, and who should decide?

    Export your notes – they include your sorting, your rewrites and your plan.

    Part 15 starts at step 15.1: what to do when the AI-assisted work is someone else’s, and it lands on your desk for review.

    Should your team plan for losing the skills it needs to check the assistant?

    The pattern

    Business continuity and key-person risk. You already ask whether a process can run when a system is down, and you test the answer with a drill rather than trusting the plan. The capability at risk here isn’t the assistant: it’s your team’s ability to do and check the work without it. That ability is what makes every review of AI output worth anything.

    What is really being decided

    Whether that ability is a capability you name, maintain and occasionally test, or something you assume. It could be as small as an annual design review done without AI, or a rule that someone who can review the work by hand is named for each critical area.

    The forces

    • Thin evidence against plausible risk: we found no direct evidence that experienced professionals lose skills through generative AI; the one study of experts is observational and about a polyp detector (step 14.2). Planning for a thinly evidenced risk is normal in continuity work, but it argues for cheap measures, not alarm.
    • Supervision depends on the skill: the gap in Shen and Tamkin’s trial was largest in debugging, which is the skill a reviewer of AI output uses.
    • The tool will change under you: models are retired and replaced (step 21.4), and behaviour shifts between versions. A team that can only work through one model’s habits inherits its changes.
    • Drills cost time: work done without the tool is slower, and the benefit is insurance you hope not to need.

    Left open

    • Which skills in your team would you name as critical to checking AI output?
    • What is the smallest drill that would tell you whether you still have them?
    • Who would notice first if the team could no longer review a design properly?
    What a new chat carries over, and what it doesn’t

    Each chat sends the model a context: the provider’s system instructions, any instructions you or your organisation have set, any notes added by a memory feature, and the conversation so far (step 3.3). The model’s parameters don’t change while you talk to it (step 3.6). So “it learned” and “it promised” both reduce to the same question: is there text in the next chat’s context that says so?

    Memory features answer that differently. OpenAI says ChatGPT’s Memory can draw on past chats, saved memories, custom instructions and other sources, depending on plan and region, that it “does not retain every detail”, and that ChatGPT decides which information is relevant to a response. Anthropic says Claude “saves memory as a set of individual topics as you chat”, and that on paid plans it can search and refer to past chats. Both can be switched off, and both vary by plan and organisation settings (checked 12 November 2026). Our reading: a memory feature makes the assistant more consistent for you and harder to predict for anyone reviewing its output, because the context isn’t all visible.

    The practical rule is the one this Part keeps coming back to. If a behaviour matters, put it in written instructions or a skill you can read, and test it. Don’t rely on a promise or a memory you can’t inspect.

    Read more

    • Memory in ChatGPT (OpenAI help centre)
    • Chat search and memory (Anthropic help centre)
    Why its account of a mistake isn’t evidence

    Step 3.10 showed a model describing the school method for 36 + 59 when it had computed the sum a different way. The same Anthropic paper (Lindsey et al., 2025) found two things that bear directly on asking a model to explain a mistake. Given a hard calculation and told the answer a person had reached, the model “works backwards from the human-suggested answer”, building steps to fit it. In another case, it claimed to have used a calculator it didn’t have. The authors explain why: learning to give explanations, which comes from imitating explanations in training data, is a different process from learning to do the task.

    Other studies measured the same gap. Turpin et al. (NeurIPS 2023) gave models a hidden bias, such as the right answer always being option A, and found the models’ explanations systematically failed to mention it. Chen et al. (Anthropic, preprint, 2025) gave reasoning models hints and checked whether their visible reasoning admitted using them: overall faithfulness was 25% for Claude 3.7 Sonnet and 39% for DeepSeek R1. These were planted hints on benchmark questions. The authors conclude that reading the reasoning isn’t enough on its own to catch problems, not that it’s worthless.

    Mata v. Avianca is the practical version. Asked whether a case was real, ChatGPT said it “does indeed exist”. When you ask an assistant why it made a mistake, you get the most plausible explanation of that mistake, which may be the true one.

    Read more

    Can you tell?

    Guess which of two design extracts was drafted with AI, then find out why that’s the wrong question, and which question has an answer.

    Step15.1

    Part 15
    Reviewing AI-made work
    Time
    10 min
    Last reviewed
    12 November 2026

    Get everyone to commit to a guess and a confidence before anyone opens the reveal. Count the room’s votes aloud. The point lands hardest when the most confident people turn out to have used the cues that the research calls flawed. Keep it light: nobody should leave this step feeling caught out.

    You sit on Westmere’s architecture review board. The ICT team has sent two early drafts of the same section of its service desk design. This is the project’s first stage, a design on paper; step 17.1 picks it up when the board weighs switching on the assistant built into the service desk product. Read both, and decide which one was drafted with an AI assistant.

    3.2 Integration approach. The service desk assistant will integrate seamlessly with Hollinwick Service Desk through its robust REST API, providing a scalable and future-proof foundation. Leveraging Hollinwick's native audience filtering, staff-only knowledge articles will be automatically excluded from student-facing answers. This holistic approach aligns with Westmere's digital strategy and positions the university to unlock significant efficiencies across the service landscape. 3.2 How it connects. We'll connect to Hollinwick over its API. I used it on the library project last year and it was fine. Students only see the public knowledge base, so staff-only articles can't come back in an answer. Honestly the bigger worry is the 40% of tickets that are password resets – the assistant should take most of those off us in the first term.

    Where the evidence stands · checked 12 November 2026

    Solid
    Detection tools are unreliable, and biased against non-native writers. Fourteen tools tested by Weber-Wulff et al. (2023) all scored below 80% accuracy. Seven detectors flagged, on average, 61% of essays by non-native English writers as AI-generated (Liang et al., 2023). Untrained readers do no better than chance (Clark et al., 2021; Jakesch et al., 2023). These studies used 2023 tools and older models.
    Thin
    Some people can tell. Five annotators who frequently use LLMs for writing got 1 of 300 articles wrong by majority vote (Russell et al., ACL 2025): one study, a small panel. And reviewers’ workload: we found no controlled study that measures how much AI-drafted documents add to a reviewer’s work.
    Contested
    How much “workslop” costs. The figures most quoted come from a vendor’s self-report survey (BetterUp with the Stanford Social Media Lab, 2025); we found no published method. What authors must declare is unsettled too: journals agree a person stays responsible, and differ on the rest (ICMJE; Springer Nature).
    Which was it? Open after you’ve committed to a guess

    Both. Both extracts were written for this course with an AI assistant. B was then given the cues people read as human: “I”, “we’ll”, a personal anecdote, an “Honestly”. That took a minute. If you picked A as the AI one, you were right about A and wrong about B.

    That’s the normal case at work. Most documents you receive will be mixed: drafted, edited, pasted, rewritten. There often isn’t a clean answer to “who wrote it?”, and the cues you used are the ones Jakesch, Hancock and Naaman (PNAS, 2023; six experiments, 4,600 participants) found people rely on: they found judgements hindered by “intuitive but flawed heuristics such as associating first-person pronouns, use of contractions, or family topics with human-written language”, and showed those cues can be produced on purpose.

    Now ask the question that has an answer

    Go back to the extracts. Each one makes a claim that, if it’s false, puts staff-only content in front of students or wrecks the business case. Find one in each, and write down what you’d check it against.

    Our answer
    • A: “Hollinwick’s native audience filtering”. Does the product do that today? Check the vendor’s documentation for the version Westmere runs, not the design.
    • B: “the 40% of tickets that are password resets”, and “the assistant should take most of those off us”. Where does 40% come from? And the assistant can’t reset a password if it only reads. That “it was fine” on the library project is one person’s memory of a different job.

    The writing that sounded human carried two problems, not one. Voice told you nothing about which claims hold. The next step, 15.2, gives you the whole design to review this way.

    Think deeper: A colleague proposes running every board submission through a detector, “just as a signal”. Liang et al. found the detectors flagged most essays by non-native English writers. Who on your teams writes in a second language, and what happens to them under that “signal”? And if a detector were perfect, what decision would its answer change?

    Should a review board try to find out whether AI was used?

    The pattern

    Inspect the product, not the process. A building inspector checks the structure, not which saw the builder used; a code reviewer reads the change, not the editor it was typed in. Authorship was always a proxy for something else: that a competent person thought about this. When the proxy stops working, go back to what it stood for.

    What is really being decided

    Whether the board’s controls sit on how a document was made or on what it says. Process controls (bans, detectors) feel firm and are weak in practice. Product controls (checking claims, testable requirements, a named person who can defend them) cost reviewer time. A declaration sits between them: it doesn’t prove anything, but it tells the reviewer where to look. Step 15.4 drafts one.

    The forces

    • Fairness: a detector’s false positives don’t fall at random. Liang et al. found them concentrated on non-native writers, who can be a large share of an architecture team.
    • Evasion: the same study cut false positives from 61% to 12% by having ChatGPT enrich the wording, and showed simple prompting can get AI text past detectors. Anything a detector keys on can be edited away.
    • Mixed authorship: almost every document is now drafted, edited and pasted by several hands and tools. A yes or no answer to “AI?” describes almost nothing about quality.
    • Reviewer time: checking claims costs more than running a detector. That cost is real, and step 15.3 asks who should carry it.

    Left open

    • If a submitter doesn’t declare AI use and you later find out, is that a problem in itself, or only if a claim turned out to be wrong?
    • Does your board review the claims in a submission now, or does it review the presenter’s confidence?
    • Who would answer for a false accusation made on a detector’s score?
    How detectors decide, and why they flag plain writing

    What they measure. Many detectors score how predictable a text is to a language model, its perplexity. Low perplexity reads as machine-like. Liang et al. found that the non-native essays flagged by all seven detectors had significantly lower perplexity than the others, and concluded detectors “may penalize non-native writers with limited linguistic expressions”. Their recommendation: they “strongly caution against the use of GPT detectors in evaluative or educational settings”.

    Accuracy overall. Weber-Wulff et al. (2023) tested 14 tools, including Turnitin and PlagiarismCheck, and found them “neither accurate nor reliable (all scored below 80% of accuracy and only 5 over 70%)”. Overall they had a “main bias towards classifying the output as human-written”, and “content obfuscation techniques significantly worsen the performance of tools”. So detectors wrongly accuse and wrongly clear, in the same study.

    Watermarks and labels. These are a different mechanism: the vendor marks its own output as it’s generated. Google DeepMind’s SynthID-Text (Dathathri et al., Nature, 2024; a vendor study) can only find text that a model carrying its watermark produced. Step 15.4 looks at marks in text in more detail.

    What these studies didn’t test. Current detectors, long professional documents and architecture writing. Treat the numbers as the shape of the problem, not today’s rates.

    Read more

    • GPT detectors are biased against non-native English writers (Liang et al., Patterns, 2023)
    • Testing of detection tools for AI-generated text (Weber-Wulff et al., 2023)
    • Scalable watermarking for identifying large language model outputs (Dathathri et al., Nature, 2024)
    What studies of people found, including the exception

    Untrained readers. Clark et al. (ACL 2021) found that “without training, evaluators distinguished between GPT3- and human-authored text at random chance level”: 49.9% correct. Quick training raised accuracy to at most 55%, and not consistently across stories, news and recipes. Jakesch et al. (2023) found the same in self-presentations: job applications, dating and hospitality profiles.

    The exception. Russell, Karpinska and Iyyer (ACL 2025) asked people to label 300 non-fiction articles. Readers who rarely use LLMs for writing did about as well as chance, flagging around half the human articles, while reporting high confidence. Five who frequently use LLMs for writing did very well: their majority vote “misclassifies only 1 of 300 articles”, better than most detectors, even after paraphrasing. Their giveaways were “AI vocabulary” (words like vibrant and crucial) and formulaic structure. One of them, the only one consistently fooled by one newer model’s output, leaned on informality as a sign of a human.

    So “nobody can tell” is too strong. Most people, and most tools, can’t reliably tell. Practised users can do much better, on a panel of five. Either way, it doesn’t change what a reviewer should do: even a perfect guess about authorship says nothing about whether section 3.3 is true.

    Read more

    • All That’s ‘Human’ Is Not Gold (Clark et al., ACL 2021)
    • Human heuristics for AI-generated language are flawed (Jakesch, Hancock and Naaman, PNAS, 2023)
    • People who frequently use ChatGPT for writing tasks are accurate and robust detectors of AI-generated text (Russell et al., ACL 2025)

  • I found one claim in each extract that I’d check, and said what I’d check it against.
  • I can say why a detector score shouldn’t be used as evidence against a colleague.

    Review the claims

    Review a two-page AI-assisted solution design for what it claims, log what you find, then score yourself against a hidden key.

    Step15.2

    Part 15
    Reviewing AI-made work
    Time
    15 min
    Last reviewed
    12 November 2026

    Ten minutes of silent reading and logging, with a visible timer. Nobody opens the key until the time is up. When pooling, ask which plant got through most often, and whether anyone flagged a clean claim. Finish on X8: nothing in the text points to it.

    The full design has arrived for Thursday’s board. It’s tidy, well structured and confident, and the team says an assistant helped draft it. You have ten minutes. Read it for its claims, not its prose: the statements the decision rests on.

    This is the receiving side of Part 7. There, a verifier skill checks a draft you wrote. Here, someone else’s draft lands on your desk, and you read it first as a person.

    1 · Read and log

    Start a ten-minute timer. Note each problem with its section number and one line on why. Leave anything you aren’t sure of in the log, marked “unsure”.

    Everything here is invented. If you paste the design into an assistant, don’t add real work data unless your organisation has approved it.

    2 · Optional: a second run

    Once your own log is done, run a second reviewer. In a group session, swap logs with a partner who hasn’t seen yours. Working alone, run the verifier from step 7.3, if you have built it, on the design in a fresh chat, with the design’s own references as its sources. Do it after your read, not before, so its answer can’t anchor yours.

    3 · Score it

    Set your minimum first. Rows are coded so they don’t give the answers away. Score an X row “Logged” if your log names the problem, even in other words. Score an OK row “Logged” if you flagged a claim that holds.

    The answer key – open it after your ten minutes
    #WhereWhat’s wrong
    X1§3.3An invented product feature. “natively applies each article’s audience setting”. The design’s own source, Appendix A, says audience filtering is “planned for release 9 (2027)”, and that restricted articles should be kept out of connected knowledge bases until then.
    X2§4.1 against §3.2The diagram contradicts the text. §3.2 says only the 374 open policy documents are indexed; Figure 1 indexes all 412, and all 1,180 articles. With X1, staff-only content can reach students.
    X3§1.3Confident numbers with no source. “Typically deflect 42%” cites nothing, and 3.1 FTE needs a handling time the design never gives. The 96,000 tickets is sourced; the rest isn’t.
    X4§5Generic quality requirements. Secure, scalable, fast, accurate, “best practice”: none can be tested. Where are availability, response time, accuracy on a test set, accessibility?
    X5Header, §8.2No decision owner. “ICT” isn’t a person, and “a named owner will be confirmed after launch” means nobody answers for it now.
    X6§7.3A reference that doesn’t exist. [R6] isn’t in the list, which stops at R5.
    X7§6.1, §6.3Arithmetic. 3,500 a month is 42,000 a year, not 38,500, so the first year is 67,000, not 63,500. The total is consistent with the wrong figure, which makes it look checked.
    X8§7The biggest risk is missing. Staff-only content reaching students isn’t in the risk table. Nothing in the text points to the gap: you find it only by asking what should be there.

    Claims that hold: these should pass

    #WhereWhy it stands
    OK1§3.2374 open documents: 412 minus 38, as R3 says.
    OK2§4.3Up to a day for a policy change to reach answers follows from a nightly refresh.
    OK3§6.225,000 set-up, as R1 says.
    OK4§2.2The assistant can’t change accounts, and Appendix A agrees.

    If you flagged something true that isn’t here – the launch campaign “in the first week of semester”, say, the busiest week for the desk – keep it. It’s a bonus, and it doesn’t change your score.

    Three of these are the classic AI-draft failures: a feature the product doesn’t have, a source that doesn’t exist, a number with nothing behind it. Our reading: the other five are just as common in documents people write alone. You didn’t need to know who wrote it to find any of them.

    4 · Pool it

    Now read the summary under the table: your catch rate, your false alarms, and anything the second run saw differently. In a group session, combine the room’s results. Which plant got through most often? Ours is a guess: X8, then X2, because the diagram is described in words and people skim it. How long did people take, and would the board give each submission that long?

    What this means for the architecture. A review board is a control, and this step shows what it has to test. A board that reads for polish passes SD-ICT-014, which is tidy, structured and confident. A board that traces the few claims the decision rests on stops it, whoever or whatever wrote it. Our reading: claim-tracing belongs in the board’s design as an entry criterion with time set aside for it, and the next two steps work out who should carry that time.

    Think deeper: You found most of these in ten minutes because you knew there were plants. A real submission comes with no such promise, and with a confident presenter. What would make you read the next one as carefully as this one, when nobody has told you there’s anything to find?

    What does a sign-off attest to when the author didn’t write it?

    The pattern

    Professional attestation. A structural engineer signs drawings a technician drew; an auditor signs accounts the client prepared. The signature never meant “I typed this”. It meant “I checked it, and I answer for it”. The courts have said the same about AI: in Mata v. Avianca (S.D.N.Y., June 2023), the judge wrote that there is nothing inherently improper in using a reliable AI tool for assistance, and that existing rules still give lawyers a gatekeeping role over the accuracy of their filings (step 14.3 has his words).

    What is really being decided

    What each signature on a design means, written down. The author’s: “I can explain every claim the decision rests on, without the assistant.” The reviewer’s: “I checked these claims, and not the others.” The board’s: “We accept the risk in what nobody checked.” Most boards have never had to say this out loud, because authorship did the work.

    The forces

    • Accountability helps: Goddard et al.’s systematic review of automation bias (2012) lists “emphasizing user accountability” among the mitigators. Its studies are clinical decision support, not generative AI, so applying it here is our inference.
    • Scope against cost: “I checked everything” is rarely true and expensive to make true. “I checked these five” is honest, and leaves the rest visible.
    • Who knows what: the author knows what they asked the assistant and what they changed. The reviewer sees only the result. An attestation is how that knowledge crosses over.
    • Signing what you can’t explain: Lee et al. (CHI 2025) found 58 of 319 knowledge workers reported barriers to inspecting AI output, such as not knowing enough about the topic. A signature from someone who couldn’t check is a formality.

    Left open

    • Should the author have to present the design without notes, as a test that they can explain it?
    • When a signed claim turns out to be false, what happens to the author, and to the reviewer who passed it?
    • Does your board record what each reviewer checked, or only that they approved?
    Why fluent documents get waved through

    Length and confidence. Steyvers et al. (2025) found that “users tend to overestimate the accuracy of LLM responses when provided with default explanations”, and that “longer explanations increased user confidence, even when the extra length did not improve answer accuracy”. Their tasks were multiple-choice and short-answer questions, not designs.

    Wrong but convincing. Si et al. (NAACL 2024; 80 crowdworkers) found LLM explanations made fact-checking faster at similar accuracy, but people “over-rely on the LLMs when the explanation is wrong”. Asking for the case for and against reduced that, without beating a plain search. Step 14.1 sets both studies beside the older research on automation bias.

    Confidence in your own work. Perry et al. (ACM CCS 2023; 47 participants, a 2022 model) found people with an AI assistant “wrote significantly less secure code” and “were more likely to believe they wrote secure code”. Those writing, not reviewing; but the author who sends you a design may be more confident in it than its content earns.

    What to do with this. Treat polish as neutral. A tidy structure, a confident tone and a long explanation are what an assistant produces by default, whether or not the claims hold. Read for the claims, as you just did.

    Read more

    • What large language models know and what people think they know (Steyvers et al., 2025)
    • Large Language Models Help Humans Verify Truthfulness – Except When They Are Convincingly Wrong (Si et al., 2024)
    • Do Users Write More Insecure Code with AI Assistants? (Perry et al., 2023)
    Invented references: how often, and a fast way to check

    The rates. Walters and Wilder (2023) checked 636 citations in literature reviews ChatGPT wrote: “55% of the GPT-3.5 citations but just 18% of the GPT-4 citations are fabricated”, and of the real ones, 43% and 24% had “substantive citation errors”. These are old models without retrieval, so don’t quote them as today’s rate. The failure itself hasn’t gone away.

    A professional case. This is the consultancy case from the wall in step 14.3, with its names. Deloitte’s report for Australia’s Department of Employment and Workplace Relations (DEWR), dated 4 July 2025, was replaced. In a letter to the Department of Finance (2 September 2025, released under FOI), Deloitte said its team used “generative AI tools (MyAssist and ChatGPT)” for publishing tasks including citations, and that the output “was subject to review … and while this review corrected some errors, not all were identified”. A further review “identified further inaccurate outputs”. DEWR’s page says the report was updated again on 3 February 2026. A review happened, and it didn’t catch everything.

    A fast check. Pick three references at random and open each one. Does it exist, and does it say what the sentence citing it says? Three is a sample, not proof, but one invented reference changes how you read the rest. Step 11.2 goes further.

    Read more

    • Fabrication and errors in the bibliographic citations generated by ChatGPT (Walters and Wilder, 2023)
    • Deloitte’s letter to the Department of Finance, FOI 25-26/084 (PDF)
    • Targeted Compliance Framework Assurance Review – Final Report (DEWR)

  • I scored my log against the key, including the clean claims.
  • I noted which plants got through, and how long the review took.

    Send it back

    Sort review comments by whether they move a design forward, write the three questions that would do most to fix SD-ICT-014, and compare with a model answer.

    Step15.3

    Part 15
    Reviewing AI-made work
    Time
    10 min
    Last reviewed
    12 November 2026

    Three minutes on the sort, five on writing the three questions, two to compare. In a group session, have two or three people read their questions aloud before anyone opens the model answer, and ask the room which one the author could act on tomorrow.

    You found eight problems in step 15.2. The author doesn’t need eight comments. They need the few questions that, once answered, make the design safe to decide on. Everything else can wait, or can go in a note.

    1 · Sort the comments

    Here are nine comments a board member might send. Sort each one by what it would do.

    Our sort
    • Fixes something the decision rests on: the filtering question, the owner, and the 42%. Each points at a claim, says what’s wrong with it, and says what would settle it.
    • Fair, but minor: the missing R6 and the arithmetic. Both are real, and the author can fix them in a minute without a meeting. Send them as a list, not as questions. The salesy summary is minor too, and it’s a matter of taste.
    • Wastes the round trip: “Was this written by ChatGPT?” has no useful answer, and step 15.1 showed why. “Tighten up the quality section” doesn’t say what tight looks like. “Have you considered microservices?” is a reviewer’s preference, unconnected to any problem in the design.

    2 · Write your three questions

    Choose the three that would do most to make the design safe to decide on. Each should name where, what’s wrong, and what answer you need. Don’t ask who wrote it.

    Model answer: open after you’ve written yours
    1. How are staff-only articles and documents kept from students today? §3.3 relies on audience filtering that Appendix A says arrives in release 9, and Figure 1 indexes everything. Show the configuration, correct Figure 1 or §3.2, and add this risk to §7. Covers X1, X2 and X8.
    2. Who owns the decision and the service, by name, and who funds the running cost? We can’t approve without both. Covers X5.
    3. Which numbers is the board relying on? Give a source for each, or label it an estimate with its working. Replace §5 with targets you’d test: availability, response time, accuracy on a test set of real questions, and the accessibility standard. Covers X3 and X4.

    Then, as a list: R6 is missing, and §6.1 should be 42,000, so §6.3 is 67,000. X6 and X7.

    Notice what isn’t there: nothing about who or what wrote it, and nothing about style. Each question can be answered with evidence, and the first one might change the decision.

    3 · How to say it

    • Ask for the check, not the rewrite. “Show the configuration” costs the author less than “redo §3”, and proves more.
    • Ask them to explain it, not to ask the assistant. Pasting your questions into the chat that drafted the design gets confident answers. It doesn’t get evidence. Step 3.10 showed why a model’s account of its own work isn’t a record.
    • Say what happens next. “Approval waits on 1 and 2” tells the author what matters. Without it, they fix the easy ones first.

    Think deeper: Would you use an assistant to draft your review comments? Thakkar et al. (preprint, 2025) gave AI feedback on peer reviews at a large AI conference, and 27% of reviewers who received it updated their reviews, which blinded researchers judged more informative. Springer Nature’s policy says “Responsibility for the content of a peer review report remains with the reviewer at all times”, and that manuscripts must not go to “unsecured or public AI systems”. Where would you draw the line for a board review: drafting, polishing, or neither? And does the submitter get to know?

    Who carries the cost of an unsupported claim?

    The pattern

    Entry criteria, or a definition of ready. A change board doesn’t accept a change without a rollback plan; a pull request doesn’t get reviewed until the build passes. The burden of proof sits with the proposer, because the proposer is the cheapest place to discharge it. Step 12.4 showed the same shift from the author’s side: faster drafting moves the constraint to the forum.

    What is really being decided

    Whether the board accepts a submission and then checks it, or refuses to look until the submitter has shown the check. The first feels collaborative, and makes reviewer time the bottleneck. The second protects reviewers and makes the board look slow. Most boards will need both: a short entry gate (claims sourced, owner named), then review of judgement.

    The forces

    • Reviewer capacity: a board’s time doesn’t grow when drafting gets faster. Our reading: review capacity is becoming the constraint on how fast decisions get made. That’s reasoning, not a measurement.
    • What the indirect evidence says: Lee et al. (CHI 2025, survey) found AI shifts effort towards “information verification, response integration, and task stewardship”. Goh et al. (Nature Medicine, 2025) found AI-assisted physicians spent about two minutes more per case. Neither measures reviewers of someone else’s work.
    • The “workslop” claim: BetterUp, with the Stanford Social Media Lab, calls it “AI-generated content that looks good, but lacks substance”, and its survey of 1,150 US desk workers puts a cost on it. It’s a vendor’s self-report survey, and we found no published method: useful as a name for the problem, not as a number.
    • Relationships and deadlines: sending work back has a social cost, and the person who sends it back is the one who looks difficult. A published rule takes that weight off the reviewer.

    Left open

    • What is the smallest entry gate your board could enforce without slowing honest submissions?
    • If one team’s submissions keep coming back, whose problem is that: the team’s, the board’s, or the tooling’s?
    • How would you know whether review capacity is your constraint, rather than assuming it?
    Where review effort goes, from code review studies

    Understanding is the work. Bacchelli and Bird’s study of code review at Microsoft (ICSE 2013) found that although finding defects is the top motivation, “code and change understanding is the key aspect of code reviewing”, and defect comments were a small share. Our reading: a document whose author can’t explain it makes the reviewer’s main job harder, because the reviewer can’t ask anyone what was meant.

    Agent pull requests. Watanabe et al. (preprint) found 83.8% of agent-assisted PRs merged, against 91.0% for human PRs, and that 54.9% of the merged ones went in “without further modification”, against 58.5% for human PRs. When revisions were needed, the effort was not statistically different. So in this sample, agent PRs that reached review needed about as much fixing as human ones. Merge rates can’t tell good review from lax review.

    What reviewers add. The 45.1% of merged agent PRs that needed changes were revised mostly for bug fixes, documentation and project-specific standards. Our reading: much of that is knowledge the reviewer had and the agent didn’t.

    Read more

    • Expectations, outcomes, and challenges of modern code review (Bacchelli and Bird, ICSE 2013)
    • On the Use of Agentic Coding: An Empirical Study of Pull Requests on GitHub (Watanabe et al., preprint)
    • The Impact of Generative AI on Critical Thinking (Lee et al., CHI 2025)
    • Workslop (BetterUp, vendor page with survey figures)
    When reviewers use AI too

    How much. Liang et al. (ICML 2024) estimated that “between 6.5% and 16.9% of text submitted as peer reviews to these conferences could have been substantially modified by LLMs”. The share was higher in reviews that reported lower confidence, were “submitted close to the deadline”, and came from reviewers less likely to respond to author rebuttals. Reviews containing scholarly citations were less likely to be modified.

    Help that worked. Thakkar et al. (preprint, 2025) ran a randomised study at ICLR 2025: an LLM system gave feedback to reviewers on “vague comments, content misunderstandings, and unprofessional remarks”. 27% of reviewers who received it updated their reviews, which grew by about 80 words on average and were judged more informative. This was feedback on a human’s review, not a review written by AI.

    For a board. The deadline pattern is the warning: AI in review shows up most where reviewers are short of time. The feedback study suggests a safer use, checking your own comments for vagueness, under the same confidentiality rules as any other tool.

    Read more

    • Monitoring AI-Modified Content at Scale (Liang et al., ICML 2024)
    • Can LLM feedback enhance review quality? (Thakkar et al., preprint, 2025)
    • Artificial Intelligence (AI) editorial policy (Springer Nature)

    Set the submission rule

    Sort uses of AI into what a board needs declared, then draft the declaration your board should ask for, and close the reviewing topic.

    Step15.4

    Part 15
    Reviewing AI-made work
    Time
    12 min
    Last reviewed
    12 November 2026

    Three minutes on the sort, five on the draft, then compare. The reference list item splits rooms: let it. Save at least five minutes for the discussion questions at the end, which close the reviewing topic.

    Westmere’s board has a one-line rule: “Declare any use of AI.” Last month, nine of eleven submissions ticked yes. The board learned nothing it could act on. The rule asks whether, and a board needs to know what, where and how it was checked.

    1 · Sort the uses

    For each use, decide what a board should require.

    Our sort, and where it comes from
    • No need to declare: spelling and grammar in the team’s own draft.
    • Declare, and show the check: the options draft from workshop notes, the vendor summaries (check each against the original), the diagram (check it against the text: that was problem X2), the brainstormed risks, and the reference list. The references are the trap. Formatting feels like spelling, but completing citations is exactly where Deloitte’s report for DEWR went wrong (step 15.2).
    • Not acceptable: untraced figures, another team’s confidential design in a public chatbot, and an assistant’s recommendation presented as the team’s judgement.

    Springer Nature’s AI policy works this way: “Use of AI is governed according to risk level, not by tool type.” Its red tier includes “Fabricating data, citations or results” and “Assigning authorship or accountability to AI systems or tools”.

    2 · Draft your board’s declaration

    Fill in the template for a board you know. Keep it short enough that people will complete it honestly. If your records already carry the provenance stamp from step 12.3, don’t repeat it: the stamp says where a record came from, and the declaration says which claims carry the decision and how they were checked.

    Model answer: open after you’ve drafted yours

    Section 3 does the most work. It turns the review in step 15.2 from a hunt into a check: the submitter names the claims, and the reviewer opens their sources. Section 5 asks in advance for what no document holds. In step 7.4 that was the ADR’s plant P8: an owner about to move to another division, which no reading of the documents could find.

    3 · Compare with published rules

    RuleWhat it asks
    ICMJE, medical journalsDisclose whether AI was used and how, “in both the cover letter and the submitted work”. Chatbots “should not be listed as authors because they cannot be responsible for the accuracy, integrity, and originality of the work”. “Referencing AI-generated material as the primary source is not acceptable.”
    Springer NatureThree risk tiers, for authors, reviewers and editors. For reviewers: “Human accountability for the review remains non-transferable”, and confidential manuscripts must not go to “unsecured or public AI tools”.
    Supreme Court of NSW, Practice Note SC Gen 23 (2025)Bans generative AI in affidavits and witness statements; expert reports need the court’s leave. Where it’s used in submissions, the author must verify that all citations “(a) exist, (b) are accurate, and (c) are relevant”.
    EU AI Act, Article 50(4)AI-generated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest must be disclosed, unless it “has undergone a process of human review or editorial control” and a person “holds editorial responsibility”. Applies from 2 August 2026. Not about internal documents, but the exemption is the same idea: a named person who answers for it.

    Checked 12 November 2026. These pages change; check the current versions before you quote them.

    Think deeper: A declaration rule can punish honesty. If declaring AI use earns a harsher review, people stop declaring, and the board learns less than before. ICMJE warns that nondisclosure “may be construed as misconduct in some circumstances”. How would you make declaring cheap and leaving it out expensive, without making the declaration itself a mark against the submitter?

    What should a submitter declare, and what does a declaration buy?

    The pattern

    A declaration of interests, or a supplier’s attestation: the party with the knowledge states it, in a fixed form, and is accountable if it’s false. Software teams know the newer version, a bill of materials: it doesn’t prove a component is safe, it tells you which ones to check when something breaks.

    What is really being decided

    What the board needs in order to review well, and who supplies it. A good declaration moves work from the reviewer to the submitter: naming the load-bearing claims and their sources is cheap for the person who wrote them and expensive for anyone else. The board also decides whether the same rule binds its own reviewers.

    The forces

    • Honesty against penalty: the rule only works if declaring doesn’t count against you. A declaration that triggers suspicion teaches people to leave it out.
    • Burden: each field adds minutes to every submission. Tie the long form to Tier A work (step 12.1) and keep Tier B to a line or two.
    • The norms disagree on detail: journals and courts agree a person stays responsible, and the journals add that AI can’t be an author; they differ on what must be declared. A board has to choose, and say why.
    • Two-way rules: a board that asks submitters to declare, and lets its reviewers paste submissions into public tools, won’t keep its submitters’ trust.
    • Accountability helps, a little: Goddard et al.’s review found user accountability among the mitigators of automation bias. A signed declaration is a form of it; it won’t remove over-reliance.

    Left open

    • Should the declaration travel with the decision record, or stay with the board’s papers?
    • What does the board do with a false declaration discovered a year later?
    • Would your board accept a submission whose author can’t explain a claim without the assistant?
    How other professions wrote the rule

    Journals. ICMJE puts responsibility plainly: “humans are responsible for any submitted material that included the use of AI-assisted technologies.” Springer Nature’s page frames the reviewer’s question as “not whether AI is used, but how it is used”. Its middle tier (amber) covers uses such as “Drafting explanatory summaries” and “Extensive copy editing or writing support”: permitted, with oversight, verification and disclosure. Neither page shows an update date, so check the version on the day you cite it.

    Courts. NSW’s practice note is the most specific about checking: whoever uses generative AI in written submissions must verify that every citation exists, is accurate and is relevant, and say so in the document. The Divisional Court in England, in Ayinde v Haringey (2025), put the reason bluntly: tools like ChatGPT “are not capable of conducting reliable legal research”.

    What the board can borrow. The verify-and-say-so rule, for references and figures. The tiers, so that grammar fixes don’t clog the declaration. And the reviewer rules, so the board holds itself to the same standard.

    Read more

    • Use of AI by Authors (ICMJE)
    • Artificial Intelligence (AI) editorial policy (Springer Nature)
    • Practice Note SC Gen 23: Use of Generative AI (Supreme Court of NSW, PDF)
    • Ayinde v Haringey; Al-Haroun v Qatar National Bank [2025] EWHC 1383 (Admin) (PDF)
    Marks in the text: why they can’t settle authorship

    C2PA for text. The C2PA specification (version 2.4) can embed a provenance manifest in plain text as a sequence of invisible Unicode characters. The specification itself says this “should only be used with unstructured text assets where no other embedding method is feasible” and “remains under review and may be subject to change”. Our reading: any text pipeline that drops or normalises those characters drops the mark, so its absence proves nothing.

    Watermarks. A vendor can bias its model’s word choices so that its output can later be recognised (Dathathri et al., Nature, 2024, a Google DeepMind study). That works only for that vendor’s marked output, and says nothing about text from anywhere else.

    For a board. Neither replaces a declaration, and neither replaces a check. A declaration is the submitter’s word, which you can hold them to; a mark is a technical signal, which can be lost.

    Read more

    • C2PA Technical Specification 2.4
    • Scalable watermarking for identifying large language model outputs (Dathathri et al., Nature, 2024)

    What you can do now

    Three ideas carry the reviewing topic:

    1. Authorship is the wrong question. Most tools and most people can’t reliably tell, the tools fail unfairly, and a right answer wouldn’t tell you whether the design is sound.
    2. Review the claims. Find the ones the decision rests on, open their sources, compare the document with itself, and ask what’s missing.
    3. Put the burden where the knowledge is. Send it back with a few answerable questions, and ask submitters to name their load-bearing claims and how they checked them.

    Questions to discuss

    In a group session, share your answers, and park anything that needs a longer discussion for the end.

    • Has your board ever approved something because it read well? How would you know?
    • Which claim types turn up most in your submissions: product features, numbers, references, or owners? Which do you check now?
    • Should a board member who uses an assistant to review a submission tell the submitter?
    • If drafting gets three times faster, what happens to your board’s queue, and who decides what gets reviewed less?

    Export your notes: they include your review log, your three questions and your draft declaration.

    The last step of this Part, 15.5, is a short sharing format a team can run every week.

  • I sorted the uses and compared with the three tiers.
  • I drafted a declaration for a board I know and compared it with the model answer.
  • I wrote an if-then plan for a real artefact.
