    Use-case clinic

    A twenty-minute weekly format for sharing how people use AI at work: what worked, what didn’t, and how they checked. Fill in a card and plan the first session.

    Step15.5

    Part 15
    Reviewing AI-made work
    Time
    8 min
    Last reviewed
    12 November 2026

    This step stands alone: run it at the end of this Part, or as the first clinic itself. If you run it as a clinic, take three volunteers, five minutes each, and hold them to the card. The first “how do you know?” sets the tone for every week after.

    Most teams share AI use in hallway stories: the time it saved a day, the time it made something up. Neither tells anyone what to do next. A clinic is a short, regular slot where people bring one real use, and the room asks the same questions every time.

    The card

    Fill it in for something you used an assistant for in the last fortnight. If you haven’t, use step 15.2. Section 4 is the one that matters: a card without a check is an anecdote.

    The card is for the room. Leave out personal, student and confidential data, and anything your organisation hasn’t approved for sharing.

    Running it

    • Rules, read aloud each time. One use each. No product pitches. Talk about the work, not the person. What’s said about failures stays in the room.
    • The facilitator asks one question every time: “How do you know?” It turns “it worked” into “it worked, and here’s how I checked”.
    • Close with a pattern, not a verdict. One line in a shared log, without names: “Vendor summaries missed caveats twice this month; check them against the original.”
    • Rotate. A new facilitator each month, and the people who haven’t presented go first.

    Keeping it honest

    • Count the “didn’t work” lines. If a month passes with none, the clinic has become a showcase. The facilitator brings a failure of their own next time.
    • Make checking the thing to admire. Praise a good check more than a good result. A check that found nothing still taught the room something.
    • Read the log back each quarter. Patterns that keep coming up belong in a template, a skill or a rule: step 15.4 is one place they land.

    Think deeper: The clinic only works if people bring failures, and they’ll bring failures only if nothing bad happens to them. But some failures matter: a confidential document in the wrong tool, a fabricated figure that reached a decision. Where is the line between what stays in the room and what someone has to report, and how will you tell people before they speak, not after?

    Should what’s shared in the clinic feed governance?

    The pattern

    A community of practice, run with the rules of a blameless post-incident review. Google’s SRE book puts the principle as “Writing a postmortem is not punishment—it is a learning opportunity for the entire company.” Architects know the same shape from design authorities that publish patterns rather than individual rulings.

    What is really being decided

    Whether the clinic is a safe space or an input to governance, and how to be both. If every card reaches the board, people bring only wins. If nothing leaves the room, the organisation repeats the same mistakes in every team. The pattern log, with no names, is the boundary, and it has to be stated before the first session.

    The forces

    • Candour against record: a written record makes people careful about what they say; no record means the learning leaves with the people in the room.
    • Learning against reporting: some things shared in a clinic are breaches that policy says must be reported. The rule for those has to be known in advance, or the first one will end the clinic.
    • Signal against noise: one week’s card is an anecdote. A pattern seen five times across teams is evidence for a change to a template or a rule.
    • Time: twenty minutes a week across a team adds up. The log is how you show the clinic paid for itself, or that it should stop.

    Left open

    • Who owns the pattern log, and who decides when a pattern becomes a rule?
    • Should managers attend, and if they do, will people still bring failures?
    • When the clinic surfaces a breach, who acts, and how do you keep the clinic alive afterwards?
    Why the card asks for failures and checks

    Safety and learning. Edmondson’s study of 51 work teams in a manufacturing company (Administrative Science Quarterly, 1999) defined team psychological safety as “a shared belief held by members of a team that the team is safe for interpersonal risk taking”, and found it associated with learning behaviour. That’s an association in one setting, not proof that a clinic works, but it’s why the rules come first.

    Why the check matters most. Lee et al.’s survey of 319 knowledge workers (CHI 2025) found generative AI moves effort towards “information verification, response integration, and task stewardship”, and that 58 reported barriers to inspecting AI output, such as lacking the domain knowledge. A clinic is a cheap place to learn other people’s checks.

    Blameless doesn’t mean no consequences. Google’s SRE guidance says a blameless postmortem must focus “on identifying the contributing causes of the incident without indicting any individual or team”. It’s practitioner guidance, not a study, and it assumes a process for the incidents that do need action.

    Read more

    • Psychological Safety and Learning Behavior in Work Teams (Edmondson, 1999)
    • Postmortem Culture: Learning from Failure (Google SRE book)
    • The Impact of Generative AI on Critical Thinking (Lee et al., CHI 2025)

    You have finished Part 15. You can explain why detecting AI is the wrong control, review a design for its claims, send it back with questions an author can answer, draft the declaration a board should ask for, and run a weekly clinic that teaches people each other’s checks.

    The if-then plan for this Part is the one you wrote in step 15.4, where the reviewing topic closed. The first-session plan above is the clinic’s own.

    Questions to discuss

    In a group session, share your answers, and park anything that needs a longer discussion for the end.

    • Where do people in your team learn each other’s checks today, if anywhere?
    • Which would be harder to bring to a clinic where you work: a failure, or a use nobody had approved?
    • After a term of clinics, what would tell you they were worth twenty minutes a week?

    Part 16 starts at step 16.1: why the same business question can get different answers depending on who asks and how, and what fixes it.

  • I filled in a clinic card, including how I checked.
  • I planned the first session: when, who facilitates, and who brings a card.
  • I decided what leaves the room, before anyone speaks.

    One question, many answers

    Ask an assistant how many students are enrolled at Westmere, from twenty invented students. Predict first, then see how many right answers there are.

    Step16.1

    Part 16
    Same question, same answer
    Time
    12 min
    Last reviewed
    12 November 2026

    Get every prediction written down before anyone opens a chat. In a group, give each table a different wording of the question, and collect the numbers on one board before you open the key. If an assistant asks which meaning you want, celebrate it and have that person read out its question: it’s the best result the exercise can produce.

    A dean opens the board pack and reads 16 enrolled students. The faculty dashboard says 12. Someone pastes the extract into a chat assistant and gets a third figure. Nobody has made a mistake in arithmetic. Each of them has answered a slightly different question, and none of them said so.

    This Part is about a kind of governance you build into the architecture: the same business question should get the same answer, whoever asks it and whichever assistant they use. Part 1 started this with entity definitions (step 1.5). Here you find out what a definition has to carry before a number stops moving.

    Where the evidence stands · checked 12 November 2026

    Solid
    On real enterprise databases, text-to-SQL scores fall far below the academic benchmarks: the Spider 2.0 team’s best agent solved 21.3% of enterprise tasks, where GPT-4-based methods had reached 91.2% on the older Spider 1.0 (ICLR 2025). Given an ambiguous question, models usually commit to one reading: AMBROSIA found a strong bias towards one interpretation, and, given no worked examples, no model found every reading for more than 1.9% of ambiguous questions (NeurIPS 2024). The same input at the same settings can produce different output, and one mechanical cause has been shown (Thinking Machines Lab, an AI lab’s own test, September 2025).
    Thin
    That adding definitions fixes it. Every study we found points the same way: BIRD’s added “evidence” raised GPT-4 by 20 points (NeurIPS 2023), and a 4 KB document of measures and rules added 17 to 23 points (Rumiantsau and Fokeev, preprint, April 2026; we read only the abstract). But most studies of semantic layers and knowledge graphs were run by companies that sell them, on 11 to 392 questions. Whether models ask before they answer: one preprint says they rarely do (Su and Cardie, May 2026). We found nothing peer-reviewed that measures it.
    Contested
    How good text-to-SQL is now. Self-submitted leaderboard entries reach 83.40% on BIRD (October 2026; we didn’t check how entries are verified), while a benchmark built from real warehouse query logs puts the best agent at 10.8% (BEAVER, preprint, May 2026). And whether to let it near business numbers: Thoughtworks moved text-to-SQL to Hold for unsupervised use (November 2025), while dbt Labs, which sells a semantic layer, reports text-to-SQL at 84% and 90% on two current models once it had remodelled the schema (April 2026, 11 questions).

    1 Predict

    Below is an invented extract from Westmere’s student system: twenty students, three tables, taken in the middle of Semester 2. Read it for a minute. Then, before you ask anyone, write down how many students you think are enrolled, and whether everyone in the room will get the same number.

    2 Ask

    Open a new chat with memory off, paste the extract, then add one of these questions on the line after it. The data is invented; don’t use real student data unless your organisation has approved it.

    • A · How many students are enrolled?
    • B · What is our Semester 2 enrolment?
    • C · How many students do we have this semester?

    In a group session, give each table one wording, and if people use different assistants, so much the better. Working alone, ask A in two separate new chats and B in a third. Note the number each answer leads with, and whether it said what it assumed. If it asks which meaning you want, write down its question, since that’s a result too, then reply “use your best judgement” and note the number it gives. Don’t argue with it yet.

    3 Compare with the key

    Pool the room’s numbers first. Then open the key: we worked out every count with a script that loads the three tables into a database and runs one query per reading, so the figures below don’t depend on anyone’s arithmetic.

    The key – open it after you’ve pooled the numbers
    AnswerWhat “enrolled” was taken to meanDefensible?
    12Enrolled today (14 October): each person once, programme status Enrolled, or still in Semester 2 units. Both routes give the same twelve people.Yes: “who is studying now”
    14Programme enrolments with status Enrolled. Tom Ackland (BA and LLB) and Priya Raman (BCOM and BSC) count twice.For “enrolments”, not “students”
    15Not withdrawn: the twelve plus three students on leave of absence, who still hold a programme.Yes: “on our books”
    16Enrolled on the census date (31 August): in units at the end of that day. Counts four who withdrew or took leave later; leaves out two who withdrew on or before it.Yes: the usual reporting figure
    17Three different routes: the census count, but treating Lucas Ferreira’s withdrawal on 31 August as still enrolled; or the count on the first day of semester (27 July), before the week-2 late enrolment; or programme enrolments not withdrawn, counting rows.The first two, arguably
    18Anyone who enrolled in Semester 2 units at any point, including the two who withdrew on or before the census date.For “enrolled this semester at all”
    20Every student in the extract.Only as “students on file”
    22Every row of programme_enrolment, whatever its status.No: a counting mistake

    Look at 17. Three routes reach it for three different reasons, so two people who agree on a number haven’t shown that they agree on a definition. Look at 12 too: it’s what a careful reader means by “currently enrolled”, and it isn’t what Westmere would report to government.

    Materials check, not evidence. On 12 November 2026 we ran this step’s wordings on three Claude models (the Haiku, Sonnet and Opus tiers), every run in a fresh session with a plain system prompt and no tools, and repeated a few runs the next day. Every run of wording A answered 12 without asking first, and most named the census figure as an alternative, usually in its last paragraph. With wording B (“enrolment”), some runs led with 16 instead; others led with 12 and gave 16 as the census figure. The second day’s runs didn’t all match the first’s, which is the point of step 16.2. That’s one vendor over two days. Your assistant may behave differently, and the exercise works either way: whatever it does, you now know the question has more than one right answer.

    What this means for the architecture

    Every answer above came from the same governed tables. Controlling access to the data didn’t keep the answers consistent, because the inconsistency lives in the step between the question and the query. When anyone can ask a data platform a question in plain words, that step happens many times a day, out of sight, once per asker. Our reading: wherever the meaning of a business term isn’t written down somewhere a machine can use it, you’ve left a design decision to whichever model happens to answer.

    Think deeper: The figure that leads an answer is the one people will copy into a slide, whatever caveats follow it. If an assistant answers 12 and mentions 16 in its last paragraph, has it done its job? Who in your organisation would be held responsible if 12 went into a ministerial return?

    Who owns the number when anyone can ask for it?

    The pattern

    A single authoritative source, the idea behind master data management and a canonical data model, applied to meaning rather than to records. Data teams have long known the dashboard version of this problem: two reports, one metric name, two numbers. Self-service BI spread it. Natural-language querying spreads it further, because every question now carries its own private definition, and nobody reviews it before the number is used.

    What is really being decided

    Whether the meaning of key business terms is designed once and enforced, or worked out afresh each time someone asks. Access control, lineage and data quality all govern the rows. None of them governs what a question means. The decision is who owns that, and where it’s enforced: in a person’s head, a document, or something every query has to pass through.

    The forces

    • Flexibility against consistency: letting each asker’s assistant interpret the question answers any question at all. It also gives different people different numbers, and makes neither of them wrong in a way you can audit.
    • Local meaning against one meaning: a wellbeing team needs “currently studying”; the planning office needs the census count. Forcing one definition erases a real difference. Allowing both needs two names.
    • Speed of asking against cost of agreeing: asking takes seconds. Agreeing a definition takes meetings, a steward and an approval route, and that cost falls on a different team from the one that benefits.
    • Visible against silent failure: a wrong number in a board pack looks the same as a right one. The cost of inconsistency shows up late, in a meeting where two figures meet.

    Left open

    • Which ten numbers in your organisation must give the same answer whoever asks, and does each of them have a named owner today?
    • When a platform assistant is switched on over your warehouse, who is accountable for what it decides a question means?
    • Is it acceptable for an assistant to answer a question nobody has defined, as long as it says what it assumed?
    How text-to-SQL does on real enterprise data

    Academic benchmarks are small. Spider 1.0 and BIRD use tidy databases with tens of columns. BIRD (Li et al., NeurIPS 2023) added dirty values and questions that need outside knowledge: 12,751 question and SQL pairs over 95 databases, with people scoring 92.96%.

    Enterprise benchmarks are not. Spider 2.0 (Lei, Chen, Ye et al., ICLR 2025) takes 632 workflow tasks from real data applications, with databases “often containing over 1,000 columns”. Its best agent, built on o1-preview, solved 21.3% of tasks. The paper sets that against the 91.2% and 73.0% that GPT-4-based methods had reached on Spider 1.0 and BIRD. BEAVER (Chen, Yang, Li et al., preprint) is built from private warehouses’ query logs: 9,128 question and SQL pairs over 812 tables. It reports the best agentic framework, using GPT-5.2, at 10.8%, and 30.1% when given hints for every subtask. We read BEAVER’s abstract, not its body.

    Leaderboards tell a different story, and it isn’t the same kind of evidence. The BIRD leaderboard’s top entry stood at 83.40% on 22 October 2026. Entries are submitted by the teams themselves, and we didn’t check how they’re verified. A benchmark can also be wrong: NL2SQL-BUGs (Liu et al., KDD 2025) found 106 errors in BIRD’s own answers, 6.91% of those it checked.

    None of these measures our problem. No study we found gives a rate for questions whose business meaning is ambiguous. Spider 2.0’s error classes are technical: schema linking, joins, dialect functions. Every answer in this step’s key would be marked correct by a benchmark that defined “enrolled” its own way.

    Read more

    • Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows (ICLR 2025)
    • BIRD: Can LLM Already Serve as a Database Interface? (NeurIPS 2023)
    • BEAVER: An Enterprise Benchmark for Text-to-SQL (preprint)
    • NL2SQL-BUGs: detecting semantic errors in text-to-SQL (KDD 2025)
    Same words, different runs

    Two people asking the same words can get different answers even when nobody changes a setting. Horace He at Thinking Machines Lab (September 2025) sampled 1,000 completions of one prompt at temperature 0 and got 80 unique completions, the most common occurring 78 times. The cause is mechanical. A server batches your request with other people’s, the batch size varies with load, and the maths kernels don’t give bit-identical results across batch sizes. Kernels written to be batch-invariant made all 1,000 identical, at a speed cost. It’s one AI lab’s measurement of one prompt, and it explains the mechanism well.

    Others have measured the effect on results. Atil et al. (preprint, v5 April 2025) ran five models set to be deterministic, ten times each on eight tasks, and saw “accuracy variations up to 15% across naturally occurring runs”. Ouyang et al. (ACM TOSEM) found that setting the temperature to 0 “does not guarantee determinism” in code generation. We found no study that measures run-to-run variation in business numbers from text-to-SQL. Our reading: on a question with several fair readings, a small difference early in the answer can tip it into another reading, which is a much bigger change than a different word.

    Read more

    • Defeating Nondeterminism in LLM Inference (Thinking Machines Lab, 2025)
    • Non-Determinism of “Deterministic” LLM Settings (Atil et al., preprint)
    • An Empirical Study of the Non-determinism of ChatGPT in Code Generation (Ouyang et al.)
  • I predicted a number before I asked.
  • I asked the question in at least two fresh chats, or with two wordings, and recorded what each assumed.
  • I found my answers in the key and can name at least three fair readings of “enrolled”.
    •
    Previous step15.5 Use-case clinic Next step16.2 Find the ambiguity

    Find the ambiguity

    Name the choices hidden in “enrolled”, see how far each one moves the count, and score whether your assistant said which way it went or asked.

    Step16.2

    Part 16
    Same question, same answer
    Time
    10 min
    Last reviewed
    12 November 2026

    Two minutes of silent listing before the figure appears. The room will find the date and the withdrawals quickly; the double-counted combined degrees and the census-day withdrawal are the ones to draw out. When you score the answers, an assistant that asked counts as a full marks result, not as a failure to answer.

    Every number in the last step’s key is arithmetic done correctly. The disagreement was in the question. So before anyone fixes it, find exactly where “How many students are enrolled?” forks. An architect would call these the unstated requirements.

    1 · List the choices yourself

    Look back at the extract in step 16.1 and at the answers you got. Write down every choice someone has to make, consciously or not, to turn the question into one number. For each, note which students it moves.

    Our list – open it after writing yours
    • What is counted: people, or programme enrolments. Two students in combined degrees add 2 if you count enrolments.
    • As at when: today, the census date, the first day of semester, or any time in the semester. The extract is a snapshot from 14 October; the census date is in its header, not in the data.
    • Withdrawals: two students withdrew on or before the census date and three after it. Whether they count depends on the date you chose.
    • Leave of absence: two took leave for the whole semester, and one from 21 September. They still hold a programme, so “on our books” includes them.
    • The census boundary: Lucas Ferreira withdrew on 31 August. Westmere’s policy lets students withdraw without penalty “up to the census date”, which a careful reader takes to include the day. That one student is the difference between 16 and 17.

    Notice what isn’t on the list: nothing about SQL, joins or the model’s skill. Each fork is a business decision, and the people who can settle it work in student administration, not in IT.

    2 · Did it ask, or guess?

    Score the answer you got in step 16.1 as run 1. Then, in a new chat, paste the extract again with the prompt below, and score that as run 2. A row scores “Said or asked” if the answer named the choice, whichever way it went, or asked you to make it.

    How many students are enrolled? Before you answer, list the ways this question could be read, and ask me which one I mean.

    Run 1: your plain question from the last step. Run 2: the ask-first prompt. Leave rows blank rather than guess.

    If your assistant asked before answering in run 1, that’s the good outcome, and it’s less common than it should be. The evidence so far:

    • Models usually commit to one reading. AMBROSIA (Saparina and Lapata, NeurIPS 2024) gave six models database questions with more than one fair reading. The models “often capture only one interpretation”, and the best of them leaned hard towards the same kind of reading each time: one reading of scope ambiguity in 80% of cases, one reading of attachment in more than 97%.
    • They can spot the ambiguity, and still don’t ask. Su and Cardie (preprint, May 2026, general questions rather than SQL; we read the abstract) found models “often identify ambiguity when explicitly asked to judge it”, yet when simply answering they “overwhelmingly default to direct answers”. Supplying retrieved context made them even less likely to ask.
    • Asking well is hard too. In BIRD-Interact (Huo et al., ICLR 2026), a simulated user answers the model’s clarifying questions. GPT-5 completed 8.67% of tasks in the scripted conversation and 17.00% when it could choose when to ask. We read the abstract only.

    What we saw, as a materials check. In our nine plain runs of wording A (three Claude models, 12 November 2026), none asked first. All nine led with 12 and then named the census figure as an alternative, so they’d score on most rows here and miss “asked”. All three runs of the ask-first prompt listed the readings with counts and asked. One vendor, one day: your results may differ, and that difference is worth bringing to the room.

    What this means for the architecture

    “Ask first” is a prompt you have to remember to write, so it doesn’t make answers consistent. It tells each person that there’s a choice, and then lets each person make it differently. Our reading: a clarifying question is a good safety net for a person at a keyboard. It is no help at all to a scheduled report, a dashboard tile or an agent calling a tool, which have nobody to ask.

    Think deeper: Suppose every assistant in your organisation were made to ask “which meaning?” whenever a term was ambiguous. Within a month, people would answer “just give me the usual one” without reading the options. What does that tell you about where the choice should be made, and by whom?

    Should an assistant ask, assume out loud, or refuse?

    The pattern

    Validating input at the boundary, and failing fast. An interface that receives an ambiguous request has three honest options: reject it, ask for what’s missing, or proceed on a stated default. Designers of APIs make this choice for every parameter. A natural-language interface makes it too, only implicitly, and differently on each run.

    What is really being decided

    The behaviour of every assistant that answers questions over your data when it meets a term nobody has defined, and whether you set that behaviour or the vendor does. It’s a policy, and it belongs in the design of a platform assistant alongside its permissions.

    The forces

    • Friction against error: asking every time slows people down and trains them to click through. Never asking produces confident, unexplained numbers.
    • People against pipelines: a person can answer a clarifying question. A scheduled report or an agent can’t, so the same assistant may need different behaviour depending on who is calling it.
    • Stated defaults decay: “assume out loud” works only if someone reads the assumption. The leading number travels; the caveat stays behind in the chat.
    • Refusing is honest and unpopular: an assistant that says “that term isn’t defined” will be called broken, even when it’s the only one behaving correctly.

    Left open

    • For which terms should an assistant refuse to give a number until a definition exists?
    • Can you configure this behaviour in the platform assistants you already own, or only in the ones you build?
    • Who should see the clarifying questions people are asked most often, as a list of definitions you still need?
    What AMBROSIA measured

    The benchmark. AMBROSIA covers three kinds of ambiguity: scope (their example, “What activities does each gym offer?”, can mean the classes every gym offers, or each gym’s classes separately), attachment (it’s unclear what a modifier attaches to), and vagueness, which they define as context creating “uncertainty about which set of entities is being referred to”. The authors built 846 databases and 4,242 SQL queries so that the ambiguity survives even with the database in view. That last point matters here: our extract has all the data a model needs, and the question is still ambiguous.

    The results. Models were asked to produce SQL for every reading they saw. On ambiguous questions, the best model (Llama3-70B) recalled 30.7% of the correct queries, against 64.5% on unambiguous ones; GPT-4o scored 27.1% against 63.4%. The share of ambiguous questions where a model found every reading was at most 1.9%. Those figures are for prompts with no worked examples; with one example, the two models’ shares rose to 3.7% and 4.5%. Looking at which readings the best model chose, the authors report “a clear bias towards one interpretation type”.

    What it doesn’t show. AMBROSIA tests whether models produce every reading, not whether they ask a person. Its models are from 2024. Business ambiguity like ours, a term whose meaning an organisation sets, is closer to its “vagueness” category than to the other two, but no study we found measures that directly. PRACTIQ (Dong et al., NAACL 2025) builds conversations around ambiguous and unanswerable data questions and reports that “state-of-the-art systems struggle to handle ambiguous and unanswerable questions effectively”; we read its abstract only.

    Read more

    • AMBROSIA: parsing ambiguous questions into database queries (NeurIPS 2024)
    • Knowing but Not Showing: LLMs Recognize Ambiguity but Rarely Ask Clarifying Questions (Su and Cardie, preprint)
    • BIRD-INTERACT (ICLR 2026)
    • PRACTIQ: ambiguous and unanswerable queries in conversational text-to-SQL
  • I listed the hidden choices before opening ours.
  • I scored a plain answer and an ask-first answer.
  • I can say why a clarifying question helps a person but not a scheduled report.

    Fix it with a definition

    Write the definition that settles the question, run the same wordings again with it pasted in, and check that the answers converge without stretching to questions it doesn’t cover.

    Step16.3

    Part 16
    Same question, same answer
    Time
    12 min
    Last reviewed
    12 November 2026

    Let people draft their own definition first, whichever reading they prefer; the point is that any agreed definition makes the answers converge. Then hand out Westmere’s. When you pool the tally, spend most of the time on row D, the question the definition doesn’t cover.

    In Part 1 you reviewed entity definitions (step 1.5), and in Part 2 you built the entity-definition-review skill, which has six checks (step 2.3): a singular business noun, what the thing is rather than where it’s stored, not circular, one concept, no attributes, distinct from its neighbours. Those checks make a definition people can agree on. They deliberately stop short of anything a machine could count with. A number needs both.

    1 · Draft one

    Choose the reading of “enrolled” you think Westmere should use, and write a definition that would make every assistant give the same number. Use those six checks for the meaning, then add whatever a counter would need.

    Now compare yours with the one Westmere’s Registrar agreed. Its top half passes the six checks: “a person who is studying at least one unit” defines the thing without using the word “enrolled”, and the “not to be confused with” lines keep it distinct from its neighbours. Its bottom half answers each fork from step 16.2.

    2 · Run it again

    For each row below, open a new chat, paste the definition, then the extract from step 16.1, then the question. Score whether the answer led with 16, the agreed figure. Row D asks something the definition doesn’t define: a good answer gives another number and says why. If you can, run row A on a second assistant or model.

    What to expect, and what we saw

    Rows A to C should all lead with 16: Chloe Martin and Lucas Ferreira out (on or before the census date), the four who left after it in, the two combined-degree students once each. Row D asks about “this week”, which the definition names only to rule out. A good answer gives 12, the students still in units on 14 October, says that it isn’t the census figure, and notes that the extract was taken on 14 October, so “this week” may have moved on. An answer of 16 to row D is the definition over-reaching.

    Materials check, not evidence. On 12 November 2026, on three Claude models, all three wordings led with 16 in every run with the definition pasted, against 12 in all nine plain runs of wording A. All three runs of row D answered 12 and said it wasn’t the census headcount. One run got the headline right and a side figure wrong: it reported Enrolled programme rows as “12 rows across 11 people”, where the extract has 14 rows across 12. A definition settles which question is being answered. It doesn’t check the arithmetic.

    What the studies measured

    Our runs are a check of the materials. These are the measurements, and they all point the same way. Read who ran each one.

    • Academic. BIRD (Li et al., NeurIPS 2023) gave models the same questions with and without short “external knowledge evidence”: synonyms, domain facts, value meanings. GPT-4’s execution accuracy on the test set rose from 34.88% to 54.89%; Claude-2’s from 34.60% to 49.02%.
    • Preprint, funding not stated. Rumiantsau and Fokeev (April 2026) gave three current models 100 questions over a retail dataset, with and without “a 4 KB hand-authored markdown document describing the dataset’s measures, conventions, and disambiguation rules”. Accuracy rose 17 to 23 points, to 67.7–68.7%, and the models were statistically indistinguishable within each condition. We read the abstract only; the affiliations aren’t shown. It’s the closest published test of what you just did.
    • Run by companies that sell the answer. Snowflake (March 2025): 392 adapted BIRD questions, 57% to 78% average accuracy with its semantic model, scored by another model, with no repeats. dbt Labs (April 2026): 11 questions run 20 times each; on the original schema, text-to-SQL 64.5% against 72.7% through its semantic layer. data.world’s authors (November 2023, preprint): 43 questions on an insurance schema, GPT-4 at 16% on SQL against 54% over a knowledge graph. The authors list the limits themselves. It’s useful history, not a current figure.

    So the direction is consistent, and the size is not established. The samples run from 11 to 392 questions, apart from BIRD. The semantic-layer and knowledge-graph studies were run by companies that sell semantic layers and knowledge graphs. We found no independent study that compares a glossary, a semantic layer and a knowledge graph on the same enterprise data.

    What this means for the architecture

    The definition you pasted did the work a semantic layer does, by hand, for one chat. That shows the definition is the thing that matters, more than where it sits. It also shows the weakness: it worked because you remembered to paste it, pasted the current version, and asked a question it covered. Each of those is a control that depends on a person remembering.

    Think deeper: Westmere’s Student Wellbeing team counts “currently studying”, because it needs to know who to contact this week. The Planning office reports the census headcount. Both call their figure “enrolled students”. Do you rename one, define both under different names, or let “enrolled” mean whichever the asker’s team uses? What does each choice do to an assistant that serves both teams?

    Is the definition the control point?

    The pattern

    A controlled vocabulary with a steward, the business-glossary practice data management has long recommended, now with a new kind of reader. It is also the canonical model pattern: agree the meaning once, at one point, and make every consumer translate to it rather than to each other. What’s new is that an AI reader will act on a missing definition by inventing one, quietly and differently each time.

    What is really being decided

    Whether the definitions of your important numbers become controlled artefacts, with an owner, a version and a change route, like any other control. In practice that means deciding which numbers count as important, and funding the stewardship nobody has had to pay for while people resolved ambiguity informally in meetings.

    The forces

    • Agreement is the expensive part: writing the definition took minutes. Getting Planning, Wellbeing and the faculties to accept it takes months, and someone has to chair that.
    • Precision against reach: the tighter the definition, the more questions fall outside it (row D). Every excluded question needs its own definition, or an assistant that says it has none.
    • Definitions change: the census date moves each semester, and policies change. A definition without a version and an effective date gives last year’s answer with this year’s confidence.
    • Evidence of benefit is thin: the direction is consistent across studies, but most were run by vendors on small samples. You can’t yet quote a reliable figure for the improvement in a business case.

    Left open

    • Who in your organisation could sign off Westmere’s definition today, and would they accept being named as its steward?
    • How many definitions would you need before assistants over your data were safe for routine reporting: ten, a hundred, all of them?
    • When an assistant answers a question a definition doesn’t cover, should it still answer?
    The with-and-without studies, side by side

    What “definitions” meant in each. BIRD added a sentence or two of evidence to each question. Rumiantsau and Fokeev added one 4 KB document for the whole dataset, closest to a pasted glossary. Snowflake added a semantic model, its description of tables, measures and their meaning, for its Cortex Analyst product. dbt routed questions through its semantic layer, which generates the SQL itself, so failures show up differently: in dbt’s words, “With text-to-SQL, failure looks like a plausible but incorrect answer. With the Semantic Layer, failure looks like an error message.”

    Limits worth knowing. Snowflake scored answers with another model (Mistral Large 2) and reported no repeats or intervals. dbt’s semantic layer scored 0% on questions needing joins its model didn’t cover, until dbt added three models to the project; after that, Claude Sonnet 4.6 scored 90.0% by text-to-SQL and 98.2% through the layer. dbt also notes that its text-to-SQL arm was given the whole schema, which “isn’t practical for larger datasets”. The 2026 dbt post gives its 2023 text-to-SQL baseline as 32.7% on its 11 questions, while the original data.world paper gives 16.7% on that benchmark’s 43 questions. The question sets differ and neither source reconciles the two figures, so don’t set them side by side.

    Read more

    • BIRD benchmark (NeurIPS 2023)

    • Agentic Semantic Model Improvement (Snowflake, vendor)

  • I reran the wordings with Westmere’s definition and recorded whether they converged.
  • I checked that the definition didn’t stretch to a question it doesn’t cover.

    Check the query

    Have the assistant write the SQL, then read any query for three things – what it counts, what it filters on, and which date it uses – and review one that returns a plausible wrong number.

    Step16.4

    Part 16
    Same question, same answer
    Time
    12 min
    Last reviewed
    12 November 2026

    Most architects can read SQL well enough for this; pair anyone who can’t with someone who can, because the three questions work without SQL fluency. Have people review the planted query before asking their assistant to, and keep the key shut until both runs are scored.

    In a real platform, the number doesn’t come from a model reading twenty rows. It comes from a query, and the query is where a definition either survives or quietly doesn’t. You don’t need to write SQL to check one. You need three questions, asked of every query that produces a number someone will use.

    1 · Ask for the query

    In a new chat, paste Westmere’s definition (step 16.3), then the extract (step 16.1), then this prompt.

    Write one SQLite query that answers "How many students are enrolled?" using the agreed definition and the three tables above. Then, in one line each, say which tables you joined and why, what you filtered on, and the exact date comparison you used.

    Read its query, not its explanation. Answer the three questions from the query text alone, then check whether the explanation describes the same query.

    If your assistant can run code, ask it to load the three tables into SQLite and run its query. Then you have a number from the query itself, rather than its own account of what the query would return.

    2 · Review someone else’s

    Another assistant wrote this query for the same question and the same definition. It runs without error and returns a sensible-looking number. Review it yourself first and record run 1. Then paste it into a new chat with the definition, the extract and the review prompt, and record your assistant’s review as run 2.

    Another assistant wrote the query below for "How many students are enrolled?" under the agreed definition above. Review it line by line against the definition. For each line, say whether it is right, and if not, what it gets wrong. Then say what number it returns on this extract.

    Run 1: you. Run 2: your assistant. Leave rows blank rather than guess.

    The key – open it after both runs
    LineVerdictWhy
    COUNT(*) after the joinFaultJoining to programme_enrolment gives one row per programme, so Tom Ackland and Priya Raman each count twice. It counts enrolments, not people. COUNT(DISTINCT t.student_id), or no join at all, fixes it.
    t.term = '2026-S2'SoundThe right semester.
    p.status <> 'Withdrawn'FaultThe status is the status today. It drops Mei Lin Zhao, Oliver Grant and Mateo Alvarez, who withdrew after the census date and should count. The definition says not to use this column.
    withdrawn_on IS NULLSound, on one conditionKeeps students who never withdrew, as long as the blanks were loaded as true empty values (NULL). Leaving the line out is a classic fault, because a comparison with an empty value is never true. If a spreadsheet or CSV import loads the blanks as empty text instead, this line silently drops all twelve students still enrolled, and the query returns 1.
    withdrawn_on >= '2026-08-31'FaultCounts a withdrawal made on the census date as still enrolled. The definition excludes it. It should be >.

    What it returns: 15. The right answer is 16. Now the uncomfortable part, which we confirmed by running each fix on its own:

    • Fix only the count and you get 13, further away.
    • Remove only the status test and you get 19.
    • Fix only the date and you still get 15, because the status test already throws out Lucas Ferreira, who withdrew on the census date. One fault hides another.
    • Fix all three and you get 16.

    So a number that looks about right tells you very little about a query. Two more things a test on this extract can’t catch. The query never checks that the enrolment started by the census date; nobody here enrolled late enough for that to matter. And it depends on how the blanks were loaded, as the IS NULL row says. A reference query that copes with both kinds of blank, and returns 16 either way:

    SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT student_id) AS enrolled_students FROM term_enrolment WHERE term = '2026-S2' AND enrolled_on <= '2026-08-31' AND (NULLIF(withdrawn_on, '') IS NULL OR withdrawn_on > '2026-08-31');

    Materials check, not evidence. On 12 November 2026 we ran both prompts on three Claude models, then ran the SQL ourselves. All three wrote a query that returns 16, and all three guarded against blanks loaded as empty text, which our own first reference query didn’t. All three reviews flagged the three faults and the missing start-date check, and worked out 15 by hand. Two of them raised the blank-value caveat. One review muddled its explanation of the status line while getting the verdict right. Remember that the definition told them which column not to use, which made the status fault easy to see. Your assistant may do better or worse, and without the definition the review would be much harder.

    What the research says about query errors

    The Spider 2.0 team (ICLR 2025) analysed 300 sampled failures on its enterprise tasks. Wrong schema linking, meaning wrong tables or columns, accounted for 27.6% of errors, and join errors for 8.3%. The largest class, 35.5%, was “erroneous data analysis”: wrong calculations, wrong dialect functions, wrong query plans. None of the classes is “answered a different question than the asker meant”, which is the error this Part is about. Benchmarks score a query against one gold answer, so they can’t see it.

    Can a model review a query instead? NL2SQL-BUGs (Liu et al., KDD 2025) built 2,018 expert-annotated examples and found models detected semantic errors with 75.16% average accuracy. That is useful as a second reader, and not enough to be the only one. Thoughtworks moved text-to-SQL to Hold in November 2025 for unsupervised use, and advised that “human review is required for all generated queries”.

    What this means for the architecture

    Reviewing every generated query doesn’t scale, and the people asking the questions mostly can’t do it. Our reading: the review belongs once, on the definition’s query, by someone who can read SQL, and then the number should come from that reviewed query every time. That is what a semantic layer does. Generating SQL afresh for each question moves the review to the moment, and the person, least able to do it.

    Think deeper: dbt Labs, which sells a semantic layer, puts the difference this way: with text-to-SQL, “failure looks like a plausible but incorrect answer”; with a semantic layer, “failure looks like an error message”. An error message makes people angry and gets fixed. A plausible wrong number gets used. Which failure does your organisation currently tolerate better, and is that the right way round?

    Who checks generated SQL, and when should nobody need to?

    The pattern

    Fail closed rather than fail open, and the old difference between ad hoc queries and reviewed, parameterised ones. Database teams learnt long ago to put business-critical logic in reviewed views or procedures rather than in every report author’s hand-written SQL. Text-to-SQL brings back the hand-written query, at a volume no reviewer can match.

    What is really being decided

    For each kind of question, whether a generated query is acceptable at all. Exploratory questions from an analyst who can read the SQL are one thing. A number that goes into a board pack, a funding return or an agent’s next action is another. The decision is where that line sits, and what enforces it: a policy people should follow, or a path that only leads through reviewed definitions.

    The forces

    • Coverage against correctness: generated SQL can attempt any question. A governed layer answers only what it models, and dbt’s did score 0% on questions needing joins its model lacked.
    • Review capacity: a query reviewed once can be reused a million times. A query generated each time has to be reviewed each time, or not at all.
    • Who can read it: the asker usually can’t judge SQL, and the model’s explanation of its query may not match the query.
    • Hidden faults: as the key shows, faults can cancel out on today’s data and surface on next semester’s. Tests on one extract prove little.

    Left open

    • Which numbers in your organisation should never come from a freshly generated query?
    • If a platform assistant shows its SQL, does that count as review, when the reader can’t check it?
    • Who maintains the test data that would catch a late enrolment, a census-day withdrawal or a combined degree?
    Where text-to-SQL goes wrong on enterprise data

    The Spider 2.0 error analysis. The team sampled 300 failures across its two agent frameworks. “Erroneous data analysis” (35.5%) breaks down into dialect functions such as date handling (10.3%), advanced calculation (7.5%) and intricate query planning (17.7%). “Wrong schema linking” (27.6%) splits into wrong columns (16.6%) and wrong tables (10.1%); the paper links the column errors to databases with far more columns than BIRD’s. “JOIN errors” (8.3%) arise, the authors say, because the BigQuery databases often lack declared foreign keys, so models have to guess how tables relate.

    What that means for a reviewer. Our reading: in Spider’s terms, two of our three planted faults are closest to schema linking: the right table for the wrong purpose (programme_enrolment.status), and a join that changes what one row means. The third is a date boundary. The things to read for are the same on twenty rows as on a thousand columns. The difference is that on a thousand columns, a person can’t check the result by eye.

    Robustness. Dr.Spider (Chang et al., ICLR 2023) rewrote questions, databases and SQL in 17 ways, rephrasings among them, and found “even the most robust model suffers from a 14.0% performance drop overall”. Its models predate today’s; we read the abstract only.

    • Dr.Spider: text-to-SQL robustness (ICLR 2023)
    • Text to SQL (Thoughtworks Technology Radar)

    Where definitions live

    Sort nine Westmere definitions into the places they could live, by who they reach and who owns them. Then close the Part with a plan and questions for the room.

    Step16.5

    Part 16
    Same question, same answer
    Time
    14 min
    Last reviewed
    12 November 2026

    Four silent minutes for the sort, then compare. The items that split rooms are the census dates and the “ask which one” rule; let that argument run. Keep the last ten minutes for the if-then plan and the questions to discuss.

    The definition worked when you pasted it. A pasted definition is a copy, though, and a copy in one chat reaches one person, once. The question for an architect is where the definition should live, so that every report, dashboard, assistant and agent gets the same one, and somebody owns it.

    1 · Sort them

    Here are nine things Westmere knows about enrolment. Put each where you think it belongs. The six homes aren’t exclusive, so choose the one that should be the source, the place you’d change first.

    • Business glossary: the organisation’s vocabulary, for people, with a steward per term.
    • Data catalogue or dictionary: what data exists, where, and what its columns mean technically.
    • Semantic layer: metrics and their logic, defined once in code and run by a machine for every consumer.
    • Retrieval source: documents an assistant searches before it answers.
    • Skill or project instructions: a procedure an assistant loads for a task.
    • Platform assistant’s system prompt: standing behaviour for one assistant.
    Our reading – open after placing all nine
    ItemOur home for itWhy
    Enrolled student: what it isBusiness glossaryMeaning, for people, with the steward and the “not to be confused with” lines.
    Census headcount formulaSemantic layerIt computes a number. It should run the same way for every consumer, and fail with an error outside its scope.
    Census datesSemantic layerAs a calendar table the formula reads. Typed into a prompt, it goes stale next semester.
    Status holds today’s valueCatalogue or dictionaryA fact about a column, the kind of “technology relevant” detail a data dictionary holds.
    Don’t use enrolment_2019CatalogueA warning about an asset. Better still, retire the table, so the warning isn’t needed.
    Load and headcount differBusiness glossaryA common misunderstanding: a field glossaries are meant to carry.
    Enrolment PolicyRetrieval sourceLong, explanatory, changes yearly, and the policy owner already publishes it.
    Ask which measureSystem promptBehaviour, not meaning. It belongs to whichever assistant meets people, and it’s the only item here that a prompt is the right home for.
    Weekly summary procedureSkillA repeatable task. The skill should call the census measure, not restate its formula.

    The two disputes worth having: whether census dates belong in a semantic layer or in a reference-data service, and whether “ask which measure” should be a prompt at all, rather than a rule the semantic layer enforces by refusing undefined questions.

    2 · What the sources say

    • Glossary, dictionary and catalogue are different things. The UK Government Data Architecture Community’s Business Glossaries Definitions (June 2020) calls a business glossary “the vocabulary of an organisation”, a data dictionary the place for “‘technology relevant’ or ‘machine readable’” detail, and a data catalogue “An inventory of available data assets supported by a collection of metadata”. For each, it lists confusion with the others as a common misunderstanding.
    • Semantic layers are worth trying, starting small. Thoughtworks put the semantic layer at Trial in April 2026: without one, “metric definitions quietly diverge”, and naive text-to-SQL often gives wrong results when business rules live outside the schema. Its advice is to “start with a single domain rather than attempting an enterprise-wide rollout”, because broad rollouts leave legacy reports running beside the new layer. It had already moved text-to-SQL to Hold for unsupervised use (November 2025), pointing agentic BI at a governed semantic layer or a semantically rich access layer instead.
    • Instructions bloat. The Radar’s next volume (35, November 2026) puts “agent instruction bloat” under Caution: instructions “become long, contradictory and stale”. Its first remedy: “convert any instructions you can into deterministic hooks or checks.” The entry is about instructions for coding agents. Our reading: a formula typed into a prompt is the same kind of instruction.
    • Loading is uncertain. Birgitta Böckeler (Thoughtworks, February 2026) notes that when a model decides whether to load context, such as a skill, “there always remains some uncertainty (dare I say non-determinism)”, and that “there are no unit tests for context engineering”. She was writing about coding agents; applying it to data definitions is our reading.
    • A shared format is coming, not here yet. Open Semantic Interchange, a specification for metrics and dimensions started by Snowflake and other vendors, entered the Apache Incubator as Ossie on 22 June 2026. Its incubator page describes “a vendor-neutral format for expressing business metrics, dimensions, and their relationships”. The incubator page listed no Apache release when we checked (12 November 2026), so it isn’t yet a standard you can require of a supplier.

    What this means for the architecture

    Our reading: a prompt or a skill is a copy of a definition, not its home. Copies drift unless they’re generated from the governed source, the way you’d generate a client from an interface definition rather than retype it. Computable definitions want a semantic layer, because it is the one place where the meaning is executed instead of described, and where a question outside it fails visibly. Explanatory definitions want a glossary with a steward, exposed to assistants through retrieval. And the definition that matters most may be the one that tells an assistant what to do when no definition exists.

    Think deeper: Your data platform, your BI tool and your CRM may each offer their own semantic layer, each with an AI assistant on top. If “enrolled student” is defined in all three, you have three sources of truth that started identical. What would keep them identical, and who would notice first if they weren’t?

    What you can do now

    You have finished Part 16. You can show a room why one business question gets several right answers, name the choices hidden in a term, write a definition with both halves (what it is, and how to count it), read any query for what it counts, filters on and dates by, and say where each kind of definition should live and who should own it. You can also say how strong the evidence for semantic layers really is, and who produced most of it.

    Questions to discuss

    In a group session, share your answers, and park anything that needs a longer discussion for the end.

    • Which three numbers in your organisation get different answers depending on who asks, and does anyone know that?
    • Who would be the steward of “enrolled student”, or your equivalent, and do they know yet?
    • Would you rather an assistant refused an undefined question, or answered it with its assumption stated?
    • The AI built into your data platforms will answer these questions whether or not you define anything. What will it use as the definition?

    Export your notes: they include your prediction, your definition and your plan.

    Part 17 starts at step 17.1: the AI assistants that vendors have already switched on in the platforms you own.

    One semantic layer, or one per platform?

    The pattern

    Hub and spoke against point to point, the choice you already know from integration architecture, now applied to meaning. A canonical model in a shared hub has one owner and one change route. Definitions held in each platform are quicker to start and multiply with every platform you add. An interchange format such as Ossie would let the spokes share definitions, once it exists as a standard.

    What is really being decided

    Where the authoritative copy of each metric sits, and what every other copy is: generated from it, synchronised with it, or maintained by hand. And, as ADR-0012 asks at Westmere, who funds the owner, because a shared layer is a shared platform.

    The forces

    • Built in against independent: a platform’s own semantic layer works with its own assistant on day one, and only there. A shared layer works across tools and needs its own team.
    • Upfront modelling: Thoughtworks names upfront modelling as the main cost. It falls before any benefit shows, which is when funding is hardest to find.
    • Coverage: a semantic layer answers only what it models. Every question outside it either gets an error or slips back to generated SQL, and nobody has measured how often that happens in practice.
    • Standards are immature: with Ossie still in incubation, moving definitions between platforms means a migration, so the first platform you model in may decide for you.
    • Who owns a metric: the data team can run the layer, but the meaning of “enrolled” belongs to the Registrar. Splitting technical and business ownership is normal, and it needs writing down.

    Left open

    • Should your first semantic layer cover one domain completely, or your ten most-used numbers across all domains?
    • When a vendor’s assistant can use only that vendor’s semantic layer, is that a reason to choose the vendor’s layer, or a reason to doubt the assistant?
    • Who decides that a metric is important enough to be governed, and what happens to the rest?
    Glossary, dictionary and catalogue, and the new interchange format

    The GDAC definitions. The UK Government Data Architecture Community’s short paper gives each term a definition, a steward and its common misunderstandings, and traces its lineage to the DAMA Data Management Body of Knowledge, among other sources. A business glossary’s entries carry, among other attributes, a name, a definition, synonyms, a term steward, “Common misunderstandings” and lineage. That list is a usable template for the top half of the definition you wrote in step 16.3. A data dictionary “bridges the gap” between content as defined and how it is implemented, and is usually extracted from the database or modelling tool. A data catalogue is an inventory, supported by metadata, that helps people find and judge data.

    DAMA-DMBOK. DAMA’s 2024 revision of its body of knowledge is described as a maintenance release, with AI governance and ethics added, and its site links to a DMBOK 3.0 project. We didn’t read its chapter on metadata, which isn’t freely available, so we don’t summarise it here.

    Open Semantic Interchange (Ossie). Snowflake announced the first version of the specification in January 2026, Apache 2.0 licensed, with a plan to move it to “a neutral, foundation-led governance model”. It entered the Apache Incubator on 22 June 2026. The incubator page lists its initial committers, but not their employers, and no releases. Whether it is adopted beyond its founding vendors is an open question.

    Find the assistants

    Vendors switch AI on inside products you already own, often by default. Find the assistants in an invented landscape, then ask who switched each one on and who knows.

    Step17.1

    Part 17
    The AI already in your platforms
    Time
    12 min
    Last reviewed
    12 November 2026

    Silent sorting first, four minutes, on their own. Then ask the room two questions about the reveal: how many of the eleven did anyone decide, and who would have known about Lowick Tutor? Keep the scope debate short here. It comes back in the last step.

    Westmere’s architecture review board has three AI projects on its list: a student help chatbot, a staff policy assistant and a service desk assistant. Each one went through intake, the process Part 8’s triage skill was built for (step 8.1). Meanwhile, AI has arrived in most of the products Westmere already pays for, and almost none of it went through anything. Nobody hid it. A release note said it was available, and a default setting did the rest.

    This Part is about that second kind of AI. Features change monthly, so it teaches the questions, not the features. The exercises use invented vendors. Real products appear only as dated examples, in their vendors’ own words. One of the three projects runs through this Part too: the service desk assistant, whose first design the board sent back in step 15.3, is at its second stage here, the choice of whether to switch on the assistant built into the service desk product. Step 19.3 follows what ICT prototypes itself.

    Where the evidence stands · checked 12 November 2026

    Solid
    Vendors document AI that is on by default: Microsoft enables Claude models in Copilot by default for most commercial-cloud customers outside the EU, EFTA and UK, and Snowflake grants its AI functions to every user by default (both vendors’ own documentation). Two government trials of an embedded assistant, the UK’s GDS (2025) and Australia’s DTA (2024), warn that it can expose or magnify poor permissions and information management. Prompt injection against an embedded assistant has a published CVE: EchoLeak, CVE-2025-32711, rated 9.3 (Microsoft as assigner).
    Thin
    How often embedded assistants actually surface overshared content: we found no measurement, only the trials’ warnings. Productivity: the UK GDS figure of 26 minutes a day was self-reported, and the UK DBT evaluation found no evidence that time savings led to improved productivity. What happens when several products each run an assistant, in conflicting answers or total cost: we found no credible study.
    Contested
    Whether AI inside a bought product counts as AI for governance. The US OMB memo M-25-22 excludes “any common commercial product within which artificial intelligence is embedded”; Australia’s DTA technical standard includes “systems with embedded AI services and products”. Notice of changes: of the texts we read, only US federal guidance asks vendors for advance notice of new AI features, as something agencies “should consider”, and Microsoft advises against a new risk assessment for its model updates (its blog, updated September 2026).

    1 · Sort Westmere’s landscape

    Here are eleven products Westmere already uses, each with the one clue someone found. Everything is invented, and any resemblance to a real company or product is accidental. For each, decide whether its AI is on, and for whom, from the clue alone. Place all eleven before you open the answer.

    Saved in this browser and included in your exported notes.

    Is it on, who switched it on, and who knows – open after you have placed all eleven
    ProductIs it on?Who switched it onWho knows
    Ecclesmere WorkspaceOn for everyoneThe vendor’s defaultWhoever read the admin notice
    Fenwold RecordsOn for everyone. The tenant move in March made Westmere a “new tenant”The vendor’s default, triggered by a migration nobody linked to AIProbably nobody
    Hollinwick Service DeskOn for some: the pilot teamICT, on purpose, with a change recordICT and the change board
    Mardle HRCan’t tell. The order form says it’s included, not whether it’s onSomeone signed the renewalProcurement, perhaps
    Lowick LearnOn for some, course by courseHundreds of course coordinators, one at a timeEach coordinator knows about their own course
    Tarnbrook MeetOn for everyoneThe vendor’s defaultAnyone who has seen a recap
    Larchfield Data CloudOn for everyoneThe vendor’s default grantWhoever reads the documentation
    Athenbury DocsNot released yetNobody, yet. The default when it arrives is unknownWhoever got the roadmap email
    Tallybrook FinanceOn for everyone, with no settingIt is part of the productFinance, as a feature, not as AI
    Carrelwood DiscoveryOn for everyone, including studentsThe vendorLibrary Services, not ICT
    MergewoodCan’t tell. Each developer decidesIndividual developersNobody centrally

    The pattern to notice is in the third column. Of eleven products, one AI feature went through a decision with a record (Hollinwick). Five were switched on by a vendor default, and two are decided by individuals, one course or one developer at a time. None of those is a decision anyone could be asked to explain.

    2 · Would your governance even see it?

    Even when you find the AI, your rules may not count it. The two government texts in the evidence summary draw the line in opposite places.

    • US OMB M-25-22 (April 2025) excludes “any common commercial product within which artificial intelligence is embedded, such as a word processor or map navigation system”. Its test is whether the product is widely available and has “substantial non-AI purposes or functionalities”. A word processor used mainly for its AI “likely would be covered”.
    • Australia’s DTA technical standard puts in scope “systems with embedded AI services and products” and “publicly available AI tools”, and leaves out “incidental use of AI”.

    Under the first, most of Westmere’s eleven would sit outside the rules. Under the second, most would sit inside, with Tallybrook’s invoice matching as the arguable case. Neither text binds Westmere, which is fictional. Your organisation needs its own line, and it should be written down.

    3 · Your own landscape

    Now list three products you use at work that have added an assistant. Describe them in general terms and include nothing confidential. For each, write who switched it on and who in your organisation would know. “I don’t know” is a useful answer: it’s the finding.

    What this means for the architecture. An application inventory records products. It doesn’t record that a product changed what it does with your data last Tuesday. If embedded AI is to be governed at all, the trigger can’t be “someone requested a new tool”, because nobody did. It has to be an event you can see: a vendor release, a subprocessor change, a setting, a renewal.

    Think deeper: Within a couple of years nearly every product you own may carry an assistant. A register that lists each one becomes a list of everything. Would you rather govern by product (every assistant is assessed), by data (any AI that reads records above a sensitivity level is assessed), or by action (any AI that can send or change something is assessed)? What does each choice miss?

    Is a vendor’s default a decision you made?

    The pattern

    Configuration management and change control for software you don’t run. Software as a service moved the release calendar to the vendor long ago; AI features make each release capable of changing what happens to your data and who can see it. The inventory you already keep (an application portfolio, a CMDB) is the right home, but it records products, not behaviours. NIST’s Generative AI Profile asks organisations to “Inventory all third-party entities with access to organizational content” (GV-6.1-007), which is close, but still a list of companies, not of switches.

    What is really being decided

    What the default is for a new AI feature in a product you own, and who holds the switch. There are three honest positions: accept the vendor’s default and review later, turn new AI features off until assessed, or let each product owner decide within a rule. Each one puts the cost somewhere different. Saying nothing is the first position by default.

    The forces

    • Pace against cadence: vendors release monthly or faster, and review boards meet monthly at best. “Off until assessed” turns the board into a queue.
    • Coverage against signal: registering every assistant makes the register complete and unreadable. Registering by data or action keeps it short, and depends on someone knowing what each feature reads.
    • Distributed switches: where a product lets each course coordinator or developer turn AI on, there is no central switch to hold. Our reading: the decision has to move into the product’s settings policy, or it hasn’t been made.
    • Leverage: a vendor feature added mid-term can usually be turned off but rarely renegotiated until renewal. The US OMB memo’s answer is to ask in the contract for notice “prior to the integration of new AI enhancements, features, or components”.
    • Scope rules that disagree: one government text excludes common products with embedded AI and another includes them. Whichever you adopt decides what your governance can see.

    Left open

    • Who owns the list of AI switches: the application portfolio owner, security, or each product owner?
    • Should a new AI feature default to off in your organisation, and who can say yes quickly when it should be on?
    • When a tenant migration or a renewal changes an AI default as a side effect, whose job is it to notice?
    How to find embedded AI, and why inventories miss it

    Where it shows up. Embedded AI leaves traces in places architects don’t usually read: admin centre notices, release notes, a vendor’s list of subprocessors (where a new AI model provider appears), and order forms at renewal, where AI arrives as a line item. Sign-in and usage logs show who is actually using it, which can differ from what is switched on.

    Measured evidence that inventories miss it. The best example we found is a US audit. In March 2026 the Government Accountability Office reported that several AI-enabled tools the IRS had contracted to help build criminal cases “were not included in the inventory”. Officials said the 2024 inventory requirements were unclear about the inclusion of commercial AI tools, and that this was partly why. That is one agency, but it is an audit, not a survey, and it shows the scope question from section 2 causing a real gap.

    The questions to ask, by source. NIST’s Generative AI Profile (July 2024) asks organisations to update due diligence for AI purchases to “Address solutions that may rely on embedded GAI technologies” (GV-6.1-009). The UK’s AI Playbook (February 2025) lists “an existing technology with bolt-on AI elements (paid or free)” as one way of sourcing AI, so it treats this as a buying decision, not a side effect.

    Not the same as shadow AI. Staff using AI tools the organisation never approved is a different problem, with its own (mostly self-reported) surveys. Embedded AI is approved software that changed under you. The controls overlap, but the owner differs: shadow AI is found by asking people, embedded AI by reading vendors.

    Read more

    • GAO-26-107522: IRS actions needed on AI (March 2026)
    • NIST AI 600-1: Generative AI Profile (July 2024)
    • AI Playbook for the UK Government (February 2025)
    • DTA technical standard: introduction and scope
    On by default: three examples in the vendors’ own words

    Dated examples, vendors’ own statements, checked 12 November 2026. These describe what each vendor says its product does. They are not evidence that anything went wrong, and they will change. Confirm them in your own tenant.

    • Microsoft 365 Copilot. Microsoft’s page on Claude models says: “Microsoft enables Claude models on by default for most customers in commercial cloud (excluding EU/EFTA and UK).” Admins turn this off under the “AI providers operating as Microsoft subprocessors” setting. The same page says Anthropic models labelled “with Data Retention” are off by default; if enabled, Anthropic stores most inputs and outputs “for up to 30 days”, under Anthropic’s terms rather than Microsoft’s. Microsoft’s privacy page adds that “Models provided by Anthropic as a subprocessor are currently excluded from the EU Data Boundary.”
    • Snowflake Cortex AI functions. Snowflake’s access page says: “By default, the USE AI FUNCTIONS privilege is granted to the PUBLIC role.” The PUBLIC role is granted to every user. The page gives the command to remove it: REVOKE USE AI FUNCTIONS ON ACCOUNT FROM ROLE PUBLIC;
    • Snowflake cross-region inference. For new accounts in new organisations in commercial regions created after 9 March 2026, “ANY_REGION is the default”, which lets requests be processed in any supported region. Snowflake says “Your customer data is not persisted in the processing region”.

    None of these is hidden. Each is documented, has an admin control and comes with a reason (model choice, convenience, capacity). The point for an architect is that the documented default is the setting you are running until someone changes it, so reading the documentation is part of the decision.

    Read more

    • Claude models from Anthropic in Microsoft Online Services (Microsoft Learn)
    • Data, privacy and security for Microsoft Copilot (Microsoft Learn)
    • Cortex AI functions: privileges and access (Snowflake)
    • Cross-region inference (Snowflake)
