    Assess one assistant

    Read a confident vendor fact sheet for the assistant in Westmere’s student records platform, then check it against twelve questions drawn from published government question sets.

    Step17.2

    Part 17
    The AI already in your platforms
    Time
    15 min
    Last reviewed
    12 November 2026

    Ask for a one-line gut reaction before anyone opens the questions, and hold people to it. When pooling, start with question 5 and question 7: they’re the two where a confident sentence sounds most like an answer. If a vendor or procurement person is in the room, ask them which questions vendors answer most readily.

    Step 17.1 found Fenwold Assist switched on in Westmere’s student records platform by a tenant move. Student Services likes it. Before the architecture review board decides whether to leave it on, someone has asked the vendor for information, and this fact sheet came back. Fenwold is invented, and so is everything in it.

    1 · Twelve questions, from published sources

    You don’t need a new questionnaire. Several government bodies have published the questions already. We drew twelve from five of them, chosen for an assistant inside a product you own, and grouped them by what they protect.

    The full sheet credits each question to its source, and adds what to capture in writing, following the National AI Centre’s format. Keep it: you’ll reuse it.

    Now mark each question against the fact sheet. Answered means you could write the answer into a contract. Partly answered means some of it is there. A claim with no detail means the sheet says something reassuring that you couldn’t check. Not answered means it’s silent.

    Saved in this browser and included in your exported notes.

    2 · Optional: let an assistant mark it

    In a new chat, paste the fact sheet and the question sheet, then ask: “For each of the twelve questions, does this fact sheet answer it? Answer Answered, Partly, Claim or Not answered, and quote the line you relied on.” Compare its marks with yours. Watch for two things: does it accept a confident sentence such as “Built-in protection against prompt injection” as an answer, and does it mark a question Partly because the sheet mentions the topic, as it does for actions and updates, without answering it? Both are the agreeable reading from step 3.6, and a person under deadline makes the same mistakes. Results vary by assistant and version. Everything here is invented; don’t paste real vendor documents unless your organisation allows it.

    Our marks – open after you have placed all twelve
    QuestionOur markWhy
    1 TrainingA claim“Never uses your data to train our models.” Assist runs on models from unnamed “AI partners”. Are theirs covered? And is it “now or in the future”?
    2 LocationPartlyRecords are stored in your region, but requests “may be processed using our global AI capacity”. That is an answer, and a worrying one: it says processing can leave the region without saying where to.
    3 Third partiesNot answered“Leading large language models from our AI partners” names nobody.
    4 Off switchPartlyOn or off for the whole institution. Nothing about turning off writes, or one group, and the default for new tenants is on. If you marked this Answered for the narrow question, that’s defensible.
    5 PermissionsA claim“Only shows staff what they are already allowed to see.” Allowed to see one record at a time, or a list of every student with a medical certificate? Nothing on its index or on what it stores.
    6 ActionsNot answeredIt drafts emails to students and updates case notes. The sheet doesn’t say whether a person approves either.
    7 Hidden instructionsA claim“Assist’s safety filter blocks malicious instructions”, in a product that reads documents students upload. The UK NCSC’s advice is to “Beware any that claim they can ‘stop’ prompt injection”.
    8 LogsA claim“Activity logging is available.” Which activity, for how long, on which licence?
    9 IncidentsNot answeredSilent.
    10 ChangesNot answeredWorse than silent: “New capabilities are delivered automatically, with no work for your IT team.” That describes the absence of notice as a benefit.
    11 ExitNot answeredSilent on data after exit, and on whether Fenwold works with Assist off.
    12 EvidenceA claim“40% faster” from a customer survey, and an ISO/IEC 42001 certificate, which covers the vendor’s management system. Whether it says anything about this feature is an open question.

    Answered in full: none. Two partly, five claims, five silences. The fact sheet isn’t dishonest. It answers the questions a buyer usually asks first, in the most reassuring words available, and that’s why a written question sheet beats reading one.

    3 · Write what you would send back

    You can’t ask all twelve again and expect a better answer. Choose the three that would block switching on until they are answered in writing, and word each so that a slogan can’t answer it. “Is your AI secure?” invites a slogan. “List every action Assist can take without a person approving it” doesn’t.

    What this means for the architecture. The fact sheet describes a product; your question is about a system: Westmere’s permissions, the vendor’s index and an unnamed model provider, joined by contracts. Questions 3, 5 and 10 are where those layers meet, which is why vendors find them hardest to answer and why they matter most.

    Think deeper: Westmere’s records permissions were designed for screens. A student adviser can open any student in their faculty, one at a time, because that’s how advising works. Assist can answer “which students in my faculty have a disability support plan and a failed unit?” in one go. Every record in that answer is one the adviser could open. Is it the same permission? If not, where should the new limit live: in Fenwold’s roles, in Assist’s settings, or in a rule nobody can enforce?

    When are contract terms part of the architecture?

    The pattern

    Supplier assurance and the shared responsibility model from cloud, with one more party. Cloud taught architects to draw the line between what the provider secures and what the customer configures. An embedded assistant adds a model provider behind the vendor, often unnamed, whose changes reach you through a contract you aren’t party to. NIST lists this as its own risk: “Value Chain and Component Integration”.

    What is really being decided

    Which unanswered questions block switching on, and which you accept on the vendor’s word and monitor. That split is a design decision, not a procurement detail, because the answers to questions 2, 5, 6 and 10 set where data goes, what the assistant can reach and do, and whether the system you approved is still the one running next month. If they aren’t in the contract, they aren’t controls.

    The forces

    • Leverage: the best time to ask is before signing, and features arrive mid-term. The US OMB memo’s answer is a clause requiring notice before new AI features. Few organisations outside US federal government have one.
    • Depth against reach: twelve targeted questions get read. The Cloud Security Alliance’s AI-CAIQ has 320 questions, which suits a full assessment and few renewals.
    • Attestation against testing: a certificate or a survey is cheap for both sides. The National AI Centre asks for “Evidence of testing, not just assurances”, which costs the vendor effort and you time to read.
    • Permissions you inherit: “respects your permissions” moves the risk to you. If Westmere’s permissions are too broad, the assistant is faithful to a mistake.
    • The supplier behind the supplier: you can require notice of a new subprocessor, but you can’t test the model provider, and its changes arrive as the vendor’s release.

    Left open

    • Who decides that an unanswered question blocks switching on: the product owner, security, or the architecture review board?
    • Should the question sheet be re-run on every model change, or only on new features, and who would notice either?
    • Does an ISO/IEC 42001 certificate held by a vendor say anything about one feature inside one product? We couldn’t check, and it’s worth asking your auditors.
    The question sets compared, and what each covers
    • ASD’s ACSC with international partners, “Engaging with artificial intelligence” (January 2024). Written for both self-hosted and third-party AI. Its questions are headings, each with mitigations, for example “understand if your organisation’s inputs will be used to retrain the AI system’s model” and “Log and monitor inputs to the AI system”. It also suggests logging “high frequency, repetitive prompts”, which can signal automated prompt injection.
    • NSA AI Security Center and partners, “Deploying AI Systems Securely” (April 2024). Explicitly “not applicable for organizations who are not deploying AI systems themselves and instead are leveraging AI systems deployed by others”. So it doesn’t govern an embedded assistant, but two of its lines make good questions: “Require the primary developer of the AI system to provide a threat model for their system”, and “Collect logs to cover inputs, outputs, intermediate states, and errors”.
    • NIST AI 600-1, Generative AI Profile (July 2024). Its governance actions name embedded AI in procurement (GV-6.1-009), ask for an inventory of third parties with access to your content (GV-6.1-007) and for contracts that consider “GAI system changes over time (e.g., fine-tuning, drift, decay)” and request “Notification and disclosure for serious incidents” (GV-6.2-007). NIST’s page says the framework is being revised.
    • US OMB M-25-22 (April 2025). Excludes most embedded AI, as step 17.1 showed, but its contract terms travel well: prohibit training on your inputs and outputs “absent explicit agency consent”, ask for notice before new AI features, and ask for “clear data and model portability practices”.
    • Australia’s National AI Centre, “Questions to ask AI suppliers” (2026). Short, plain and built for buyers. Each section has questions, what to check for and what to capture. It is the closest thing to a ready-made sheet, and most of our twelve come from it.
    • Cloud Security Alliance, AI Controls Matrix v1.1 (July 2026). “247 control objectives across 18 domains”, with an AI-CAIQ of 320 questions and guidance by role. An industry body with vendor members; we didn’t open the questionnaire itself.

    Two we couldn’t read today: ISO/IEC 42001 (the standard isn’t freely available) and EDUCAUSE’s HECVAT for higher education (its pages were blocked). If your sector has its own questionnaire, map it to the four groups before adding questions.

    Read more

    • Questions to ask AI suppliers (National AI Centre, 2026)
    • Engaging with artificial intelligence (ASD’s ACSC and partners, 2024)
    • Deploying AI Systems Securely (NSA and partners, 2024)
    • NIST AI 600-1: Generative AI Profile (2024)
    • OMB M-25-22: Driving Efficient Acquisition of AI in Government (2025)
    • AI Controls Matrix v1.1 (Cloud Security Alliance, 2026)
    Prompt injection inside the product: two documented cases

    Question 7 matters because Fenwold Assist reads what students upload. Two published cases show the same pattern in assistants built into products.

    • EchoLeak (CVE-2025-32711), Microsoft 365 Copilot. Microsoft, as the CVE’s assigner, describes it as “Ai command injection in M365 Copilot allows an unauthorized attacker to disclose information over a network”, rated 9.3 (critical), published 11 June 2025. Reddy and Gujral’s paper describes “remote, unauthenticated data exfiltration via a single crafted email”, chaining several bypasses of Microsoft’s defences. They call it the first real-world zero-click prompt injection exploit in a production system; that is the authors’ claim. We read the abstract only.
    • ForcedLeak, Salesforce Agentforce. Reported by Noma Labs, a security vendor, in September 2025. Hidden instructions in a web-to-lead form ran when staff later asked the agent about the lead, and data could be sent to an allowed domain that had expired, which Noma bought for $5. Noma reported it on 28 July 2025 and says Salesforce implemented Trusted URLs Enforcement on 8 September 2025 and re-secured the domain. This is the researcher’s account.

    Both were fixed. The lesson isn’t about either vendor. It’s that an assistant which reads outsiders’ text and can send anything anywhere is the combination to look for, whatever the product. The UK NCSC’s position (December 2025) is that “prompt injection attacks may never be totally mitigated”, that a model is an “inherently confusable deputy”, and that design should favour “deterministic (non-LLM) safeguards that constrain the actions of the system”. Part 11 tested this on a skill (step 11.3). For an embedded assistant you can’t change the design, so the questions are what it reads, what it can do next, and which of those you can switch off.

    Read more

    • Prompt injection is not SQL injection (NCSC-UK, December 2025)
    • CVE-2025-32711 (Microsoft Security Response Center)
    • EchoLeak (Reddy and Gujral, arXiv, 2025)
    • ForcedLeak (Noma Labs, September 2025)

    Which assistant answers?

    One question, three platform assistants, three numbers. Work out why they differ, which is authoritative for what, and what each answer should have told its reader.

    Step17.3

    Part 17
    The AI already in your platforms
    Time
    12 min
    Last reviewed
    12 November 2026

    Take a show of hands on which number people would forward before anyone opens the diagnosis. Most rooms split between B, because it looks careful, and C, because it names a document. The point to land is that authority belongs to a kind of question, not to a tool.

    Monday morning. The Dean of Health’s executive assistant needs one number for a meeting at ten: how many first-year Nursing students have withdrawn this semester? She has three assistants within reach, all switched on by their vendors, all answering from inside a product Westmere already owns. She asks all three.

    1 · Why three numbers?

    Before you open the diagnosis, write down for each answer what it read, how fresh that was, what it counted and what the asker could see through it.

    The diagnosis – open after you have written yours
    A · Records (37)B · Reporting (22)C · Office suite (41)
    SourceLive student recordsThe Student Load model in the reporting platformA draft slide deck in a faculty file share
    FreshnessThis minuteLast night’s load, as at 8 NovemberUnknown. Draft v3, last edited in October
    What it countedWithdrawn statuses in first-year Nursing units. A student who dropped one unit and stayed counts, and so does a Midwifery student taking a Nursing unitStudents who withdrew from the course after the census date. Earlier withdrawals are treated as never enrolled for reportingWhatever the deck’s author counted. The deck doesn’t say, and its total may include deferrals
    What she could seeEvery record in the faculty, and it offered to list the students by nameAggregates onlyA draft shared with “Everyone in Health” that was never meant for her
    What did it tell her?Nothing about its definitionIts source, date and definitionIts source document, nothing else

    None of the three is wrong about what it read. B is the only one that told its reader enough to judge it. A offered names to someone who asked for a count, which is the permissions problem from step 4.5: it showed nothing she couldn’t open, and still more than she needed. C found a file that was shared too widely and gave its number the authority of a citation.

    2 · Authoritative for what?

    Asking “which assistant is right?” has no answer. “Which source is authoritative for this question?” does. Place each question with the assistant whose source should answer it, or with “None yet” if no source should be trusted without its owner.

    Our placements – open after you have placed all six
    QuestionOur placementWhy
    The official count for the Dean’s reportBA governed model with a stated definition and date. Only if the faculty has agreed that “after census, by course” is what it means by withdrawn, which is the point of Part 16.
    Whether one named student is enrolled todayAThe system of record, live. A nightly copy or a deck can only be out of date.
    What the faculty told its retention committeeC, with careThe deck is authoritative only for what it says, and only if v3 is the version presented. Otherwise ask the faculty.
    The figure for a funding submissionNone yetA number that leaves the organisation needs its owner’s sign-off on definition and date. B is where the owner would start.
    Which students an adviser should call this weekAIt needs names, current status and unit-level detail, and an adviser’s access.
    Whether withdrawals are up on last yearBOnly a model that holds both years under one definition can compare them. If last year’s figure used another definition, the answer is “None yet”.

    3 · What every answer should say about itself

    The executive assistant couldn’t have known any of this from the answers she got. Write the few lines you would require every platform assistant to show under a number, so that a reader could judge it in ten seconds.

    One version

    Answered from: system, dataset or document. As at: date and time of the data. Counted as: the definition used, linked to where it is governed. Your view: what this answer could see as you. For official figures: the authoritative source, if this isn’t it.

    Answer B already shows the first three. Few products let you require this, so it belongs on the list of things to ask vendors for, with the questions from step 17.2, and in any assistant Westmere builds itself.

    Where the definitions behind “Counted as” should live, and who owns them, is the subject of step 16.5. This step adds the platform-scale version of the same problem: every product with an assistant brings its own index and, silently, its own definitions.

    4 · Optional: ask an assistant to reconcile them

    In a new chat, paste the three answers and ask: “Which of these numbers is correct?” Then note what it did. Did it pick one, average them, explain why they might differ, or ask what you meant by “withdrawn”? Assistants differ here, and the same one can differ between runs. A reconciling assistant has the same problem as the three it reconciles: it can only reason about what it was given. Everything here is invented.

    What this means for the architecture. Each embedded assistant inherits its product’s index, permissions and definitions. Switch on five and you have five versions of the truth, each permission-trimmed and each confident. The architecture question isn’t which assistant is best. It is which source is authoritative for each kind of question, and how a reader finds out which one answered.

    Think deeper: Should the office suite assistant be allowed to answer a reporting question at all? Blocking it means building or buying something that recognises the kind of question. Allowing it means accepting answers from whatever deck it finds. A third path is to let it answer and require it to say where official figures live. Which would your organisation actually maintain, and who would own the list of question types?

    Which assistant is the front door?

    The pattern

    System of record against systems of engagement, and master data management’s old rule: one authoritative source per fact, with every copy labelled as a copy. Platform assistants are new systems of engagement that answer in the voice of a system of record. A front door that routes by kind of question is the familiar API gateway or channel pattern, applied to natural language.

    What is really being decided

    Whether Westmere accepts many front doors (every product’s assistant answers whatever it’s asked) or designates which assistant answers which kind of question, and how. The first is free and fragments the truth. The second needs someone to define question types, keep the routing current and own the edge cases. Most organisations will end up somewhere between: many doors, with a few kinds of question (official figures, policy rulings) that every door must hand on.

    The forces

    • Convenience against authority: people ask whatever assistant is open. A rule that says “ask the reporting platform” loses to a button already on screen.
    • Each assistant is good at home: inside its own product it is permission-trimmed, current and in context. The trouble starts when it answers questions whose authority lives elsewhere.
    • Copies multiply: connectors that let one product’s assistant search another’s content add indexes, and each index is another copy, under another vendor’s terms.
    • Overlapping cost: paying for assistants in five products may buy the same capability five times. We found no credible measurement of this; it’s our reading, and worth checking in your own licence bill.
    • Testing what you don’t control: you can test that two assistants agree today. Either vendor can change its model tomorrow.

    Left open

    • Who decides which assistant answers which kind of question, and is that an architecture decision or a data governance one?
    • Should a platform assistant be blocked from answering questions outside its product, if the vendor even allows that?
    • How would you notice that two assistants have started to disagree?
    Five reasons platform assistants disagree
    • Source. Each embedded assistant searches its own product’s index. The records assistant can’t see the warehouse; the office assistant can’t see either, but can see decks about them.
    • Freshness. Live data, a nightly load and a document last edited weeks ago are all “current” to the assistant reading them.
    • Definition. “Withdrawn” by unit, by course, before or after census. On ambiguous database questions, Saparina and Lapata’s AMBROSIA benchmark (NeurIPS 2024) found that “even the most advanced models struggle to identify and interpret ambiguity in questions”. In practice they tend to pick one reading and answer it. Part 16 works through this (step 16.2).
    • Permissions. Each assistant is trimmed to what the asker can open in that product, so two people asking the same assistant can get different answers, and both are working as designed.
    • Sampling. The same model, asked the same question twice, can give different outputs. Thinking Machines Lab ran one prompt 1,000 times at temperature 0 and got 80 unique completions (September 2025, an AI lab’s own test). Part 16’s first step covers it in a Going deeper panel (step 16.1).

    What has and hasn’t been measured. We found no credible study of what happens when several products in one organisation each run an assistant: how often they conflict, which one people believe, or what the total costs. The nearest practitioner advice runs the other way, towards reuse: Thoughtworks’ Technology Radar (Vol 35, November 2026) puts Microsoft Copilot Retrieval API at Trial because it “applies security trimming based on the calling user and respects access controls defined within the tenant”, letting a team reuse the platform’s index rather than build its own. That reduces copies; it doesn’t settle which source is authoritative.

    Read more

    • Thoughtworks Technology Radar, Vol 35 (November 2026)
    • Step 16.5: where a definition can live, and who it reaches
    “Respects your permissions”: why that is the problem, not the fix

    Every embedded assistant we read about promises to show people only what they can already open. Microsoft’s privacy page, for example, says Copilot “only surfaces organizational data to which individual users have at least view permissions”, and asks customers to use the permission models in their Microsoft 365 services to get access right (vendor’s own statement, checked 12 November 2026). That is the right design, and it hands the problem straight back to you.

    • The UK’s cross-government Copilot experiment (GDS, 20,000 staff, late 2024) found that its “ability to search and query using a user’s access may highlight issues when users have access to files they shouldn’t”.
    • Australia’s whole-of-government trial evaluation (DTA, 2024) found that “Copilot may magnify poor data security and information management practices”, and says agencies “must configure their information systems, permissions, and processes to safely accommodate generative AI products”.
    • Microsoft’s own deployment blueprint names remediating oversharing first among the steps to a secure and governed foundation for Copilot (vendor guidance).

    What isn’t known. Nobody we found has measured how often embedded assistants actually surface overshared content in practice. The trials give warnings, not rates. Step 4.5 explains the underlying rule (the model must never see what the asker couldn’t open), and step 11.4 turns it into a design. For an embedded assistant, the only lever left is your own permissions, and the work of tightening them is usually the real cost of switching on.

    Read more

    • Microsoft 365 Copilot Experiment: Cross-Government Findings Report (GDS, 2025)
    • Whole-of-government Copilot trial: summary of evaluation findings (DTA, 2024)
    • Secure and governed data foundation for Copilot (Microsoft Learn)

    Switch on, buy or build

    Place nine Westmere cases as switch on, buy, build or not yet, compare with a decision ladder, then write your if-then plan and discuss.

    Step17.4

    Part 17
    The AI already in your platforms
    Time
    14 min
    Last reviewed
    12 November 2026

    Five minutes of silent sorting, then compare. The student chatbot and the Fenwold writes usually split the room. Leave ten minutes for the if-then plan and the discussion questions, and read two or three plans aloud before the close.

    The choice for an AI capability is rarely “AI or not”. It is usually one of four: switch on what a product you own already offers, buy a separate product, build your own, or not yet. The first is the cheapest to start and the easiest to forget. “Not yet” is a real decision with a reason and a date, not a refusal.

    1 · Place the cases

    Here are nine Westmere cases, all invented, built on the products from step 17.1. Place each one before you open the ladder.

    Saved in this browser and included in your exported notes.

    A ladder, and our placements – open after you have placed all nine
    CaseOur placementWhy
    Tarnbrook Meet recapsSwitch onThe meetings already live in the product, and the controls that matter (retention, confidential meetings) exist. Set them first.
    Ecclesmere Helper for all staffNot yet1,900 overshared files are exactly what the government trials warned about. Fix sharing, then switch on, perhaps for a pilot group first.
    Service desk how-to answersSwitch onThe articles live in Hollinwick and the pilot is running. Configure it first: step 15.2 found the product can’t yet filter answers by audience, so staff-only articles stay in a knowledge base the assistant isn’t connected to. If the agent starts acting on tickets, Part 20’s containment applies (step 20.4).
    Student help chatbotBuildNo single product sees the Policy Library, course rules and the student’s record. This is the shared policy service proposed in the ADR from Part 7 (step 7.4), and it needs the funded owner that ADR-0012 requires.
    Mardle InsightsNot yetQuestions 1 and 2 on the sheet (training and location) are unanswered. Turn it off and ask in writing.
    Larchfield survey commentsSwitch on, narrowlyThe capability is in the platform where the data already is. Revoke the AI privilege from every role, then grant it to Planning and Analytics.
    Fenwold writes to studentsNot yetIt reads text that students write and can send email. That is the combination from step 17.2, with no answer on approvals. Reading could go on while writes wait.
    Lecture captionsBuyNothing Westmere owns does it, specialist products do, and building speech recognition is nobody’s idea of core work.
    Review board assistantBuildThree sources, one team, a funded owner and a small audience. A skill with read-only connectors (Parts 9 to 11) may be enough.

    Two placements are close calls. The student chatbot could be “buy” if a product covered all three sources and could keep the 38 staff-only policies away from students; the ADR’s sources say two of the three vendor products couldn’t filter restricted documents by audience. Fenwold’s writes could be “switch on” with every email held for approval, if the vendor can show that holding works. Notice what decided both: not the AI, but permissions, sources and who approves.

    What this means for the architecture. “Switch on” isn’t free. Its cost moves into work that doesn’t look like AI: tightening permissions, revoking default grants, reading the vendor’s answers, and setting a review date. Count that work when you compare it with buying or building, and send anything that reaches “not yet” through the same intake as any other AI request (step 8.1).

    Think deeper: Westmere is funding a service desk assistant as a project, and Hollinwick’s own agent now does part of the same job. The project’s first design proposed simply using it, and went back to its authors with questions (step 15.3). Whoever owns the project now has every reason to build; whoever owns the Hollinwick contract has every reason to switch on. Who should decide when a vendor’s feature overlaps a funded project, and what evidence would settle it?

    What you can do now

    You have finished Part 17. You can find the AI already running in your platforms and say who switched it on, assess an embedded assistant with twelve questions drawn from published question sets, explain why three platform assistants give three answers and which source should answer which question, and place a capability as switch on, buy, build or not yet.

    Questions to discuss

    In a group session, share your answers, and park anything that needs a longer discussion for the end.

    • Which product in your landscape switched on AI most recently, and who found out first?
    • Should a new AI feature in a product you own default to off in your organisation? Who could say yes quickly?
    • Which of the twelve questions does your procurement process already ask, and which would be new?
    • When an assistant’s number reaches a board paper, what would you want to know about where it came from?
    • Should “not yet” come with an expiry date, and who reviews it?

    Export your notes: they include your sorts, your three blocking questions and your plan.

    Part 18 starts at step 18.1: using AI to draw models and diagrams, and checking what it invents.

    Who holds the switch, and for how long?

    The pattern

    Reuse before buy before build, the principle Part 22 tests (step 22.1), with a twist: the thing you reuse keeps changing. A switched-on feature is a dependency you don’t version, on a release schedule you don’t set. The closest familiar pattern is a managed service with a change calendar, except that most AI features don’t come with one.

    What is really being decided

    Who holds each switch, what a “yes” is valid for, and what reopens it. A one-off approval assumes the thing approved stays the same. An embedded assistant doesn’t, so the decision needs a review date and a trigger: a model change, a new action, a new data source, a new subprocessor. Without those, the original decision quietly becomes permission for whatever comes next.

    The forces

    • Speed of value against assurance: switching on gets value this week. Assessing first delays it, and people will use the button anyway if it’s there.
    • Hidden cost of switching on: permissions clean-up, default grants and reading vendor terms are real work, usually unfunded because “the feature was free”.
    • Lock-in through use: once staff rely on an assistant, turning it off has a cost, and the value builds up in the vendor’s index, not yours.
    • Changes you didn’t make: vendors update models on their schedule. Microsoft’s blog on Copilot model changes (updated September 2026), for example, advises customers against a brand-new risk assessment for its model updates; your policy may say otherwise, and only one of you decides.
    • Overlap with funded work: a vendor feature that does part of a project’s job can save money or strand an investment. Neither the vendor nor the project team is neutral.

    Left open

    • What reopens a switch-on decision in your organisation, and who is told when it happens?
    • When an AI feature that was included becomes a paid add-on, who decides whether to pay, keep it off or replace it?
    • Should the architecture review board see every switch-on, or only the ones that reach records, actions or outsiders’ text?
    What three government evaluations found when they switched one on

    The best public evidence on switching on an embedded assistant comes from three government evaluations of the same product. They are worth reading for their methods as much as their findings.

    • UK Government Digital Service (June 2025). 20,000 staff from 30 September to 31 December 2024. Participants reported saving an average of 26 minutes a day, calculated from the middle of self-reported ranges. The report also warned about access to files people shouldn’t have.
    • Australia’s Digital Transformation Agency (2024). A whole-of-government trial. Its summary carries the warning quoted in step 17.3: Copilot can magnify poor data security and information management, so agencies must configure permissions and processes for generative AI.
    • UK Department for Business and Trade (August 2025). 1,000 licences, October to December 2024, about 70% to volunteers and 30% to a random sample, evaluated without a counterfactual. It “did not find evidence that time savings have led to improved productivity”. Some tasks, such as scheduling and generating images, took longer, and “Respondents reported observing hallucinations”. A value-for-money assessment was still under way.

    How to read them. These are evaluations of one vendor’s product in government settings, not of embedded AI in general. Self-reported time saved is a weak basis for a business case, and the DBT report is explicit that it found no productivity evidence. Our reading: the consistent finding across all three isn’t about productivity at all. It is that the product exposes whatever is wrong with permissions and information management, so that is where switching on starts.

    Read more

    • Microsoft 365 Copilot Experiment: Cross-Government Findings Report (GDS, 2025)
    • Whole-of-government Copilot trial: summary of evaluation findings (DTA, 2024)
    • Microsoft 365 Copilot pilot: DBT evaluation report (2025)
    Model changes you didn’t make

    Models change under named products. Chen, Zaharia and Zou compared two versions of the same named model three months apart in 2023: GPT-4’s accuracy at telling prime numbers from composites went from 84% in March to 51% in June. That is one task on an old model, and step 21.4 sets out the argument that its habits changed more than its ability. Either way, “the same product” can behave differently from one month to the next.

    Dated example, vendor’s own statement, checked 12 November 2026. Microsoft says the models behind Copilot “are regularly updated and enhanced” and that updates “don’t change your security, privacy, or compliance settings”. Its blog on foundation model changes (August 2025, updated September 2026) says updates are “generally rolled out to users in phases”, that “Customers do not need to make changes to their environment”, and that “we advise against performing a brand-new risk assessment”, while noting that some organisations’ policies require one and offering documentation for them. The post says it is not a contractual commitment.

    What the question sets ask for. The National AI Centre asks suppliers “How are updates managed and communicated?” and “Can we test or review changes before they are applied?”. NIST AI 600-1 (GV-6.2-007) asks you to consider “GAI system changes over time” in contracts. The US OMB memo goes furthest: agencies should consider requiring notice before new AI features, and are encouraged to require vendors “to meet performance standards before deploying a new version” or to roll back if a new version fails them. We found no common norm for advance notice of model changes inside software as a service outside US federal guidance, and there it is “should consider”.

    What you can do without the vendor. Keep a small set of your own test questions with known answers for each assistant you rely on, and rerun them on a schedule and whenever a release note mentions a model. Part 5’s method applies (step 5.3), and Part 21 plans for the day a model is retired.

    Read more

    • How is ChatGPT’s behavior changing over time? (Chen, Zaharia and Zou, arXiv)
    • OMB M-25-22 (April 2025)
    • Questions to ask AI suppliers (National AI Centre, 2026)

    From description to diagram

    Turn a written system brief into a container diagram as text, predict where it will go wrong, and read the text whether or not you can render it.

    Step18.1

    Part 18
    AI for models and diagrams
    Time
    12 min
    Last reviewed
    12 November 2026

    Get predictions written before anyone sends a prompt. Not everyone will be able to see their diagram drawn, and that’s fine: the exercise is reading the text. Keep each person’s output for step 18.2, and don’t open the reference until most of the room has an output.

    A container diagram used to take an afternoon with a drawing tool. Now it takes a paragraph and a prompt, and comes back in seconds as text that a tool can draw. That text is the useful part. You can read it, check it against rules, keep it in version control and see exactly what changed. The catch is that a generated diagram looks finished long before it’s right.

    Where the evidence stands · checked 12 November 2026

    Solid
    Generated models can parse cleanly and still be wrong in meaning. Several small studies agree: every class diagram in NOMAD was syntactically correct while, with a single prompt, relationships scored lowest (Giannouris and Ananiadou, MODELSWARD 2026), and architecture views generated from code “consistently exhibit granularity mismatches” (Sathvika et al., preprint 2026). Every one of the ten models tested by Kourani et al. (2025, workshop paper) at times drifted back to the familiar process when the input described an unusual one.
    Thin
    How much rules in the prompt help: few-shot examples cut clarity failures from 40.0% to 30.8%, as scored by an LLM judge, which the authors class among “marginal improvements” (Sathvika et al.); telling a model to stick to the input about halved the clear cases of drift and can “mitigate, but not eliminate” it (Kourani et al.). For capability maps there is one case study with no numbers (Jung and Wienke, 2024). We found no study of generated C4 diagrams scored by human experts against a reference.
    Contested
    Which model or setup works best. Results swing widely and most tested models are now a generation or two old: in one study, four models, each run as a single agent, scored between 28% and 100% on a rule check for keeping a C4 diagram at the right level, and their diagram text compiled between 58% and 97% of the time (Szczepanik and Chudziak, HICSS 2026); in another, two of the authors rated a general coding agent as missing the right level of detail on 82% of 22 repositories and their own purpose-built agent on 14% (Sathvika et al.).

    Most of this evidence is preprints and workshop or conference papers with small samples: five briefs, 22 repositories, four processes. Treat every number as a sign of direction, not a rate to plan with. Two popular claims need care. “Mermaid’s C4 diagrams are now stable” didn’t check out: the “experimental” notice was removed on 30 October 2026 in a documentation tidy-up that removed such notices from every diagram type not in beta, and the page still lists Legend as unfinished. Our reading: no longer labelled experimental, not declared stable. “Claude and ChatGPT render Mermaid” is documented only in part. OpenAI’s help centre lists “Mermaid diagrams” among the code blocks that may offer a Preview in ChatGPT, depending on device, plan and workspace settings. Anthropic’s lists “mermaid diagrams” among the artifacts Claude can create. Both are the vendors’ own pages, checked 12 November 2026, and neither names a Mermaid version or says which diagram types work. Third-party guides say more, and they aren’t evidence.

    1 · Read the brief

    This is a fictional system at Westmere University: the shared service that answers policy questions for the three planned assistants, owned by Digital Platforms. Read it once, slowly. Notice anything that works differently from how such systems usually work.

    2 · Predict

    You’re about to ask for a C4 container diagram with no further guidance. A container in C4 is an application or a data store that runs on its own: a web app, a worker, a database. Before you send it, write down what you expect to go wrong.

    3 · Ask for the diagram

    Open a new chat and send this, with the brief pasted in place of the last line. Everything in it is invented, so it’s safe to paste. Don’t use real system details unless your organisation has approved the assistant for them.

    Draw a C4 container diagram of the system described below, as Mermaid flowchart text. Give only the diagram text. [paste the brief]
    Why a flowchart, and not Mermaid’s C4 syntax?

    Mermaid’s flowchart is the first diagram type in its documentation, carries no beta or experimental notice, and is the type GitHub’s own Mermaid example uses. It knows nothing about C4, so the C4 rules have to go into the labels, which is what step 18.2 asks for. Mermaid also has a C4 syntax (C4Container), compatible with C4-PlantUML. It’s worth trying, with two limits on its own page: Legend, tags and links are “unfinished features”, and layout is set by “the order in which statements are written”. Its experimental label went only in October 2026. C4’s notation guidance says every diagram should have a key, so the missing Legend matters. If you try it, keep the flowchart version too and compare what each gets wrong.

    4 · See it drawn, or read it

    Reading the text is the exercise. Drawing it is a bonus, so try it only where you’re allowed to:

    • In your assistant. Some assistants may draw it in the chat or a side panel. OpenAI’s help centre says a code block may offer a Preview in ChatGPT, with “Mermaid diagrams” among the supported types, depending on your device, plan and workspace settings. Anthropic’s help centre lists “mermaid diagrams” among the artifacts Claude can create. Those are the vendors’ own statements, checked 12 November 2026, and neither says which Mermaid version it runs. Whatever you see drawn, check it against the text.
    • In GitHub, if your organisation uses it. GitHub’s documentation says Markdown supports “four different syntaxes: mermaid, geoJSON, topoJSON, and ASCII STL” in issues, pull requests, wikis and Markdown files, and tells you to check which Mermaid version it runs. That’s GitHub’s own statement, checked 12 November 2026.
    • In an editor your organisation allows. Many editors have Mermaid previews. A web-based editor sends your text to someone else’s site, so check before you paste anything that isn’t invented.

    No renderer? Read the text. Each box is one line with a name in brackets. Each arrow is a line with -->, and a label, if it has one, sits between bars, -->|"label"|, or in quotes before the arrow, -- "label" -->. Count the boxes, the arrows and the labelled arrows. Then find every box that isn’t named in the brief.

    A reference diagram: open it once you have your own

    This is our version, written by hand from the brief. It isn’t the only right answer, but every box and arrow traces to a sentence in the brief. We checked that it parses and renders with Mermaid’s own command-line tool.

    Two details in the brief carry the design, so check that your output kept them. The Index updater waits for change notices rather than running on a timetable. And the Answers API checks the asker’s groups with Westmere Identity before it searches, so the model provider only ever receives passages the asker may see. That second detail is how the service keeps staff-only documents away from students, the first driver in the decision brief that Parts 6 to 13 used. A diagram that drops it has dropped the control.

    Think deeper: In review, people look at the picture. But the picture is one rendering of the text, and two tools may lay out the same text differently. If a board approves a diagram, what exactly has it approved: the image in the slide pack, the text it came from, or the system the text describes? And if the assistant redraws it next month, which of those has changed?

    Is the model or the picture the source of truth?

    The pattern

    Single source of truth, and the old split between modelling and diagramming. The C4 model’s own tooling page puts it plainly: “As an industry, we’ve tended to prefer diagramming over modelling, primarily because the barrier to entry is relatively low”. In a drawing tool, “if you rename a box, you need to rename it across every diagram where it appears”. In a model, “A model is just data!” Generative AI changes the cost on both sides: drawings get cheaper to produce, and models get cheaper to write.

    What is really being decided

    Where architecture knowledge lives, and so what an AI is allowed to change. If the picture is the truth, every generated picture is a new, unreviewed claim about the system. If a text model is the truth, the assistant edits the model and people review a diff, and every picture is a view that can be thrown away and regenerated. The second needs someone to own the model and a team willing to work in text.

    The forces

    • Speed against consistency: asking for a fresh diagram each time is fastest. Each one is also a fresh chance to drift: Cámara et al. (2023), modelling UML classes with an early ChatGPT, found that the same prompt gave very different models in different chats.
    • Audience against rigour: a picture is for people. Mike Loukides argues that C4 diagrams “are drawn on whiteboards—and that shows precisely what they are for” (O’Reilly Radar, 2024). A model is for checking and reuse. Few teams need only one.
    • Inclusion: Structurizr, a model-as-code tool, says of its own approach that it “does isolate non-technical people and architects that don’t write code” (vendor’s own statement). An assistant that writes the text may lower that barrier, or hide it.
    • Lock-in to a notation: the text you keep is in one syntax. Moving between syntaxes is translation, and translation is where generated output drifts.

    Left open

    • Which of your diagrams would anyone notice were wrong, and how long would it take?
    • If an assistant generates the picture from the model, who reviews the picture, if anyone?
    • Should a generated diagram carry a provenance stamp, as step 12.3 suggests for other generated work?
    Four ways to write a diagram as text

    Mermaid flowchart. Nodes and edges with optional labels, written as A -->|label| B. It has no idea what a container is, so C4 types live in the labels by convention. GitHub renders it in Markdown, per GitHub’s documentation.

    Mermaid C4. Five C4 diagram types (Context, Container, Component, Dynamic, Deployment), with syntax “compatible with plantUML”. The docs list sprite, tags, link and Legend as “unfinished features”, and say there is “no plan to support” C4-PlantUML’s layout statements. Its sister syntax, architecture-beta, is for cloud and CI/CD resources, and its page says “the syntax may still change in a backwards-incompatible way before it is declared stable”.

    C4-PlantUML. MIT licensed, and PlantUML ships its C4 files in its standard library, so “no additional files or Internet is required”. You need a PlantUML renderer, which is a separate install or service.

    Structurizr DSL. A text language for a model: you define people, systems, containers and relationships once, then declare views of them. Structurizr’s inspections check that model against C4 notation rules, such as “Container with no technology” and “Relationship with no description”. Step 18.4 comes back to what that does and doesn’t prove.

    From a picture instead of a description. You may be tempted to photograph a whiteboard and ask for the text. The benchmark evidence is on clean digital diagrams, not photos: in SADU, the best of 11 models answered 70.18% of questions about 154 behavioural, structural and entity-relationship diagrams correctly, as graded by an LLM judge (Ouyang et al., preprint 2026), with failures including missed and spurious elements. We found no benchmark on whiteboard photos of architecture diagrams.

    Check the abstraction

    Check a generated diagram against written rules for level, labels and invention, then put the rules in the prompt and see how much they fix.

    Step18.2

    Part 18
    AI for models and diagrams
    Time
    12 min
    Last reviewed
    12 November 2026

    Everyone scores the same invented sample first, so the room can compare. Agree the scoring rule before anyone opens the key. The FastAPI row usually splits the room: let it, because it’s the kind of error that survives review. Keep the retry for those who have an assistant; others can pair.

    A generated diagram that won’t parse is the easy case: the tool tells you. The harder failures parse cleanly. The diagram is drawn at the wrong level, adds things nobody asked for, or quietly redraws the system the way most systems work. None of that is visible at a glance, so you need written rules and a slow read.

    1 · The rules

    Rules 1 to 5 and 8 come from the C4 model’s notation guidance, which asks that “The type of every element should be explicitly specified” and that every line be labelled, “ideally avoiding single words like, ‘Uses’”. Rules 6 and 7 are ours, written for the two errors the studies keep finding: invented elements, and a familiar pattern replacing the one described.

    2 · Check a generated diagram

    Below is an invented output, planted with the errors the studies in this Part keep finding. Yours may have far fewer: a brief this detailed leaves a model little to fill in, and when we tried the bare prompt on two current models (13 November 2026, a check of these materials, not evidence) both drew something close to the reference. Everyone scores the same one, so results can be compared. Use your own output from step 18.1 as a second check afterwards.

    Our scoring rule. A row breaks a rule if any part of it breaks any of the eight rules or contradicts the brief. Keep the brief from step 18.1 open beside you.

    The answer key – open it after you have scored every row
    RowVerdictWhy
    Line 2, the commentBreaks 1, 3, 8“Architecture” states neither the diagram type nor its scope, no element says what type it is, and there’s no key.
    student, staffBreaks 7The brief says students and staff never use the service directly. The three assistants that do are missing altogether.
    API GatewayBreaks 6Not in the brief, which gives each assistant its own credential to call the Answers API. A gateway is what most designs have, so it appeared.
    Westmere Identity, and its arrowBreaks 7In the brief, the Answers API checks the token with Identity. Here Identity points at the gateway, and the check that limits the search to what the asker may see has gone.
    Answers API (Python, FastAPI)Breaks 4The container is right. “FastAPI” is invented: the brief says a Python web application. A plausible specific is the error most likely to survive review, because it sounds like knowledge.
    Redis CacheBreaks 6Not in the brief.
    PromptBuilder classBreaks 2A class is code, two levels below a container. It also makes the call to the model provider look as if it comes from a class rather than the Answers API.
    Search Index (search DB)PassesNamed differently from “Policy index”, but it’s the same container with the brief’s technology.
    Answer Log (PostgreSQL), “Writes answers”PassesRight container, right technology, and a label that says what the arrow does.
    Nightly Sync JobBreaks 7The brief says the updater “doesn’t run on a timetable: it waits for notices”. The diagram drew the usual pattern instead: a nightly pull from the Policy Library, where the brief has the Library sending a notice.
    ChunkerBreaks 2Splitting a document is a step inside the Index updater: a component, not a container.
    Embedding ServiceBreaks 2, 6A component at best, and embeddings aren’t mentioned in the brief at all.
    Policy LibraryPassesRight system, outside the boundary.
    LLM ProviderPassesThe brief’s model provider, outside the boundary. The arrow into it is the PromptBuilder row’s problem.
    11 arrows with no labelBreaks 5Only 2 of 13 arrows say what they do.

    Missing: the three assistants; the Answers API’s check with Westmere Identity; any sign that the search is limited to the asker’s audience; and the Index updater as one container, which has become three boxes. Eleven rows should be flagged and four should pass. Now score your table, and read the summary under it.

    3 · Retry with the rules in the prompt

    In a new chat, send the same brief with the rules in front of it: copy the prompt, then replace its two bracketed lines with the rules and the brief. Then compare the two outputs blind: paste your step 18.1 output as the bare prompt, and this one as the other arm. Shuffling your own outputs is less blind than having a partner do it, so swap with someone if you can.

    Draw a C4 container diagram of the system described below, as Mermaid flowchart text. Follow every rule. Give the diagram text, then any questions. RULES: [paste the rules] BRIEF: [paste the brief]
  • Only people, software systems and containers: no components or classes
  • Nothing the brief doesn’t mention: no gateway, cache or queue
  • The three assistants appear, and nobody calls the service directly
  • The Answers API checks with Westmere Identity before it searches
  • The Index updater waits for change notices
  • Every arrow has a label that says what it does
  • Every element states its type, and every container its technology
    •

    What to expect. The evidence says rules help and don’t fix it. Sathvika et al. found prompting strategies gave “marginal improvements”, with few-shot examples cutting clarity failures from 40.0% to 30.8%, as scored by an LLM judge. Kourani et al. found that telling models to follow the input cut the clear cases of drift back to the standard process from 27 to 13 for text descriptions, across ten models and four processes. In their words it can “mitigate, but not eliminate” the problem. Both are small studies of older models. One pair of runs from you is smaller still: run each prompt twice before you conclude anything. If your bare output already followed the brief, expect the rules to add mainly the title, the key and the element types.

    Think deeper: The errors that survived the rules are probably the ones that match how most systems are built: a gateway, a nightly job, a cache. Those are also the errors a reviewer who knows how most systems are built is least likely to notice. Who on your review board would spot that the diagram describes a typical system rather than yours, and what would they need in front of them?

    What should a diagram review attest?

    The pattern

    Attestation and segregation of duties: the person who signs isn’t the one who produced the work, and the signature says what was checked. The C4 model’s review checklist is a good start. It asks “Do you understand the type of every element? (i.e. the level of abstraction…)” and “Does the description match the relationship direction?” But every item is about whether the diagram can be understood. None asks whether it’s true.

    What is really being decided

    What a reviewer’s name on a generated diagram means. Before AI, a diagram’s author had usually worked out every box, so a review mostly tested communication. Now the author may have checked nothing. Either the review attests to truth, which needs someone who knows the system and takes longer, or it attests to notation, and the board needs to know that’s all it got. Step 15.2 makes the same point for written designs.

    The forces

    • Volume against attention: diagrams now cost nothing to make, and review still costs an hour. A board that receives three times as many will read each one less closely.
    • Notation against truth: notation checks are fast, repeatable and partly automatable. Truth checks need the system’s owner and the brief, and can’t be automated.
    • Plausibility against familiarity: the errors that survive are the typical ones. Reviewers fluent in typical architecture are well placed to miss them.
    • As designed against as built: a diagram can be true of the design and false of production. A signature needs a date and says which one it attests.

    Left open

    • Should a submitter declare that a diagram was generated, and what would change if they did?
    • Who signs that a diagram is true when the system spans three teams?
    • Would you accept a diagram that passed every notation rule but that nobody who runs the system has read?
    What the studies measured, and how

    Szczepanik and Chudziak (HICSS 2026) generated C4 context, container and component diagrams in C4-PlantUML from five briefs for familiar systems, such as a library and a point-of-sale system, with four models. “Abstraction adherence” was a regex check that flagged “level-inappropriate elements (e.g., Component in Context/Container)” and missing boundary constructs. That is a rule, not a judgement, so the 28% to 100% spread between single-agent runs is the most solid number here. Their semantic and clarity scores came from an LLM judge, and they say “We did not directly benchmark LLM judgments against human expert evaluations”. A three-round multi-agent set-up used about 500,000 tokens against about 40,000 for one agent.

    Sathvika et al. (preprint, 2026) generated architecture views from the source code of 340 repositories, 4,137 views in all, with DeepSeek-V2.5, Claude 3.5 Sonnet and GPT-4o and two agents. Two of the authors, not told which approach made each view, rated 110 views from 22 repositories for accuracy and level of detail. Their conclusion: “structural correctness does not necessarily imply architectural accuracy or appropriate granularity”. The general coding agent “generated code-level granularity with excessive components”. Clarity was judged by an LLM.

    Error types elsewhere. NOMAD’s taxonomy for class diagrams lists missing elements, a “Spurious class introduced”, and misclassified relationships such as a “generalisation arrow reversed”. In domain models, relationships scored worst, with F1 of 0.34 against 0.76 for classes (Chen et al., MODELS 2023, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 on ten examples: an old result, not current performance, and we read only the abstract). IcePanel, which sells a C4 tool, compared four models on one scenario in August 2025 and found one of them drawing containers “as Python classes”; its conclusion was that “these LLMs aren’t yet mature enough to produce C4 diagrams of a real-world architecture”. It’s a vendor’s blog with no rubric, so treat it as an illustration.

    Read more

    • Knowledge-Driven Hallucination in LLMs: process modelling (Kourani et al.)
    • NOMAD: UML class diagrams from requirements (Giannouris and Ananiadou)
    • Comparison: LLMs for creating software architecture diagrams (IcePanel, vendor)
    • Review checklist (C4 model)

    Critique a capability map

    Score a generated capability map against its source glossary and five quality criteria, and find what it invented, duplicated, misplaced and left out.

    Step18.3

    Part 18
    AI for models and diagrams
    Time
    10 min
    Last reviewed
    12 November 2026

    Silent scoring first, five minutes. Then ask which fault took longest to find. It’s usually 2.2, because a name that repeats its parent looks tidy. The optional generation exercise works well as homework.

    A capability map may be the diagram most likely to be trusted without being checked. It looks complete by design, every box is phrased the same way, and an invented capability looks exactly like a real one. The one detailed case study we found of generating them reports the same thing: Jung and Wienke (2024) report that “GenAI tends to hallucinate by inventing non-existing capabilities for filling in the gaps”.

    In their words, a map should be “disjoint (BC should not overlap), complete (the whole business model needs to be covered), minimal (it does not contain unnecessary BC)” and stable, meaning it “should not change over time”. Our reading: a capability named after a system fails that last test, because the system will change before the capability does.

    1 · Read the source, then the map

    The glossary is the source: the terms Westmere’s Student Services uses for its own work. The map was generated from it. Both are invented.

    2 · Score it

    Our scoring rule. Flag a capability if it fails any of the five criteria, or can’t be traced to a term in the glossary. Where two capabilities overlap, flag the one in the wrong place.

    The answer key – open it after you have scored every row
    CapabilityFailsWhy
    1.3 Marketing Campaign ManagementMinimalNo glossary term supports it. Recruitment “should” have marketing, so the gap was filled.
    2.2 Enrolment and RecordsCoherent, disjointIt repeats its parent’s name and overlaps 2.1 and 2.3. The case study had to forbid this in its prompt: “GPT does not care for naming without a clear statement” that a child may not share its parent’s name.
    3.3 Grade Prediction AnalyticsMinimalInvented. It’s also a solution idea, not something Student Services said it does.
    4.3 Student Enquiry HandlingDisjointThe same capability as 1.1 Enquiry Management. If you flagged 1.1 instead, count it.
    4.4 Fee InvoicingCoherentFees belong with Student Finance, next to 5.1 Fee Collection.
    4.5 Chatbot OperationsStableIt names a system. The chatbot is in the glossary as a tool for enquiries; the capability is 1.1, whichever tool does it.

    Missing: complaints (term 15) and placements (term 16), so the map isn’t complete. The census date has no capability, and that’s right: it’s a date that governs enrolment, not something the organisation does. If you flagged it, that’s a useful argument to have. Six capabilities should be flagged and twelve should pass. Now score your table.

    3 · Optional: generate one yourself, twice

    In two separate new chats, send this prompt with the glossary pasted in place of its last line. Then compare the two maps: do they have the same level-1 groups? The same number of capabilities? Jung and Wienke’s own verdict was that “determinism is yet to be achieved”.

    From the glossary below, write a two-level business capability map for Westmere's Student Services. Use only what the glossary supports. Level-2 capabilities must not repeat their parent's name. Give each capability a one-line description. [paste the glossary]

    Think deeper: A capability map outlives the projects that use it. Funding cases cite it, portfolio reviews map applications to it, and roadmaps are drawn against it. An invented capability like “Grade Prediction Analytics” can attract an application, a budget line and an owner before anyone asks where it came from. How would you find, a year later, which capabilities in your map nobody ever confirmed?

    Who owns a generated view?

    The pattern

    Reference data management: a shared reference has an owner, a change process and a version, or it isn’t a reference. Capability maps already work this way in mature practices. What’s new is that a plausible complete draft now costs minutes, so the draft can go into circulation before it has an owner. Step 13.4 covered ownership for skills; the same logic applies to the views they produce.

    What is really being decided

    Whether generated content can enter your reference layer, and through which door. The case study kept the door narrow: every map “still has to be revised by a senior consultant”. That makes generation a drafting aid for the owner, not a source of truth. The harder decision is what happens on regeneration. A second run is a different map, so “refresh it with AI” replaces a reviewed reference with an unreviewed one unless someone compares them.

    The forces

    • Speed against provenance: the consultants’ impression was “a couple of hours rather than days”. That’s an impression, not a measurement, and the hours saved move into review.
    • Source quality: the case study found the tool “only capable to recognise capabilities mentioned in the text documents provided”. Thin or inconsistent sources produce inventions.
    • Reference models against your own terms: a sector reference model gives a complete-looking skeleton. It can also fill your map with capabilities your organisation doesn’t have, which looks like completeness.
    • Stability against regeneration: a map is meant to change slowly. A generator that gives a different map each run works against that by design.

    Left open

    • Who in your organisation could sign that a capability exists, and would they agree with each other?
    • Should a capability added by generation be marked as such until someone confirms it?
    • When a reference model and your own documents disagree, which should a generator follow?
    How the case study generated maps, and what has been measured

    BCMGen was built by three students over three months for a consultancy in the finance sector, and first tried on public transport. Zero-shot prompts took client documents, industry reference maps and a list of client terms, and produced two levels of capabilities in three tiers (corporate, core and support). Two consultants then used and refined it for several months. The paper reports their impressions, not measurements: no accuracy against a reference, no agreement between raters, and no count of invented capabilities.

    Two other papers describe capability modelling with an assistant. Samarasekara et al. (ACIS 2024) put definitions in the prompt and report “preliminary evaluation results”; we read only the abstract. Oaj et al. (ER 2025 companion) describe a business architecture copilot, validated by the authors on one insurance scenario with no metrics; without its knowledge graph, they say, it “lacks semantic precision”. Both have a co-author from a capability-modelling vendor.

    What we didn’t find: a measured study of generated capability maps against a reference, or any peer-reviewed study generating complete ArchiMate models with a stated sample. If someone quotes accuracy figures for generated capability maps, ask where they come from.

    Read more

    • Generating Business Capability Maps using GenAI: A Case Study (Jung and Wienke, 2024)
    • LLM Driven Approach for Capability Modelling (Samarasekara et al., ACIS 2024)
    • Business Architecture Copilot (Oaj et al., 2025)

  • I found which glossary terms the map left out.
  • I can name the five criteria and say which fault each one catches.

    Keep models as text

    Read a diff of a regenerated diagram for changes nobody asked for, sort review problems by the layer that could catch them, and close the Part.

    Step18.4

    Part 18
    AI for models and diagrams
    Time
    11 min
    Last reviewed
    12 November 2026

    The diff takes three minutes and lands best if people count the changes before they list them. Most rooms find the removed line and miss the reworded label. Leave five minutes for the if-then plan and the discussion questions.

    A drawing shows you what the system looks like now. A text model also shows you what changed, line by line, and that matters more once an assistant is editing your diagrams. The C4 model’s tooling page puts two questions to anyone choosing a tool: is the data “stored in git next to your source code”, and is it “Easy to diff source to use in pull requests?” Thoughtworks put diagrams as code in “Trial” on its Technology Radar in October 2020, citing “easy version control”. That’s an old position and the item is no longer on the current Radar, but the reason has only got stronger.

    1 · Read the diff

    The reference diagram from step 18.1 was reviewed and approved. A month later, someone asked an assistant for one change: “Add a container for the review dashboard, a web page that reads the Answer log.” This is the diff between the approved text and what came back. It’s invented, and modelled on the errors in this Part. Both versions parse and render.

    Lines starting - were removed and lines starting + were added. A changed line shows as one of each.

    Open after you have listed them
    • The identity check is gone. Westmere Identity is still drawn, connected to nothing. The search arrow still says “the asker may see”, but nothing now shows how the service finds that out.
    • “Permitted” went from a label. One word, and it was the only place the diagram stated what the model provider may receive.
    • The change notice became a nightly sync. The familiar pattern came back, as it did in step 18.2.

    Cámara et al. (2023) saw the same thing in UML: asking a model to fix one part of a class model sometimes introduced new errors elsewhere. With two drawings you’d be comparing pictures by eye. With text, the change is four lines long, and you can see it.

    2 · Which layer could catch it?

    A parse check, such as Mermaid’s mermaid.parse, “validates graph definitions without rendering a graph” (Mermaid docs). Structurizr’s MCP validate tool “Returns "OK" if the DSL is parseable” (Structurizr docs). Both check syntax only. Sort these twelve problems by the cheapest layer that could reliably catch them.

    Compare your sort – open it after you have placed all twelve

    Problems 3, 4 and 8 are on Structurizr’s list of inspections for models written in its own DSL: “Relationship with no description”, “Container with no technology” and “Disconnected element”. So a check of that kind would catch the removed identity arrow, but only because Identity was left floating. Had the assistant drawn some other arrow to it, nothing would fire. Problem 5 isn’t on that list (its “view key” inspections concern a view’s identifier, not a legend), but in diagram text it’s a simple check of your own: is there a title, and a subgraph called Key? Problem 6 becomes a rule only if every label states its type. Szczepanik and Chudziak could check level with a regular expression because C4-PlantUML’s element keywords state the type. Problem 7 needs an approved list of systems to check against.

    That is the lesson of step 10.1 again: a script earns its place when the rule is exact and the input it needs is available. And step 10.3 showed the risk on the other side. A model told to “fix it until the checks pass” can label an arrow “Uses”, or connect Identity to anything, and pass. A clean inspection report means the notation is complete, not that the diagram is true.

    What this means for the architecture. If diagrams live as text beside the systems they describe, an assistant’s edit becomes a change request like any other: a diff, a check run on every change, a named reviewer. Our reading: that’s the main reason to keep models as text in an AI-assisted practice. It isn’t that a model reads text better than pictures; it’s that people can review a change to text and can’t review a redrawn picture.

    Think deeper: The two changes that mattered most, the dropped “permitted” and the nightly sync, both need a person who knows what the system is supposed to do. A diff makes them visible; it doesn’t make anyone look. If assistants make diagram changes cheap and frequent, review becomes the bottleneck. What would you have to stop reviewing so that someone still reads changes like these?

    What you can do now

    You have finished Part 18. You can turn a written description into diagram text and read it without a renderer, check a generated diagram for level, labels and invention against written rules, say how much rules in the prompt are likely to help, score a generated capability map against its source, read a diff for unrequested changes, and say which problems a parse, a rule or a person must catch.

    Questions to discuss

    In a group session, share your answers, and park anything that needs a longer discussion for the end.

    • Which of your architecture diagrams is the source of truth for something, and does anyone keep it as text?
    • Your review board receives a generated diagram. What should the submitter declare, and what should the reviewer’s signature mean?
    • Which errors in this Part would your own reviews have caught, and which would have looked normal?
    • Who owns your capability map, and could anything be added to it today without them knowing?

    Export your notes: they include your scores, your diff findings and your plan.

    Part 19 starts at step 19.1: MCP as an integration concern, beside the APIs and gateways you already run.

    Which notation should the organisation standardise on, and who decides?

    The pattern

    Standardising a modelling language, as organisations have done with UML and ArchiMate, now with a new force: the assistant is one of the authors. Choosing a notation is choosing what a machine can check, what a diff can show, and who can take part.

    What is really being decided

    How much of your architecture knowledge is a model and how much is pictures, and who maintains the model. A drawing tool keeps everyone in. Diagram text adds diffs and a parse check. A model as text, such as Structurizr DSL, adds consistent views and rule checks, and Structurizr’s own documentation names the cost: “The biggest downside of an ‘as code’ approach is the increased learning curve.” The decision is rarely one notation for everything; it’s which artefacts must be models.

    The forces

    • Checkability against participation: everything a script can check is something a non-technical stakeholder may not be able to edit.
    • Maturity: notations change under you. Mermaid’s architecture diagrams are in beta and “may still change in a backwards-incompatible way”, and its C4 support still lacks a legend.
    • Vendor claims: Structurizr’s AI page says it “can therefore enforce the hierarchy of abstractions”. That’s true of the model’s structure. It says nothing about whether the elements are real.
    • Fitness functions: Mike Loukides argues architects should write fitness functions “to encapsulate descriptions of the properties we care about” (O’Reilly Radar, 2024). A model in text is something such checks can run against; a picture isn’t.

    Left open

    • Which of your artefacts must be a model, and which can stay pictures?
    • Who maintains the model when the architect who started it moves on?
    • Would you let an assistant commit a change to the model, or only propose one?
    Checking a generated diagram in layers

    Parse. Mermaid’s mermaid.parse(text) returns the diagram type or throws an error. Structurizr’s MCP server has validate, parse and inspect tools. Every invented diagram in this Part parses; we checked ours with Mermaid’s command-line tool.

    Inspect. Structurizr’s inspections are “a Checkstyle inspired approach to verifying workspace content”. The default severity is error, adjustable per workspace, element or view. They include missing descriptions and technologies, disconnected elements, elements in no view, and “Software system with containers, but no decisions”. They check completeness against C4 notation, not whether the architecture is right.

    Rules. Your own checks: allowed levels, an approved list of systems, required relationships such as “the API must call Identity”. Szczepanik and Chudziak’s regex check is an example, and one model scored only 28% on it. We found no study measuring whether such a check reduces the errors that reach a human reviewer.

    A person. NOMAD found every generated diagram syntactically correct; Sathvika et al. that structural correctness doesn’t imply accuracy. The closest evidence on validators comes from systems engineering, covered in step 10.4: a validator drove errors per 100 lines to zero, and the author’s conclusion was still that “A clean model still requires expert review”.

    Read more

    • Why “as code”? (Structurizr, vendor)
    • AI (Structurizr, vendor)
    • Usage: syntax validation without rendering (Mermaid)
    • Tooling (C4 model)
