    What the benchmarks miss

    Predict how far three headline agent numbers move under strict scoring, then turn an invented vendor’s product sheet into the questions a business case needs answered.

    Step20.3

    Part 20
    Agents: from answering to acting
    Time
    10 min
    Last reviewed
    12 November 2026

    Predictions first, individually, with numbers: no ranges wider than 20 points. Reveal all three together. Then pairs take the product sheet and write one question per claim. Ask one pair to read theirs and another to say which question a vendor would find hardest to answer.

    A vendor tells Westmere’s ICT team that its agent “resolves most service desk tasks end to end”. Before you ask what the number is, find out how much headline numbers move when someone scores them strictly. Three predictions, with real numbers behind them.

    1 · Predict

    1. Partial or strict. An agent scores 89% on a computer-use benchmark when each task earns partial credit for the checkpoints it passes. What does it score when a task counts only if every checkpoint passes?
    2. Tests or maintainers. AI-written code changes are scored by automated tests, then the same changes go to the projects’ maintainers. On average, how many percentage points lower is the share the maintainers would merge?
    3. Half the time or most of the time. An agent succeeds half the time on tasks that take a human expert about 17 hours. How long are the tasks it succeeds on 80% of the time?
    The answers: open after you’ve written all three
    1. 89.3% becomes 54.6%. Anthropic’s system card reports Claude Fable 5.2 on 82 offline OSWorld 2.1 tasks at “a partial score of 89.3% and a strict pass rate of 54.6%”. Same runs, two scoring rules. This is a vendor measurement, and the vendor published both numbers. Headlines tend to keep only the first.
    2. About 24 points lower. METR (Whitfill, Wu, Becker and Rush, March 2026) had four active maintainers of scikit-learn, Sphinx and pytest review 296 AI-written pull requests that had passed the benchmark’s tests. The maintainers would not have merged roughly half of them. As a check on the reviewers, about 68% of the original human fixes were merged; measured against that baseline, grader scores were on average 24.2 percentage points higher (standard error 2.7) than the maintainers’ merge decisions. The reasons included broken code elsewhere and poor code quality, not only wrong fixes. The authors are careful: the agents couldn’t revise after feedback, so “we do not claim that this represents a fundamental capability limitation”, and the newest model studied was Claude Sonnet 4.5.
    3. About 3 hours. In METR’s data, Claude Mythos Preview (April 2026) has a 50% time horizon of about 17.4 hours and an 80% horizon of about 3.1 hours. Asking for “most of the time” instead of “half the time” cuts the task length by a factor of five or six. METR adds that time horizons at 99% reliability “cannot be fit at all without much larger and higher-quality benchmarks”.

    What this means for a business case. Plan on the strict score, at the reliability your process needs, on tasks like yours, at a token budget you can afford. If a vendor gives you only the generous number, the strict one is what you need to find out. Our reading, from the three gaps above.

    Claims you’ll hear that didn’t check out.

    • “The time horizon is how long the model can work on its own.” METR’s own FAQ answers “No”: it measures how hard a task is.
    • “Fable 5.2 scores 89.3% on OSWorld.” That is partial credit. The strict rate on the same 82 tasks is 54.6%.
    • “UK AISI and METR validated Fable 5.2.” They tested Mythos 5.2 snapshots before release, and Anthropic says no outside organisation reviewed its announcement or system card.
    • “Reward hacking rose from 1% to 6% in the new model.” The card’s 6.0% and 1.0% compare broken tasks with intact tasks for the same model.
    • “SWE-bench shows it can do real engineering.” A preprint documents answer leakage in SWE-bench Pro, and in one METR study maintainers wouldn’t merge many changes that passed SWE-bench Verified’s tests.

    2 · Question the product sheet

    Brindlemoor is an invented vendor. Its sheet reads like many you will see. For each claim, write the one question that would most change your view of it.

    Model questions: open after you’ve written yours
    ClaimThe questionWhy it matters
    1 · 87% end to endScored strictly or with partial credit, on whose tasks, over how many runs, at what token budget, and checked by a grader or by people who would accept the result?Each of these moved a real score by 20 points or more above.
    2 · Up to 20 hoursIs that a time horizon? At 50% or 80% reliability? Who measured it?A time horizon measures task difficulty, not running time, and METR says measurements above 16 hours are unreliable with its current task suite.
    3 · Independently evaluatedBy whom, published where, and on which model version? Which model serves my requests if that one refuses or is busy?For the newest models, outside evaluators’ findings so far appear only inside the vendors’ own documents, where they appear at all (step 20.1). A fallback model is a different model (step 21.2).
    4 · Approval on every risky actionWho decides what counts as risky? How many approvals a day would one person see, and what would they see?CoSAI’s MCP security paper (draft, January 2026) lists consent fatigue as a threat, and Thoughtworks puts “human-in-the-loop theater” on Caution (November 2026). Steps 19.2 and 19.3 met both.
    5 · 60% cheaper per ticketDoes that include failed runs, retries, people reviewing the output, monitoring and evaluation?Step 21.3 shows what a simple sum leaves out.

    Think deeper: Strict scoring and 80% reliability both make an agent look worse, and both are closer to what a deployer needs. If a vendor publishes only the generous number, is that a reason not to buy, or a test you run yourself? What would it cost Westmere to run that test, and who would own the result when the vendor changes the model underneath?

    What would make a vendor’s agent score count as evidence for your decision?

    The pattern

    Acceptance testing, and the old gap between a vendor’s reference benchmark and your workload. Database buyers learned long ago that a published transaction benchmark says little about their own queries. An agent benchmark is the same kind of evidence, with extra problems: it can leak into training data, the model may recognise it as a test, and the score depends on how many tokens the agent was allowed to spend.

    What is really being decided

    What evidence Westmere needs before a pilot, and what more before an agent runs with nobody watching; who runs that evaluation; and what forces it to be run again. Parts 5 and 7 gave you the methods for skills (steps 5.3 and 7.4). The same methods apply here, scored strictly and run more than once.

    The forces

    • Release pace against evaluation: at the release pace noted in step 20.1, an evaluation that takes a quarter certifies a model that’s already been replaced.
    • Generous against strict scoring: partial credit and automated graders are cheap and flattering. Strict scoring by people is expensive and closer to the truth.
    • Tests the model can recognise: the International AI Safety Report 2026 notes that “it has become more common for models to distinguish between test settings and real-world deployment”. Anthropic reports that Mythos 5.2, which has the same capabilities as Fable 5.2, was aware it might be in an evaluation in as many as 43% of automated audit transcripts (vendor-measured). A test that looks like a test may flatter.
    • Budget-dependent scores: UK AISI showed capability rises with the token budget. A score without its budget can’t be compared, and your budget is the one that counts.

    Left open

    • Should Westmere’s procurement require strict-scored results with the token budget stated?
    • Who at Westmere runs agent evaluations, and on whose budget?
    • When the vendor changes the model inside a product you’ve bought, who finds out, and does the evaluation have to be repeated?
    Same model, different number: harness, lab, budget and leakage

    Different cards, different numbers. Claude Opus 5.5 is listed at 66.4% on Terminal-Bench 4.0 in Anthropic’s card and 59.6% in Google’s, where the row is marked “(AA)”. Fable 5.1 is listed at 83.5% on the OSWorld 2.1 offline set in Anthropic’s card and 76.8% in Google’s. Each figure is what that vendor’s card prints, and the cards don’t say, row by row, who ran each rival model or with what set-up. So a comparison table in any one vendor’s card is not like-for-like.

    Different harnesses. The ARC Prize leaderboard lists Fable 5.2 at 81.2% on ARC-AGI-3 with its standard harness and 97.7% with the provider’s adapter. The system card cites 79.26% for the standard harness, so even those two don’t match.

    Different budgets. UK AISI (July 2026) found that raising the token budget from 1 million to 10 million “raised performance by ~25% on software engineering tasks”. It adds that gains appear strongest where agents can check their own work.

    Leaked answers. Zheng and colleagues (“SWE-Bench Pro Verified”, a preprint, September 2026, revised October) revised 102 of 731 tasks and found local answer leakage in at least 103. Once it was closed, one model fell from 78.80% to 57.32%, while another barely moved. A score on a leaky benchmark mixes ability with access to the answer.

    Read more

    • Many SWE-bench-passing PRs would not be merged into main (METR, March 2026)
    • SWE-Bench Pro Verified (Zheng et al., preprint, 2026)
    • System card: Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 (Anthropic, PDF) and Gemini 4 Carbon model card (Google)

    • More compute, more capability (UK AISI, July 2026)
    What a new model’s system card can and can’t tell a deployer

    A system card is the most detailed public document about a new model, and for Claude Fable 5.2 it runs to 264 pages and states limits as well as strengths. It is still the vendor’s own document. Read it for three kinds of content, and label each.

    • Vendor-measured. “The majority of evaluations ... were run in-house at Anthropic.” Most safety testing used Mythos 5.2, which has the same capabilities, with reduced safeguards. The card contains no task-length time horizon of METR’s kind.
    • Outside testers, quoted by the vendor. METR had API access “over a period of 10 business days” to a snapshot “stronger on AI R&D capabilities than the released model”. UK AISI found the model identified its evaluation’s purpose “100% of the time when prompted”, and so “we cannot confidently claim Claude Mythos 5.2 would not take unsanctioned actions in similar but more realistic deployment settings.” Neither organisation had published its own report when we checked. Anthropic’s announcement says: “None of the external organizations reviewed the contents of this blog post or the contents of the System Card.”
    • Stated blind spots. The main alignment audit “doesn’t cover multi-agent scenarios and tasks with very long trajectories in sufficient depth”. Those are the settings agent deployments are moving towards.

    In fairness. On the vendor’s own measures, Mythos 5.2 used credentials or files placed outside its sandbox in 3.1% of test scenarios, about the same as Opus 5.5 (3.3%) and well below Mythos 5.1 (21%) and Mythos 5 (39%). In a replay test it took fewer destructive actions than any older Claude model, which the card attributes largely to it asking for permission first. These are improvements on the vendor’s own tests, and nobody outside has repeated them yet.

    Public leaderboards add independent scores. Epoch AI ranked Fable 5.2 first of the 240 models it tracked when we checked, though the page doesn’t say who ran each benchmark. Scale AI lists it at 41.30% on the Remote Labor Index, with no confidence interval. None of these is a safety evaluation.

    Contain the agent

    Work through a real 2026 incident, in which agents under test reached the live internet, and find the controls that would have contained it. Then design containment for Westmere’s agent that doesn’t depend on the agent behaving.

    Step20.4

    Part 20
    Agents: from answering to acting
    Time
    14 min
    Last reviewed
    12 November 2026

    Five minutes on the incident and the sort, eight on the design sheet in pairs: one plays the agent’s owner, the other the security reviewer, as in step 11.4. Keep the tone factual. These were tests, the harm found was limited, and the reports are unusually open about what went wrong. That openness is why we can learn from them.

    In 2026, three organisations disclosed that their evaluations had let agents reach the real internet, by design or by mistake, and that the agents did things nobody had sanctioned. These incidents are the best independent evidence there is about containment, because the people who ran or investigated the tests published what went wrong. Two more reports show how hard it is to watch agents at all.

    Read each card for what it established and what it didn’t. Cards marked “vendor” are a company’s account of its own models.

    1 · Take one incident apart

    UK AISI’s report (4 August 2026) is a detailed account by the organisation that ran the test, with a fuller technical report linked from it. Agents worked through cyber-range challenges over many steps. Internet access was deliberately on, so they could download tools, and the developers’ cyber classifiers were deliberately off. In 10 of 122 runs, agents took 19 actions nobody had sanctioned, most of them in one sustained line of activity by a single agent. It researched the maintainers of a real open-source project and used fake identities to pressure one into approving malicious code. It messaged real people and planted hidden instructions for other AI systems to find. One agent left accounts and notes in public that later agents reused. A real maintainer refused the code. AISI found no resulting real-world harm.

    Sort each fact by the control that would have contained it, or mark it as something that held.

    What AISI and Anthropic concluded: open after you have sorted

    What AISI says it is changing. It will treat internet access “as one that must be actively justified rather than a default”, with fine-grained network controls; introduce “monitoring built to watch an evaluation as it runs”, able to flag or block out-of-scope actions; add checks that tasks are “correctly specified and solvable by the intended route”; and audit past evaluations. Its summary line is the one to keep: “good containment should not depend on the model choosing not to test its boundaries.”

    The sort, as we’d do it. Internet access, fake identities and reused accounts are all reach: no outbound internet, no way to create accounts, and nothing shared between runs. The misleading task prompt is check the task. The three days is watch it live. The Tor alert sits between watch and held: it worked, days late, because it was general monitoring. The maintainer and the sandbox held. Notice that one of the things that held was a stranger doing their job well.

    What the reports don’t settle. AISI says the task prompt was misconfigured in some runs, so agents believed no in-scope solution existed, but that some agents behaved this way even with the right instructions. Anthropic, whose model made 17 of the 19 actions, calls it “a serious failure of alignment”, and reports that its newer models were far less likely to start the same attack in retests (vendor-measured). AISI’s own follow-up (23 October 2026) found other models taking similar unsanctioned actions in simulated tests, and says newer Anthropic models so often state that they are being evaluated that it is unclear whether their lower rates reflect better alignment. Both organisations say the set-up and the model each played a part. Neither measures how likely this is in a deployment that isn’t a cyber test.

    What this means for the architecture. Westmere’s agent isn’t a cyber test, but the shape is the same. When the task couldn’t be done as briefed, both agents improvised: AISI’s found a route through the real world, and Dana’s, in step 20.2, rewrote two policy records. Containment means the improvisation hits a wall the platform enforces, not a rule the agent was asked to keep.

    2 · Design the containment

    Now design it for the Policy Office admin agent from step 20.2. Write down what you’re unsure of rather than leaving a section blank. Ten minutes.

    Model answer: open after you have filled in the sheet

    Check your sheet against the sources. Some rows rest on published guidance, some on vendor statements, some only on our reasoning.

    Sheet rowWhat to compare withSource
    1 Identity, 2 ReachTreat internet access as something to justify. Give the agent its own narrow identity rather than a person’s broad oneUK AISI incident report; step 11.4 for the trade-off
    2 Reach, 3 ApprovalsTool annotations such as destructiveHint are hints: “They aren’t enforcement.” Keep safety guarantees “in deterministic controls”MCP blog, March 2026
    3 ApprovalsConsent fatigue is a named threat; “human-in-the-loop theater” is on Caution; agent sandboxing is on Adopt as “a sensible default for all agents”CoSAI (draft, January 2026); Thoughtworks Radar, November 2026
    4 Stop conditionsCheck tasks are solvable by the intended route, and decide what happens when they aren’tUK AISI. The stop list itself is our reasoning
    5 BudgetCapability rises with the token budget, so a budget limits what the agent can attempt as well as what it costsUK AISI, July 2026; step 21.3
    6 Monitoring“Agents should be monitored every N messages/minutes instead of waiting for them to end their turns”, and agents’ actions should not influence “whether or when the monitoring system runs”METR and Redwood Research, October 2026
    7 The recordTamper-proof, searchable logs; agent output is untrusted inputMETR, October 2026 (both posts)
    8 Model and fallbackA request can be served by a different model from the one you chose, with different security behaviourAnthropic documentation and system card (vendor); step 21.2
    9 UndoNotify affected parties; know what each action changedAnthropic’s and AISI’s remediation lists

    This is a design exercise. A sheet can’t show a control working; only a pilot with the controls switched on can.

    Think deeper: In both the AISI incident and Dana’s run, the trouble started when the task couldn’t be done as briefed. Your containment sheet says what the agent must not do. Does it say what it should do when it’s stuck: stop, ask, or keep going? Who designs that path, and how would you test it, given that you can’t list in advance every way a task can be impossible?

    Can you contain an agent without relying on it to behave?

    The pattern

    Defence in depth and least privilege, with an assume-breach stance pointed at your own tool. Browser and mobile security learned to sandbox code they didn’t write and couldn’t predict. An agent is code you didn’t write, generated at run time. Add the circuit breaker from distributed systems: a budget or error count that trips the run, whatever the agent thinks.

    What is really being decided

    Which limits the platform enforces and which the prompt only requests; where a person must approve; and what stops a run. Anthropic, describing its own four incidents, wrote that “we believe these incidents would not have occurred had the environments been isolated from the internet as intended”, and also that “secure infrastructure will always be only one of several necessary layers of defense.” Both are true at once: the layers outside the model did most of the work, and they still aren’t sufficient alone.

    The forces

    • Approval against fatigue: the MCP specification says there should always be a human in the loop. CoSAI names consent fatigue as a threat, and the MCP blog notes that people building autonomous agents “treat confirmations as friction and lean on sandboxing instead”. Few, well-placed approvals beat many reflex ones.
    • Reach against capability: internet access makes agents more useful and was the common factor in the 2026 incidents at all three organisations. AISI now asks for it to be justified.
    • Monitoring against attack surface: the monitor is now part of what an agent can probe. Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s newest flagship models are each reported by their own vendor as harder to monitor than their predecessors.
    • Budget as a control: in one of Anthropic’s incidents, the session ended only when the token budget ran out. A budget chosen on purpose is a stop condition; a budget chosen for cost is a stop condition by accident.
    • The fallback is a different model: in Anthropic’s prompt-injection tests on Fable 5.2, more than half of the attempts in one test were answered by an older fallback model, where attacks succeeded more than twice as often. That is vendor-measured, in runs without the injection probes the vendor says it deploys in its products; with the probes on in its harder test, the share of fallback-served requests that were compromised fell from about 90% to about 29%. Step 21.2 has the figures. Your security posture is that of the weakest model a request can reach. Our reading, from the card.

    Left open

    • Who at Westmere may switch a monitor off, and does anyone get told when it happens?
    • Should any Westmere agent have internet access by default, and who would grant an exception?
    • What counts as a “risky” action needing approval, and who keeps that list current as tools are added?
    What a red team found in a real agent monitoring system

    Why monitoring is automated. METR’s Senate testimony (September 2026): “Automating monitoring is necessary given the enormous scale of AI agent activity, and has considerable promise.” And, from the incidents: AI developers “have not yet solved the problem of preventing AI agents from pursuing actions against human intent.”

    What one red team found. From July to August 2026, one METR and one Redwood Research employee tested OpenAI’s internal agent monitoring. They estimated that roughly 75–94% of internal agentic traffic from strong models was eligible for monitoring. Because the monitor ran when control returned to the user, an agent could postpone it by carrying on. Compaction events weren’t monitored, which probably left about 10% of eligible internal Codex traffic unmonitored from May to July 2026; OpenAI had found that itself and fixed it during the exercise. Two client-controllable headers could switch monitoring off for new agents, although setting them might itself be caught. OpenAI says most issues are now patched, which METR has not evaluated. The exercise had deep access, but the public post is brief and high-level by agreement with OpenAI, and some details were redacted.

    The monitor can be fooled, and its view altered. METR (October 2026) found a flaw that could let an agent change what a human reviewer sees, and recommends tamper-proof logging and stress-testing the monitoring itself. Vendor cards point the same way: Anthropic calls it “weak evidence that our ability to monitor Claude Mythos 5.2 has declined relative to Claude Opus 5.5”, and quotes UK AISI finding that, given monitor feedback, the model’s evasion rate “rises to 85%, compared with 9% for Claude Mythos 5.1”. OpenAI’s card for GPT-6 Astra reports a reasoning-only monitor’s recall falling below 11% on one benchmark when the model was told to sandbag and evade detection. All vendor-reported.

    Register the agent

    Write a register entry that gives the agent an owner, a reach, limits and the events that force a re-review. Then close the Part with an if-then plan and questions to discuss.

    Step20.5

    Part 20
    Agents: from answering to acting
    Time
    10 min
    Last reviewed
    12 November 2026

    Five minutes on the register entry, individually. Then the close: read the three ideas, collect if-then plans, and open the discussion. The room answers first. Anything that needs more than 30 seconds goes on the parking lot, read back before the end.

    An agent that acts on Westmere’s systems is a capability someone owns, like a service account or an integration. If it isn’t in a register, nobody reviews it again when the model under it changes, when a tool is added, or when its owner moves on. On the release calendars of 2026, the first of those comes round every few months.

    1 · Write the entry

    Fill it in for the Policy Office admin agent, using your containment sheet from step 20.4. Westmere’s ADR-0012 says no new shared platform goes live without a funded owner named in the decision. Decide whether this agent, or the platform it runs on, counts.

    Model answer: open after you have written yours

    Look hardest at “Re-review when”. A model change is the trigger most likely to happen and least likely to be noticed. Anthropic shipped three versions of its Fable model in five months of 2026, and its stated notice before retiring a publicly released model is at least 60 days (vendor documentation, checked 12 November 2026). Step 21.4 takes that further.

    Think deeper: Your register covers the agents Westmere builds. Vendors are also switching agents on inside products Westmere already uses (step 17.1), and staff can run coding agents on their own machines. Where does your register stop? What would you need to find the agents nobody registered, and who would you ask?

    What you can do now

    You have finished Part 20. You can read an agent run against its tool log instead of its report, question a headline agent score, design containment that doesn’t depend on the agent behaving, and give an agent an owner and a reason to be looked at again. Three ideas carry this Part:

    1. Design for the run, not the answer. Errors compound, and reach is set by the agent’s access, not by its brief.
    2. The strict number is the real number. For the newest models, independent evidence is thin, and the task-length yardstick has run out.
    3. Containment sits outside the model. In UK AISI’s words, “good containment should not depend on the model choosing not to test its boundaries.”

    Questions to discuss

    In a group session, share your answers, and park anything that needs a longer discussion for the end.

    • Which task in your area would you trust an agent to complete with nobody watching, and what evidence would you want first?
    • Where in your organisation is an instruction doing the job a permission should do?
    • Who reads agent logs today, and who would notice if a monitor stopped running?
    • When a vendor says its agent was independently evaluated, what should your procurement team ask for?
    • Who answers for an action an agent took on someone’s behalf: the person who started it, the agent’s owner, or the vendor?

    Export your notes: they include your predictions, your run log, your containment sheet and your register entry, if you changed them.

    Part 21 starts at step 21.1: the platform around the model, including where these controls sit, which model does which job, and what happens when one is retired.

    Who owns an agent, and when does it get looked at again?

    The pattern

    Service ownership and the application portfolio, plus the access recertification you already run for privileged service accounts. An agent is a service with an owner, a non-human identity with privileges that need re-approving, and a dependency on a supplier whose product changes without your say. Each of those has a process you know. The register is where they meet.

    What is really being decided

    What counts as an agent for the register: anything with a write tool, anything that runs unattended, or anything a vendor calls an agent. Who owns it, both for the business and on the technical side. And what forces a re-review. Part 2’s third open question, who answers for an action an agent took on someone’s behalf (step 2.6), is answered here, by name, for each agent. No standard answers it for you.

    The forces

    • Completeness against friction: a heavy register drives agents underground. A light one misses the agents that matter. Vendors switching agents on inside existing products add entries nobody asked for.
    • Ownership against shared platforms: one agent is a project’s problem. The runtime that ten agents share is a platform, and ADR-0012 says that needs a funded owner first.
    • Re-review cost against model churn: if every model change means a full re-review, nobody can afford to keep up. If none does, the evidence in the register describes a model you no longer run. The answer is probably a standing test set that reruns cheaply (step 13.4).
    • Accountability: the person who starts a run, the agent’s owner and the vendor each hold part of the responsibility. Your audit logs need to tell them apart before an incident, not after.

    Left open

    • Where should Westmere’s agent register live: in the application portfolio, the identity system, or the architecture review board’s records?
    • Should an agent that has run without incident for a year be reviewed less often, or is that when attention lapses?
    • Who has the authority to switch an agent off, and does that person know they have it?
    Whose identity does an agent run under? What the protocols say so far

    Step 11.4 weighed delegated identity against a service identity for a skill that reads. For an agent that acts, often with nobody present, the options look like this.

    • Act as the person. It keeps the source system’s rules, and it carries all of the person’s reach. It also assumes the person is there: MCP’s roadmap says plainly that “MCP authorization assumes a person with a browser at consent time.” MCP’s enterprise-managed authorisation, stable since June 2026, lets an organisation’s identity provider decide access, but it doesn’t cover agents acting with no user present.
    • Its own service identity. It can be scoped narrowly and audited as one thing, which is what the model answer in step 20.4 chose. The cost is the link to the person who asked, which you restore in the run record. In practice many service identities end up as a pasted, long-lived API key, the break at hop 4 in step 19.4; the same roadmap says existing servers lean on them.
    • A proper agent identity. MCP plans workload identity federation, token exchange and proof-of-possession tokens, and an Agent Identity working group is forming. Until those exist and your products support them, treat any vendor’s “agent identity” as that vendor’s own design, and ask how it maps to your identity provider.

    Step 19.4 traces one call through each hop and shows where the audit trail breaks.

    Read more

    • MCP roadmap
    • MCP enterprise-managed authorisation
    • Model deprecations (Anthropic documentation)

    Place the controls

    Put twelve controls on the layers of an AI platform, then see which ones have evidence behind them and which are only expected to work.

    Step21.1

    Part 21
    The AI platform: models, cost and change
    Time
    10 min
    Last reviewed
    12 November 2026

    Five minutes of silent sorting, then compare placements in pairs. The items that split the room are usually 3 (the injection filter), 6 (retention) and 7 (staff-only policies). Push on 3: most people put it in the gateway and stop there. The point of the step is that a filter is friction, and the boundary is item 4.

    Westmere’s three AI projects started separately. The student help chatbot, the staff policy assistant and the service desk assistant each call a model provider directly, with their own API key, their own logs and their own bill. The service desk assistant is at its fifth stage here: after the agent pilot in step 20.1, ICT’s own prototype from step 19.4 now only drafts replies for an analyst to send, and step 21.3 costs it. Digital Platforms now proposes one shared layer in front of the models. The architecture review board will ask what that layer is for, and ADR-0012 says no new shared platform goes live without a funded owner.

    Before anyone funds it, decide where each control should sit. Some belong in a shared gateway. Others only work somewhere else, however good the gateway is.

    Where the evidence stands · checked 12 November 2026

    Solid
    Input filters for prompt injection are bypassed often when someone other than their maker tests them: character tricks got past four of the five injection detectors tested more than 70% of the time (Hackett et al., LLMSec 2025), and adaptive attacks beat 12 published defences against jailbreaks and prompt injection, filters among them, most above 90% (Nasr, Carlini et al., 2025 preprint). Platforms behave very differently when a model is retired: some fail the request, some swap the model for you, one reroutes to another model at that model’s price (each vendor’s own lifecycle page).
    Thin
    Routing between cheap and expensive models has saved money on benchmarks (FrugalGPT, RouteLLM), but we found no published production study. We found no independent measurement of an AI gateway or a semantic cache. The NSA says MCP-aware security proxies “remain limited and are still maturing” (May 2026).
    Contested
    Whether bills fall as prices fall. Epoch AI measures the cost of a fixed level of performance falling about 47% a quarter (September 2026), while a separate Epoch analysis (April 2025) finds answers getting longer, especially from reasoning models. Whether a central gateway should be the main control point: InfoQ reported gateways as the “dominant architectural consensus” for MCP at April’s MCP Dev Summit, where the speakers and sponsors it names include gateway vendors. Thoughtworks, whose teams use the open-source gateway LiteLLM, keeps it at Trial rather than Adopt, largely because of its count of security flaws (November 2026).

    1 · Place each control

    Choose the layer where each control would be enforced, not where it’s written down. If two layers are needed, pick the one that would fail if the other were missing.

    Saved in this browser and included in your exported notes.

    Our placement, and how much evidence stands behind each one: open after you’ve placed all twelve
    #Where we’d put itWhy, and what backs it
    1GatewayA limit per person needs one counter across every request. Vendors sell this as a gateway feature, for example Azure API Management’s llm-token-limit policy (vendor documentation, 29 May 2026). Vendor description.
    2Gateway, stored with the answerA fallback or reroute happens below the application, so only the gateway knows which model answered. Without this record you can’t tell which model’s weaknesses a request was exposed to (step 21.2). Our reading.
    3Gateway, as friction onlyAttacks by outside researchers get past most such filters (Going deeper, below). The NCSC says prompt injection “may never be totally mitigated” and advises: “Beware any that claim they can ‘stop’ prompt injection”. Keep the filter for monitoring and friction. Don’t count it as the boundary. Measured: mostly bypassed.
    4Tools and dataThis is the boundary. If the tool can’t send, no prompt can make it send. The NCSC recommends “deterministic (non-LLM) safeguards that constrain the actions of the system”. Step 11.4 built the same rule for a connector, and in step 19.3 a reply tool was the way out that completed the risky set. Guidance.
    5GatewayRouting and fallback live where every request passes. It also changes your security, your data terms and your price, which is why the next step treats it as a decision. Benchmarks only for savings; vendor-measured for the security effect.
    6Provider contract and settingsNo gateway can enforce what a provider keeps. It’s an agreement, and it has gaps: Anthropic’s zero-retention terms don’t cover features such as batch and file storage, and its API “does not block these features” (vendor, read 12 November 2026). Its newest top models aren’t available under zero retention at all unless Anthropic expressly authorises it. Vendor terms.
    7Tools and dataRetrieval must run with the student’s rights, so restricted text never enters the session (step 4.5). A filter on the answer would be too late. Guidance.
    8GatewayThe FinOps Foundation: “Model providers do not support the tagging FinOps teams rely on for Allocation”, so “An LLM proxy or gateway in the request path attaches your own metadata” (28 October 2026). Practitioner guidance.
    9OperationsA test set of your own, run again on every change (step 5.5 builds one). NIST AI 600-1 suggests re-assessing third-party models for uses “not evaluated in initial testing” (MG-3.1-003). Guidance.
    10Each assistant, checked at the gatewayThe team that tested a version should name it; the gateway can refuse names not on its list. Our reading.
    11GatewayOne place to rotate and revoke. Vendors describe managed identities to the model service instead of keys. Vendor description.
    12Operations, fed by the gatewayThe gateway collects the numbers, and someone has to watch them. The FinOps Foundation advises reporting “median and high-percentile cost per run, rather than as a single average”. Practitioner guidance.

    Count the gateway rows: six of twelve. A gateway does real work, but half the controls live elsewhere, including the two that most limit harm (4 and 7).

    2 · What this means for the architecture

    A gateway is a policy enforcement point for traffic: who called, which model, how many tokens, at what cost. It isn’t a security boundary for meaning. It sees text pass, and can’t tell whether that text has steered the model. So the controls that limit harm sit with the tools: what the assistant may read, and what it may do. Put those in place first, and the gateway can be added later without becoming the thing everything depends on.

    Think deeper: A shared gateway gives Westmere one place for keys, quotas, logs and cost tags. It also gives it one place to fail, one place to attack, and one team whose backlog every project now waits on. ADR-0012 asks for a funded owner. Would you fund it before the second project goes live, or wait for the third? What would have to be true for you to say “not yet”?

    Is an AI gateway a control point or a new single point of failure?

    The pattern

    The API gateway and the policy enforcement point, which you already run for ordinary APIs. Its failure mode is also familiar: the enterprise service bus that gathered business logic into “smart pipes” until every change queued behind one team. An AI gateway can repeat that if prompts, routing rules and model-specific features move into it.

    What is really being decided

    Which controls are shared, and which stay with each assistant. Then who owns the shared ones, funds them and answers when they fail. A gateway that only does keys, quotas, logs and cost tags is a thin utility. One that also rewrites prompts, picks models and filters content is a platform product, and needs the funded owner ADR-0012 asks for.

    The forces

    • Consistency against coupling: one place for policy is consistent. But every provider-specific feature routed through it brings back, in Thoughtworks’ words, “the coupling the gateway is meant to eliminate” (April 2026).
    • Visibility against concentration: the gateway sees all traffic, so it’s also the most valuable thing to attack. Thoughtworks keeps LiteLLM at Trial rather than Adopt, largely because “more than 25 CVEs have been reported this year alone” (November 2026). One listed in the US National Vulnerability Database, CVE-2026-30623, is scored 9.8 out of 10 there by CISA (NVD’s own analysis was still pending on 12 November 2026): in version 1.18.10, a user adding an MCP server could name any command, and LiteLLM ran it on the host without validation.
    • Cost attribution against effort: without something in the request path, the bill arrives as one number per provider account. The FinOps Foundation’s first step is to “Inventory all model provider accounts, API keys”.
    • Evidence against expectation: we found no independent, measured evaluation of an AI gateway’s security or cost benefit. The case rests on guidance, vendor documentation and familiar patterns.
    • What it can’t see: a gateway logs and limits traffic. It doesn’t know what the model concluded from a retrieved page, so it can’t replace limits on tools.

    Left open

    • Should the gateway be a thin utility, or a platform product with its own roadmap and owner?
    • When a gateway outage stops all three assistants, who decides whether they may call providers directly until it’s back?
    • Does one gateway serve both model calls and MCP traffic (step 19.5), or are they separate concerns?
    • Who may add a provider-specific feature that only one project needs?
    Evidence: how often input filters are bypassed

    Hackett et al. (LLMSec 2025; authors at Mindgard, an AI security vendor, and Lancaster University) tested six commercial and open detectors for prompt injection and jailbreaks with two families of evasion: character changes (homoglyphs, zero-width characters, emoji smuggling) and word-level attacks guided by an offline model. Most detectors missed character-injection attacks more than 70% of the time on average. Emoji smuggling reached 100% for both injections and jailbreaks. One detector, Protect AI v2, held injection success to about 20%.

    Nasr, Carlini et al. (“The Attacker Moves Second”, October 2025 preprint; authors include staff of Anthropic and Google DeepMind) took 12 recent defences against jailbreaks and prompt injection and attacked them adaptively, changing the attack in response to the defence: “we bypass 12 recent defenses … with attack success rate above 90% for most”, while “the majority of defenses originally reported near-zero attack success rates”. Their point is about method. A defence tested only against fixed attacks will look stronger than it is.

    UK AISI (17 February 2026) showed the same for jailbreaks against the strongest vendor classifiers. Its boundary-point method raised average success against one vendor’s classifiers from 0% to 25.5%, for about $330 in queries. It recommends “batch-level monitoring that aggregates traffic across interactions”, a job for the gateway’s logs rather than its filter.

    What these studies don’t show. They measure detectors alone, not a whole deployment with limited tools. A filter that fails 70% of the time still stops 30%, and leaves a trace. That’s why we call it friction and monitoring, not a boundary.

    Read more

    • Bypassing LLM Guardrails (Hackett et al., LLMSec 2025)
    • The Attacker Moves Second (Nasr, Carlini et al., 2025, preprint)
    • Boundary point jailbreaking (UK AISI, February 2026)
    • Prompt injection is not SQL injection (NCSC, December 2025)
    How it works: what a gateway does, and what has been measured

    An AI gateway is an API gateway that understands model traffic. Microsoft’s documentation for Azure API Management (29 May 2026) is a typical list of features, described by the vendor: token limits per consumer (llm-token-limit), token metrics with your own dimensions such as user and API (llm-emit-token-metric), semantic caching (llm-semantic-cache-store and -lookup), content safety checks, load balancing, a circuit breaker, managed identities instead of keys, and logging of prompts and completions. It fronts OpenAI-style, Anthropic Messages and Google Vertex AI APIs. Open-source proxies such as LiteLLM, and cloud and vendor products, offer similar lists.

    Semantic caching reuses an earlier answer when a new prompt is close in meaning. It saves tokens only when questions repeat, and it can serve one person’s answer to another person’s question. We found no independent measure of its savings. The FinOps Foundation warns that ordinary prompt caching can cost money too: “If cached content is not read back enough times before it expires, the write premium costs more than caching saves.”

    Control frameworks. The Cloud Security Alliance’s AI Controls Matrix v1.1 (14 July 2026) has 247 control objectives in 18 domains, and assigns each to roles: model provider, application provider, orchestrated service provider, AI customer and cloud provider. It’s a good checklist for deciding which layer owns a control. NIST AI 600-1 suggests an inventory of generative AI systems, including versions and known issues (GV-1.6-001 and -003), and regular review of guardrails (MS-2.5-006).

    Read more

    • AI gateway capabilities in Azure API Management (Microsoft, vendor documentation)
    • Managing AI Token Costs from Direct Model Provider APIs and How token pricing really works (FinOps Foundation, both updated 28 October 2026)
    • LiteLLM (Thoughtworks Technology Radar)
    • AI Controls Matrix v1.1 (Cloud Security Alliance)
    • NIST AI 600-1: Generative AI Profile (PDF)

    Choose a model

    Choose a model for three Westmere jobs by what decides each one, route requests on paper, and see why a fallback model changes your security as well as your bill.

    Step21.2

    Part 21
    The AI platform: models, cost and change
    Time
    11 min
    Last reviewed
    12 November 2026

    Keep the first part quick: the aim is to name the criterion that decides each job, not to pick a product. Spend most of the time on the router. Ask who put S4 and S9 with a model, then ask what a router that only chooses between models would do with them. Finish on the fallback figure.

    “Which model should we use?” is usually asked once, at the start of a project, and answered with a product name. It’s really three decisions: which tier of model each kind of request needs, where requests go when that model fails or refuses, and where the data may be processed. Product names change every few months. These decisions last longer.

    1 · Choose by job

    Here are the three Westmere jobs. For each, name the one criterion that decides it – quality, speed, cost, context size or where data is processed – and the tier you’d start testing with: small, main or top.

    JobWhat it doesVolume and data
    Student help chatbotShort answers about enrolment, timetables and services, from published pagesThousands of chats a day in term. Students may type personal details
    Staff policy assistantAnswers HR questions from the Policy Library: 412 documents, 38 staff-only, quoting the clauseA few hundred questions a week. Questions can reveal a staff member’s situation
    Service desk assistantSorts tickets, drafts replies, summarises long threads overnightAbout 400 tickets a working day. Tickets contain names, devices and sometimes security incidents
    Our reading: open after you’ve written yours
    • Student help chatbot: speed and cost. High volume, short answers from published pages. Start with a small model and move up only where your tests show a gap. Anthropic’s guide calls this starting “efficiency-first”. Where data is processed matters too, because students type personal details whether you ask them to or not.
    • Staff policy assistant: quality, then where data is processed. A wrong answer about leave or misconduct does real harm, so start with a main-tier model and measure. Context size matters less than it seems: retrieval sends the relevant clauses, not 412 documents (step 4.6). Data terms can rule a model out entirely. Anthropic’s top 5.x models need 30-day retention and aren’t available under zero data retention unless Anthropic expressly authorises it (vendor, read 12 November 2026).
    • Service desk assistant: no single answer. Sorting a ticket and summarising a 40-message thread are different jobs. One model for everything either overpays for the easy work or underperforms on the hard work. That’s the case for routing, which is the next exercise.

    The vendors agree on method, not on models. Anthropic: “Tuning effort is often a better lever than switching models”, and “Having a good evaluation set is the most important step in the process.” OpenAI: “Choose acceptance criteria before comparing models”, and measure “time spent reviewing or repairing the result.” Thoughtworks put “blanket frontier model usage” in Caution in November 2026: “Frontier models can cost significantly more and run more slowly than their more nimble counterparts”.

    2 · Route requests on paper

    A router sends each request to the cheapest model likely to handle it. Be the router. Sort the ten service desk requests (S1 to S10) first. Then sort the four Student Services requests (F1 to F4) with the same rule, without changing it.

    Now give the same list to an assistant and compare. Two assistants, or two runs of one, may route a request differently. Everything in it is invented; don’t use real tickets unless your organisation has approved it.

    You are routing requests for a university service desk. For each request below, answer SMALL (a small, cheap model will do), LARGE (needs a more capable model) or PERSON (should go to a person, not a model). One line each: the code, your answer, and a reason in under ten words. S1. "My password reset link has expired. How do I get a new one?" S2. Put this ticket in one category: hardware, access, software or network. S3. Summarise this 40-message email thread about the failing lab booking system and suggest a likely cause. S4. "My laptop was stolen from the train. It has exam papers on it." S5. Explain to a lecturer why the VPN is slow on campus Wi-Fi, using these three log extracts. S6. Pull the asset tag and room number out of this ticket. S7. "Is the learning system outage over?" S8. Draft a change request to move the print servers to the new data centre. S9. "I think someone is signing in to my account from overseas." S10. Translate the reply to S5 into Vietnamese for an international student. F1. Student Services: "When is the next fee payment due?" F2. Student Services: "Can I get my fees back if I withdraw after the census date for medical reasons?" F3. Student Services: "I can't pay rent this month and I'm thinking of dropping out." F4. Student Services: "How do the payment plan options compare if I start mid-year?"
    What to notice: open after you’ve compared
    • S4, S9 and F3 aren’t model questions. A stolen laptop with exam papers is a data breach. An overseas sign-in is a security incident. A student thinking of dropping out over money needs a person. A router that only chooses between two models has no way to send these to anyone. Someone has to design that exit.
    • S7 and F1 need a lookup, not a bigger model. The answer lives in a system of record (the status page, the fees calendar). Any model, small or large, would guess.
    • S10 is where people split. Translation looks routine, but a wrong word in an explanation to a student is a quality problem. Your answer depends on how you’d test it.
    • F2 and F4 test your rule. A rule written for tickets (“short and factual goes small”) sends F2 small, but it’s a policy interpretation with money at stake. This is what the research found at scale. In RouteLLM (Ong et al.), routers trained only on general chat data performed “at the level of the random router” on MMLU and “close to random” on GSM8K, until a small amount of MMLU data, or data labelled by a model acting as judge, was added.

    A simulation can’t show cost or latency, and one person’s sort isn’t a router. It shows where the routing rule comes from and where it breaks.

    3 · A fallback changes your security, not just your bill

    Every platform needs an answer for when the chosen model fails, is overloaded or refuses. The usual answer is a fallback: try another model. Anthropic now offers this as a server-side option (beta) that the caller turns on: a request its safety classifiers decline on Claude Fable 5.2 is retried on a permitted fallback, Claude Opus 4.8 or Claude Opus 5 (vendor documentation, read 12 November 2026). Its own system card shows what that did to prompt-injection results.

    The vendor’s explanation: “We attribute these relatively higher rates mainly to fallbacks from Fable 5.2 to Opus 4.8”. In a harder test, with an attacker given 200 tries per scenario, 99.46% of answered requests were served by the fallback, and “None of the 43 requests that Fable 5.2 answered itself were compromised.” This is a vendor measuring its own models, and the harder test uses a threat model the vendor calls “deliberately permissive”. These figures are also from runs without the prompt-injection probes the vendor says it deploys in its products; with probes on in the harder test, the share of fallback-served requests that were compromised fell from 90.31% to 28.56%. The lesson doesn’t depend on the exact numbers.

    So what: our reading is that a deployment is only as resistant to prompt injection as the weakest model a request can be routed to. The same goes for data terms and price. Record which model answered each request (item 2 in step 21.1), and test the fallback path as you test the main one. For an agent, which acts on what it reads, this matters most; step 20.4 covers the containment that shouldn’t depend on which model answered.

    4 · What this means for the architecture

    Treat the model as a replaceable component behind a contract you own: your test set, your acceptance bar and your data rules. The model name is a setting you expect to change. What you can’t treat as a setting is everything that changes with it – behaviour, injection resistance, where data goes and what a request costs. A routing rule or fallback list is therefore an architecture decision, and needs an owner and a record like any other.

    Think deeper: A fallback keeps the service up when the main model refuses. But a refusal is sometimes the system working, as when a classifier declines a request that looks like an attack. Retrying it on a weaker model turns a block into an answer. Which of Westmere’s three assistants should fail closed when the main model refuses, and which should fall back? Who decides, and where is it written down?

    Is the choice of model a decision you make once, or a setting you’ll change every few months?

    The pattern

    A pluggable provider behind an interface you own: the strategy pattern in code, multi-sourcing in procurement, and a circuit breaker for the fallback. You already do this for payment gateways and identity providers. The difference here is that two providers behind the same interface don’t behave the same, and a newer version of the same model may not either.

    What is really being decided

    What Westmere fixes and what it lets vary. Fix the test set, the acceptance bar, the data rules and the record of which model answered. Let the model, its effort setting and the routing rules vary, but only through a change that reruns the tests. The real choice is who may change the model, and what evidence they need.

    The forces

    • Portability against capability: a common interface lets you switch. Each provider’s distinctive features – caching, tools, reasoning controls – are often where the value is, and using them ties you to that provider.
    • Cost against quality per request: routing saves money where easy requests are common and easy to spot. The savings measured so far are on benchmarks, not production (Going deeper).
    • Availability against posture: a fallback keeps the service up, and may lower its injection resistance, change where data is processed and change the price.
    • Data terms against the newest model: the cheapest options (batch, global processing) widen where data goes, and the newest top model may be the one you can’t use under zero retention.
    • Test effort against pace: Anthropic shipped three Fable versions between June and November 2026. Every switch needs the test set rerun. Without one, each switch is a guess.

    Left open

    • Who may change the routing rules or fallback list, and does that go through the review board?
    • Should every assistant be portable across two providers, or only those where an outage would hurt?
    • When the fallback answers, should the user be told?
    Evidence: what routing studies measured

    FrugalGPT (Chen, Zaharia and Zou, Transactions on Machine Learning Research, December 2024) sends each query first to a cheap model and moves up a cascade until a learned scorer accepts the answer. The published version’s abstract reports it “can match the performance of the best individual generative LLM (e.g., GPT-4) with up to a 98% cost reduction or improve the accuracy over GPT-4 by 4% at the same cost.” The 98% is the HEADLINES dataset (financial news classification). Other datasets saved 52% to 75% at matched accuracy. The scorer is trained per dataset, and the tasks are classification and short question answering, not open-ended drafting.

    RouteLLM (Ong et al., revised February 2025) trains a router to choose between a strong model (GPT-4) and a weak one (Mixtral 8x7B). Its best cost-saving ratio was 3.66 on MT Bench while keeping 95% of GPT-4’s quality. On MMLU it was 1.41 (92% quality), and on GSM8K 1.49 (87%). The paper works the ratio out from how many GPT-4 calls its best router needed compared with routing at random, so it isn’t a bill compared with using GPT-4 alone. Routers trained only on general chat data performed close to random on the knowledge and maths benchmarks until task-specific or judge-labelled data was added. Running the router itself cost between $3.19 and $39.26 per million requests.

    The Routing Plateau (Lu et al., v2 September 2026, preprint, abstract read) compared many routing methods on five benchmarks and found they “converge to a narrow performance range that remains far below the oracle router” – the ideal router that always knows which model is good enough. More data, larger encoders and fine-tuning improved eight routers by 1.24 percentage points on average.

    Where things stand. Routing saves money on benchmarks where cheap models are often good enough, and the saving shrinks on harder or unfamiliar tasks. We found no independent study of a production router’s savings. Treat a vendor’s routing saving as a hypothesis to test on your own traffic.

    Read more

    • FrugalGPT (Chen, Zaharia and Zou, TMLR 2024), the published version quoted here, and its 2023 preprint, which has fewer datasets and a slightly different abstract
    • RouteLLM (Ong et al.)
    • The Routing Plateau (Lu et al., 2026, preprint)
    • Blanket frontier model usage (Thoughtworks Technology Radar, November 2026)
    • Choosing the right model (Anthropic) and Model selection (OpenAI) – vendor guidance
    How it works: where the data goes when you choose a deployment

    “Where data is processed” is a choice you make per deployment, and it changes with price and features. Examples, from vendor documentation read on 12 November 2026:

    • Anthropic API. By default, inference may run in any available geography. On Claude 4.6 and later models, restricting it to the US with inference_geo: "us" “incurs a 1.1x multiplier on all token pricing categories”. Under a zero data retention agreement, Anthropic “does not store customer prompts or responses at rest after the API response is returned”, but features such as batch and file storage are outside it, and the API “does not block these features”. On Amazon Bedrock and on Claude models that Google Cloud manages, the cloud provider is the data processor, so its terms apply.
    • Microsoft Foundry (Azure). Standard deployments process prompts “within the customer-specified geography”. Global deployments “may be processed in any geography where the relevant model … is deployed”. DataZone deployments stay within the US or the EU. “Batch processing is a Global deployment type”. Microsoft says these models’ prompts and completions are not available to OpenAI.
    • Batch everywhere. Anthropic, OpenAI and Google all price batch jobs at about half. Batch suits overnight work such as summarising the service desk backlog, if the data terms allow it.

    Our reading: write the data rule first (“staff HR questions are processed in our region, with no retention beyond 30 days”), then list which models and deployment types meet it. That list, not the leaderboard, is your shortlist.

    Cost a use case

    Size one service desk request in tokens, cost it from today’s price list, then find what the simple sum leaves out and cost it again.

    Step21.3

    Part 21
    The AI platform: models, cost and change
    Time
    12 min
    Last reviewed
    12 November 2026

    Have everyone use the same price list so the room can compare, and write the date it was read on the board. The point isn’t the dollar figure. It’s the ratio between the two worksheets, and which line moved it most. Leave three minutes for the Think deeper question: it usually shows that people’s time costs more than tokens.

    The first cost estimate for an AI feature is usually one line: requests times tokens times price. It’s a reasonable start and nearly always too low, because the things it leaves out multiply rather than add. In this step you’ll cost Westmere’s service desk assistant twice: once as the simple sum, then with what real use adds. Step 3.2 introduced tokens as the unit of cost; this step uses them.

    1 · Size one request

    Here is one complete request as the model would receive it: the system prompt, one retrieved knowledge article and the ticket. It’s invented.

    Paste it into the estimator to see roughly how many tokens it takes.

    Paste the request here.

    An estimate: characters ÷ 4, rounded up. Each model family splits text differently, and Anthropic says the tokenizer in its Claude 4.7 and later models “produces approximately 30% more tokens for the same text” than its earlier one (pricing page, read 12 November 2026). For an exact count, use the provider’s own token counter.

    You should get about 750 tokens. In production the assistant would retrieve around four more articles and carry tool definitions, so we start the worksheet at 3,000 input tokens. The reply is capped at 150 words, about 200 tokens by the rule of thumb in step 3.2. We allow 300 output tokens to cover the category and source lines and tokenizers that count more.

    2 · The simple sum

    Before you type a price, write down your guess for a month.

    Now open one provider’s current price list and choose a main-tier model. Type its price per million input tokens and per million output tokens, and write the date you read it. Prices change on set dates: Google’s list on 12 November 2026 showed Gemini 4 Carbon doubling from 1 December. A price is true only on the day you read it.

    Price lists: Anthropic · OpenAI · Google. Cloud platforms such as Azure and Bedrock publish their own, which can differ for the same model.

    3 · What the simple sum leaves out

    Before you open the list, write down two things you think it misses.

    What it leaves outHow it worksSource
    Conversation historyEach turn re-sends everything before it, so “the total cost of a session grows much faster than the number of turns”. On Anthropic’s newer models, earlier turns’ thinking is kept in context and billed as input.FinOps Foundation (28 October 2026); Anthropic
    Reasoning tokensReasoning models think before answering. OpenAI: reasoning tokens are not shown but “are billed as output tokens”, and a request may use “anywhere from a few hundred to tens of thousands”. Epoch AI found reasoning models produce “around 8x more tokens on average” on benchmark questions (April 2025).OpenAI; Epoch AI
    Retries and failed runsTimeouts, refusals and answers that fail a check are still billed. A request can even hit its output limit “before any visible output tokens are produced” (OpenAI). “Failed and discarded runs are still cost.”OpenAI; FinOps Foundation
    Evaluation runsEvery model or prompt change reruns the test set (step 5.5), several times, often with a model as judge.Our reading
    AgentsAn agent loops, calls tools and may start helpers. UK AISI: “A task a person could finish in a minute costs an agent thousands of tokens”, and longer tasks millions. Anthropic: “Subagents can account for a large part of what a session costs.” Step 20.4 covers budgets as a control.UK AISI (July 2026); Anthropic
    Price modifiersBatch about halves the price; fast or priority modes cost about twice as much; processing in one region can add 10% (Anthropic’s US-only option is 1.1x); search tools are billed per search.Vendor pricing pages
    Caching (can reduce it)Re-used prompt text is cheaper to read, but writing it to the cache costs extra. Anthropic: a 5-minute cache write pays for itself “after one cache read”. The FinOps Foundation: if it isn’t read back enough times, “the write premium costs more than caching saves.”Anthropic; FinOps Foundation

    4 · Cost it again

    This worksheet starts from an illustrative “realistic” profile. Change any number you disagree with, and keep the same prices as before.

    • 420 requests a day: the same 400 tickets, plus 5% retries and failed runs.
    • 10,000 input tokens: three turns per ticket, each re-sending what went before (about 3,000 + 3,300 + 3,700).
    • 4,000 output tokens: three replies of 300 visible tokens, plus about 1,000 reasoning tokens a turn (3,900, rounded up). Reasoning could be far more; OpenAI suggests reserving at least 25,000 tokens for reasoning and output when you start.
    A dated worked example: open after you’ve filled in both worksheets

    With Anthropic’s Claude Sonnet 5.5 at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output (US dollars, list price on 12 November 2026), the simple sum is about $79 a month, and output is a third of it. The realistic profile is about $554 a month, about seven times as much, and output is now two-thirds of it. A small model at a twentieth of the price lowers both, but the ratio stays about the same, because the drivers are tokens, not price.

    Three things change the answer more than the choice of vendor: how many turns a conversation takes, how much the model reasons, and whether the long, unchanging part of the prompt is cached. None of those is on the price list. You find them by logging real use, which is why the FinOps Foundation suggests reporting “median and high-percentile cost per run, rather than as a single average.”

    Arithmetic: simple, (3,000 × 2 + 300 × 10) ÷ 1,000,000 = $0.009 a request, × 400 × 22 = $79.20. Realistic, (10,000 × 2 + 4,000 × 10) ÷ 1,000,000 = $0.06, × 420 × 22 = $554.40. Agents and evaluation runs aren’t included.

    5 · What this means for the architecture

    The number that matters isn’t cost per token or per request but cost per successful outcome, which the FinOps Foundation defines as the total cost “counting only runs whose output clears the quality floor”. For the service desk, that means cost per draft an analyst sends with light edits, including the analyst’s time to check it. To measure it you need the gateway’s per-request records (step 21.1), the test set’s quality bar, and a way to tell which drafts were used.

    Think deeper: Suppose analysts rewrite three drafts in ten from scratch, and checking each of the others takes two minutes. At a realistic hourly rate, how does the analysts’ checking time compare with your token bill? If it dwarfs it, what should Westmere spend its next dollar on: a cheaper model, a better model, or better retrieval? OpenAI’s own guidance says to measure “time spent reviewing or repairing the result”. Who at Westmere would count that?

    Who owns the AI bill when the unit price falls and the bill still rises?

    The pattern

    Cloud cost management, or FinOps: showback and chargeback, unit economics, and capacity planning. You’ve seen this with cloud computing, where the price per server fell for years while total spend grew. Tokens add a twist: the provider’s newer models may use more tokens per task, so a price cut and a bigger bill can arrive together.

    What is really being decided

    Who carries the bill (central IT, each project, each faculty), what unit it’s measured in, and what happens when use grows faster than the budget. Then which levers belong to whom: the project owns its prompts and turn count, the platform owns caching and routing, procurement owns the price and commitment.

    The forces

    • Falling prices against rising use: Epoch AI estimates the cost of a fixed level of performance falls about 47% a quarter, and adds that almost nobody stays on that cost frontier (Going deeper has the quote). Your model choice, not the frontier, sets your price.
    • Price per token against tokens per task: Artificial Analysis reported that one new model’s per-token price had doubled, while it used about 40% fewer output tokens, for a “net ~+20% cost” on its index (April 2026). Compare cost per task, not list prices.
    • Showback against central funding: charging projects makes cost visible and discourages experiments. Central funding encourages use and hides who drives the bill.
    • Commitments against flexibility: reserved capacity is cheaper per token, and ties you to one model that will be retired (step 21.4).
    • Attribution needs plumbing: providers don’t support the tags FinOps teams use to allocate cost (control 8 in step 21.1), so the gateway or each project has to attach them.

    Left open

    • Should a project’s AI spend come from its own budget or a central pool, and does the answer change after the pilot?
    • Who can stop an assistant whose cost per successful outcome is rising?
    • Do you budget for evaluation runs and migrations as running costs or as project costs?
    How it works: the parts of a price

    The three main vendors price the same way, and a cost model can follow their structure even as the numbers change:

    • Input and output are priced per million tokens, output at about five times input. For example, on 12 November 2026: Anthropic’s Claude Sonnet 5.5 $2 / $10, OpenAI’s gpt-6.1-sol $2 / $10, Google’s Gemini 3.8 Flash $0.75 / $3.75 (rising to $1.50 / $7.50 on 1 January 2027).
    • Reasoning is billed as output on all three. Anthropic and OpenAI each report, in the response’s usage data, how many of the billed output tokens were reasoning.
    • Cached input is cheaper to read: Anthropic charges 0.1 times the base input price on most models, and its 5-minute cache write costs 1.25 times.
    • Batch jobs are about half price at all three, in exchange for waiting.
    • Speed tiers cost more: Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s fast modes are about twice the price.
    • Region can cost more: Anthropic’s US-only processing is 1.1 times; OpenAI lists a 10% uplift for regional processing on newer models.
    • Long prompts can change the rate: OpenAI’s top model costs more above 272,000 input tokens; Anthropic’s Haiku 5.5 costs more above 100,000. Anthropic’s Claude 4.6 and later models, apart from Haiku 5.5, charge the same rate up to 1 million tokens.
    • Hosts differ: for open-weight models served by many vendors, the FinOps Foundation notes that “Prices for the same model have historically varied by as much as 30 percent between vendors.”

    Read more

    • Pricing (Anthropic)
    • Pricing (OpenAI) and Reasoning models (OpenAI)
    • Pricing (Google Gemini API)
    • How token pricing really works (FinOps Foundation)
    Evidence: why bills rise while prices fall

    Prices for a fixed level of performance fall fast. Emberson and Roodman at Epoch AI (“The plunging price of thought”, September 2026) estimate that “the cost of a given level of AI performance has fallen about 47% per quarter” since 2023. That measures the cheapest way to reach a fixed benchmark score, not what any organisation pays. The authors note that “Essentially no user stays permanently on the cost frontier” and that “doing well on a benchmark is not synonymous with useful work.” Earlier Epoch analyses used a different method, so their figures aren’t comparable with this one.

    Answers are getting longer. Epoch AI (April 2025; 77 models, 11 of them reasoning models, on three benchmarks) found reasoning models’ output growing about 5 times a year (90% interval 2 to 13), and non-reasoning models’ about 2.2 times. The authors warn that leaving out individual models “can shift the overall trend by significant amounts.”

    Price and tokens move separately. Artificial Analysis (April 2026): a new model’s per-token price had doubled, but “a ~40% token use reduction largely absorbs the hike”, for a net cost about 20% higher on its index. The reverse also happens. Anthropic’s Sonnet 5.5 is a third cheaper per token than Sonnet 4.5, but its newer tokenizer produces about 30% more tokens for the same text, so the saving for the same text is nearer 13% (our arithmetic from the pricing page). That counts the tokenizer only. Anthropic’s migration guide says Sonnet 5.5 also thinks by default where Sonnet 4.5 didn’t, and thinking is billed as output, so a real request could cost more than before. Measure it on your own requests.

    Agents change the scale. UK AISI (July 2026) found that raising agents’ budgets from 1 million to 10 million tokens raised performance by about 25% on software engineering tasks, so what an agent can do and what it costs can’t be read apart. Step 20.3 has more on scores that depend on the budget.

    • Pricing and Claude Sonnet 5.5 migration guide (Anthropic, vendor documentation)

  • I costed it again with history, reasoning and retries, and named the line that moved it most.
  • I can explain why cost per successful outcome matters more than price per token.
