    Plan for retirement

    A retirement notice arrives for the model in production. Work out what happens on the day on each platform, what must be re-tested and who decides, then close the Part.

    Step21.4

    Part 21
    The AI platform: models, cost and change
    Time
    12 min
    Last reviewed
    12 November 2026

    The sort takes three minutes and usually surprises people: most expect every platform to behave the same way. Give the plan ten minutes in pairs, one person as the service owner and one as the reviewer. Then allow about fifteen minutes for the discussion questions at the end of the step.

    On 30 September 2026 Anthropic told developers that Claude Sonnet 4.5 would be retired on its API on 30 November 2026, and recommended Claude Sonnet 5.5 instead. Suppose Westmere’s staff policy assistant runs on Sonnet 4.5. That gives the HR service owner 61 days to choose, test and switch, or the assistant stops. And ICT’s prototype uses the same model through Amazon Bedrock, which has its own dates.

    A model is a dependency with a published end date. Notice periods are short by enterprise standards: Anthropic promises “at least 60 days’ notice before model retirement for publicly released models”; OpenAI gives generally available models “At least 6 months”; Microsoft Foundry sends a retirement notice at least 60 days before for generally available models. Anthropic shipped three versions of its top model between June and November 2026. Our reading: a system built on one of these models should expect a forced migration within one to two years, and each one is real work.

    1 · What happens on the day?

    For each Westmere deployment, predict what happens to requests once the model is retired on that platform. The platforms’ behaviour is real, as published on 12 November 2026; the deployments are invented.

    What each platform says: open after you’ve placed all six
    #What happensWhat the vendor says
    E1Requests failAnthropic: “Retired: The model is no longer available for use. Requests to retired models fail.”
    E2Requests fail, on Bedrock’s later dateBedrock: after end of life, requests “will fail” and “Migration will not happen automatically.” In Legacy, “existing customers may lose access to Legacy models after 15 days of inactivity”, so a prototype nobody uses for a fortnight can lose access early. Its dates “may differ from dates published by model providers”.
    E3Swapped for youMicrosoft Foundry: Global Standard, Data Zone Standard and Standard deployments are upgraded automatically when a version retires, on a rolling, region-by-region basis. A deployment can opt out with NoAutoUpgrade (“never auto-upgrade—deployment stops working at retirement”), so check the setting rather than assume it.
    E4Requests failMicrosoft: “Provisioned deployments are NOT auto-upgraded.” At retirement, “All inference requests return 410 Gone.” “Retirement dates aren’t extendable.”
    E5Sent to a different model, at its priceGoogle: from 1 December 2026, requests to gemini-2.5-pro “automatically route to” gemini-3.8-flash and are billed at that model’s rates. That price itself doubles on 1 January 2027. The page doesn’t say whether the response tells you a reroute happened.
    E6Wherever your gateway sends itA configured fallback turns a loud failure into a quiet swap to an older model, with the security effects from step 21.2. LiteLLM’s drop_params mode “silently discards unsupported parameters”, as Thoughtworks noted (April 2026).

    The quiet cases are the risky ones. The service keeps answering, so nobody runs the tests, and the first sign of a changed model is a complaint.

    2 · Plan the migration

    Fill in the plan for the staff policy assistant, or for an assistant you know, described only in general terms. Write down what you’re unsure of rather than leaving it blank.

    Two parts of the plan draw on earlier Parts. The re-test in section 3 is the comparison from step 5.3, scored as in step 5.4, using the test set from step 5.5. If you don’t have a test set, that is the first finding of this plan. The security tests are the planted-page tests from step 11.3.

    Model answer for the staff policy assistant: open after you’ve filled in yours

    Notice three things the notice didn’t say. A parameter the assistant relies on now causes an error. The tokenizer changes and thinking is on by default, so the saving is smaller than the price cut and may not be a saving at all. And the same model has a second deadline on another platform.

    3 · What this means for the architecture

    Plan model migration as a running cost, not a project. NIST’s Generative AI Profile suggests that organisations “test and manage risks related to rollover and fallback technologies” and acknowledge “that rollover and fallback may include manual processing” (GV-6.2-006). In practice that means three standing things: an inventory of which assistant uses which model on which host, a test set that can run against a new model in a day, and a named owner who can decide to switch, or to pause the assistant if nothing passes.

    Think deeper: Auto-upgrade keeps the student chatbot running and moves it to a model nobody tested. A pinned version stops working at retirement and forces the test. Which would you choose for each of Westmere’s three assistants? And is a service that stops on a known date better or worse than one that changes behaviour quietly on a date you don’t control?

    Who owns a dependency that changes behaviour without a code change?

    The pattern

    Technology lifecycle management: end-of-support dates for operating systems and databases, kept in a register and planned for. Two things differ. The notice is weeks or months, not years. And a model can change behaviour with no change to your code – through an auto-upgrade, a reroute, a fallback, or a provider changing what it serves under the same name.

    What is really being decided

    Pin or float. Pinning a dated version means you control when behaviour changes, and you must migrate by the deadline. Floating on a moving name or an auto-upgrade keeps things running, and lets the provider decide when your behaviour changes. Then who owns each migration: the project that built the assistant, or the platform team that runs the gateway.

    The forces

    • Control against continuity: a pinned model stops on a known date; an upgraded one keeps going on an untested model.
    • Notice against effort: 60 days is enough to rerun a ready test set, and not enough to build one.
    • One model, many hosts: the same model retires on different dates and terms on different platforms, so the register needs the host, not just the model.
    • Behaviour against capability: a newer model can be more capable and still break your assumptions about length, format or refusals.
    • What you can verify: research suggests customers can’t reliably check which model an API is serving (Going deeper). Your own test set is the practical check.

    Left open

    • Should every assistant pin a dated version, or only those whose answers carry weight?
    • If no replacement passes the bar before the deadline, who may decide to pause the service?
    • Who reads retirement notices – the project, the platform team or procurement – and how do they reach the owner?
    Evidence: does behaviour change between versions?

    Chen, Zaharia and Zou (arXiv, 2023) compared March and June 2023 versions of GPT-3.5 and GPT-4. “GPT-4 (March 2023) was reasonable at identifying prime vs. composite numbers (84% accuracy)”, and the June version “was poor on these same questions (51% accuracy)”. They also found “GPT-4’s ability to follow user instructions has decreased over time”, and called for “continuous monitoring of LLMs”.

    Narayanan and Kapoor challenged the paper’s first version (July 2023), which tested only primes: “They picked 500 numbers, but all of them were prime!” On that test a model that tends to say “prime” scores well and one that tends to say “composite” scores badly, whatever it can actually do. The revised paper, quoted above, tests 1,000 numbers, half prime and half composite. Our reading: 51% on that test is about what a model scores by giving the same answer every time, which fits their account. They argue that capability stayed much the same while behaviour shifted, and they point at who pays: “Code that is deployed to users might simply break if the model underneath changes its behavior.”

    Can you tell which model you’re getting? Gao, Liang and Guestrin (ICLR 2025) note that API providers “may quantize, watermark, or finetune the underlying model”, “possibly without notifying users”. Testing endpoints that offered four of Meta’s open Llama models in mid-2024, they found “11 out of 31 endpoints serve different distributions than reference weights released by Meta.” Cai et al. (2025, preprint, abstract read) argue that software-only checks for model substitution are unreliable. This is about third-party hosts of open models, not a finding about any particular vendor.

    Where things stand. Behaviour changes between versions are documented. Silent changes under the same name are shown for some hosts. We found no published, reliable way for a customer to verify the model behind an API, so your own test set, run regularly, is the evidence you’ll have.

    Read more

    • How is ChatGPT’s behavior changing over time? (Chen, Zaharia and Zou)
    • Is GPT-4 getting worse over time? (Narayanan and Kapoor, 2023)
    • Model Equality Testing: Which Model Is This API Serving? (Gao, Liang and Guestrin, ICLR 2025)
    • Are You Getting What You Pay For? Auditing Model Substitution in LLM APIs (Cai et al., 2025, preprint)
    How it works: notice periods by platform
    • Anthropic API: “at least 60 days’ notice” for publicly released models, and new models list a retirement date of “Not sooner than” a year after release. Amazon Bedrock and the Claude models that Google Cloud manages “set their own retirement schedules”.
    • OpenAI API: “At least 6 months” for generally available models, “At least 3 months” for specialised variants and image models, and preview models “may be retired with much shorter notice, such as 2 weeks.” Platform features retire too: the Evals platform and Agent Builder are scheduled to shut down on 30 November 2026.
    • Google Gemini API: listed shutdown dates are the “earliest possible dates”. Retired models may be rerouted to another model at that model’s price.
    • Google Cloud’s Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform (formerly Vertex AI): generally available models are listed either for at least 12 months after release or, for shorter-term models, with a fixed date that gives at least 45 days to migrate. Listed dates won’t be moved earlier. Gemini 2.5 Pro, Flash and Flash-Lite retired there on 20 October 2026, six weeks before the Gemini API starts rerouting 2.5 Pro and 2.5 Flash on 1 December. On the Gemini API, 2.5 Flash-Lite stays available.
    • Microsoft Foundry: generally available models have an 18-month lifecycle (12 months for models from Anthropic, DeepSeek, Fireworks and Mistral), a notice at least 60 days before retirement, and dates that “aren’t extendable”. Standard deployment types auto-upgrade; provisioned ones don’t.
    • Amazon Bedrock: for models launched from 7 September 2026, the Legacy period before end of life is 6 months or 45 days. For older models, at least 6 months, with a “public extended access” period where “you should expect higher pricing, which will be set by the model provider”. Yet in some regions Claude 3 Haiku went from Legacy on 10 October to end of life on 13 November 2026, about a month, though the same model had entered Legacy in other regions on 10 March. Read the dates for your region, not just the rule.

    • Foundry Models lifecycle and support policy (Microsoft)
    • Model lifecycle (Amazon Bedrock) and Model lifecycle (Legacy)

    What you can do now

    You have finished Part 21. You can place a control on the layer that actually enforces it, and say which controls have evidence behind them. You can choose a model by the criterion that decides the job, and explain why a fallback changes security, data terms and price. You can cost a use case from today’s prices and name what the simple sum leaves out. And you can plan a model’s retirement before the notice arrives.

    Questions to discuss

    In a group session, share your answers, and park anything that needs a longer discussion for the end.

    • Which AI services in your organisation would fail loudly on a model’s retirement day, and which would change quietly? Does anyone know?
    • Who reads model retirement notices where you work, and how does one reach the person who owns the service?
    • Would you fund a shared AI gateway now, or wait? What would it have to do that each project can’t?
    • Where should a fallback be allowed, and where should the service fail closed instead?
    • What would you need to measure cost per successful outcome for one assistant, and who would own the number?

    Export your notes – they include your control placements, your cost worksheets and your retirement plan.

    Why reuse came first

    “Reuse before buy before build” was written when code was dear. Sort its reasons into the ones cheap code changes and the ones it leaves alone.

    Step22.1

    Part 22
    Build, buy or generate
    Time
    9 min
    Last reviewed
    12 November 2026

    Open with the question as someone in the room would ask it, and take two or three answers before anyone reads the evidence box. Give the sort four silent minutes, then compare. The argument worth having is over the reasons people put under “Stronger”.

    Someone in your organisation will soon say it, if they haven’t already: “An agent built a working version of that in an afternoon. Why are we paying for the renewal?” It’s a fair question. A first working version has become much cheaper to produce, and the principle many architecture teams work by, reuse before buy before build, took shape when it wasn’t.

    Step 17.4 leaned on that order for AI features: switch on what you own, then buy, then build. This Part tests the order itself. Our starting view, and the one that prompted this Part, is that cheap code is changing that principle, and that nobody has yet worked out how to make vibe-coded software reliable in production. The evidence supports some of that and not the rest. This Part shows you both, with dates, because the evidence is moving.

    Where the evidence stands · checked 12 November 2026

    Solid
    The principle’s published reasons are cost, duplication, lock-in and the upkeep people forget; the effort of writing code is only part of the cost (US Office of Management and Budget, 2016; European Commission’s architecture principles, undated). In the one trial we read that measured both, experienced developers believed AI had made them 20% faster when their tasks had taken 19% longer (METR, July 2025, 16 developers). METR adds that survey estimates of AI’s effect have tended to run above experimental ones (May 2026).
    Thin
    That organisations are now building what they used to buy. There are anecdotes, including the UK NCSC’s (March 2026), and one vendor’s survey of builders, its own customers among them (Retool, February 2026). We found no independent data. Practices for making generated code reliable in production: none has a controlled trial behind it that we found. Their support is agency guidance, practitioner agreement and what went wrong in reported incidents.
    Contested
    How much faster AI makes developers. Controlled trials run from 26% more tasks completed (Cui et al., an autocomplete-era assistant) to 19% slower (METR, 2025, which METR now marks out of date), and METR calls its 2026 follow-up “an unreliable signal”. Whether AI-written code costs more to maintain: repository studies find more warnings and complexity (a conference paper and preprints, 2025 and 2026, abstracts read), and a controlled experiment found no maintainability difference (Borg et al., preprint).

    Where the principle comes from

    We couldn’t trace the phrase to a single origin. The earliest dated statements we could read come from governments in 2016 and 2017. Architects often meet it as an enterprise architecture principle, and you may hear it credited to TOGAF. We couldn’t confirm that, because the chapter we would need is behind a login. If someone tells you where it comes from, ask to see the page.

    What the published versions do agree on is the reasons:

    • The European Commission’s library of architecture principles states it as “Existing IT systems are reused, before deciding upon buying or even building them.” Its reasons: “Taxpayers’ money can only be spent once”, and the costs of maintaining and supporting new systems “are often forgotten and are much higher than the cost related to the initial development.” Building is “only considered a last resort”. The page gives no date. It cites the European Interoperability Framework’s reusability principle as its source, and is now marked archived.
    • The US Office of Management and Budget’s memorandum M-16-21 (August 2016) sets the same order as a three-step analysis, to avoid “duplicative acquisitions for substantially similar code and an inefficient use of taxpayer dollars” and to reduce “Federal vendor lock-in”.
    • The Scottish Government’s Digital Directorate (March 2017) calls “re-use before buy before build” one of its underlying principles, “potentially saving time, money and effort.”
    • The UK Technology Code of Practice (updated October 2026) puts reuse first, “Before building something new, find out whether government has already solved this problem”, but doesn’t rank buying against building.

    Sort the reasons

    Here are ten reasons the principle’s authors give, in their words or close to them. For each one, decide what happens when an agent can write the first version of a system in an afternoon. Is the reason now weaker, unchanged, or stronger? Place all ten before you open our reading.

    Our reading – open after placing all ten
    Where we put itReasonsWhy
    WeakerReuse is much cheaper · saving time, money and effort · vendor lock-in · effort to switch vendorsOnly the build part of each. A first version is now quick, and a credible rebuild makes it cheaper to walk away from a vendor. That changes the renewal negotiation even if you never build.
    UnchangedSecurity and privacy · quality supportNothing we read shows generated code is safer, and some studies suggest otherwise (step 22.2). Somebody still has to answer when it breaks.
    StrongerUpkeep · duplication · solved elsewhere · adapting your processIf code is cheap to make, more of it gets made, and each copy needs running. The cost pressure that made teams accept a standard process has gone, so that discipline has to come from somewhere else.

    Reasonable people put “solved elsewhere” under Weaker: rebuilding a solved problem wastes less when building is cheap. Our reading is that the waste moves from building to running, and that is the part this Part keeps returning to.

    What this means for the architecture. The principle is mostly a statement about lifetime cost and risk, written as an order. Cheap code shrinks one part of lifetime cost. So, by our reading, the order still holds wherever the rest of the bill dominates: anything durable, shared, regulated or holding data people rely on. Where a tool’s whole life is short, such as one team using it for one term, the build is most of the cost, and that is where the order can change.

    Think deeper: The European Commission’s text says to adapt your processes to standard systems where you can. That advice leaned on building being expensive. If any team can now build to its own process in an afternoon, what stops you ending up with forty slightly different booking tools? Should anything stop it, and who would notice it happening?

    Is your principle a cost rule or a risk rule?

    The pattern

    The make-or-buy decision and total cost of ownership, and pace layering, which many architects know from Gartner’s application strategy: systems of record change slowly, systems of innovation change fast, and each layer deserves its own governance. Reuse before buy before build was always a shortcut for a cost-of-ownership calculation. It worked because building was dear at every layer.

    What is really being decided

    Whether to keep one ordered rule or to give it a scope. The order stood in for three reasons: lifetime cost, duplication and risk. With cheap code, the shortcut and its reasons now point different ways at the fast-changing edge, and agree everywhere else. A principle that states its reasons can survive that. One that states only the order will be argued around tool by tool.

    The forces

    • First cost against lifetime cost: the first can now be close to nothing, and the second hasn’t moved that anyone has shown.
    • Fit against standardisation: a tool built to your own process fits better. A standard one gives you comparable data, shared upkeep and a supplier that fixes it.
    • Vendor lock-in against author lock-in: a generated tool is locked to whoever understands it, and that may be one person.
    • Procurement time against build time: for a small tool, the purchase process can now take longer than the build. That is a pressure on procurement, not only on architecture.
    • Duplication: copies are cheap to make and dear to run, and each one is a separate thing to patch.

    Left open

    • Does your principle say why, or only in what order? If only the order, which reason would you add first?
    • Who may grant an exception, and do they see the running costs or only the build cost?
    • Should “reuse” now also mean reusing a platform – a pipeline, an identity, a hosting environment – even when the application itself is new? Step 22.5 comes back to this.
    Five statements of the principle, side by side

    US OMB M-16-21 (8 August 2016). The Federal Source Code Policy’s “Three-Step Software Solutions Analysis”: prefer an existing federal solution, then look for a commercial one, and only then consider custom-developed code. It already allows mixtures: “Solutions containing a mixture of existing Federal, commercial, and/or custom-developed solutions should be considered throughout each step”. Step 22.3 quotes the three steps and scores a decision against the memo’s seven “Targeted Considerations”. We didn’t check whether the memo is still in force.

    European Commission, European Library of Architecture Principles. “Reuse, before buy, before build”, citing as its source “Reusability Underlying Principle (4) of the European Interoperability Framework”. The page itself carries no date. Its implications go further than the order: check first whether similar systems exist in the organisation or on the market, challenge requirements existing systems don’t meet, and adapt processes to standard systems where that is acceptable. The page is marked archived.

    Scottish Government Digital Directorate (7 March 2017). A blog post by Hugh Wallace calls “re-use before buy before build” an underlying principle of how the directorate works.

    UK Technology Code of Practice (point 8, updated 29 October 2026). Share, reuse and collaborate. Its reasons: “Duplicating work across government wastes time and money”, and working in isolation risks “building a solution for a problem which has already been solved elsewhere.” It ranks reuse first and says nothing about buy against build.

    Australia’s Digital and ICT reuse policy (the fifth row). The Digital Transformation Agency’s page marks the policy current and mandatory. It applies to non-corporate Commonwealth entities, and carries a notice that the government will revise it in the second half of 2026. It has three requirements: “Reuse whenever possible”, “Design and build for reuse” and “Enable reuse by others”. Its stated purpose is that it “reduces duplication of investment and ongoing costs involved in digital and ICT delivery across government”, and the agency assesses proposals against it when their whole-of-life ICT cost is $10 million or more. Like the UK code, it puts reuse first and doesn’t rank buying against building. We read the page on 13 November 2026.

    What we couldn’t read. TOGAF’s architecture principles chapter (behind a login) and NHS England’s reuse guidance (refused the request). So we make no claim about them.

    Read more

    • Reuse, before buy, before build (European Library of Architecture Principles)
    • Re-use it, don’t lose it (Scottish Government Digital, 2017)
    • The Technology Code of Practice (GOV.UK)
    • Share and reuse technology (GOV.UK)

  • I placed all ten reasons before opening our reading.
  • I can say which of the principle’s reasons cheap code weakens, and which it leaves alone or strengthens.
  • I can say what is and isn’t known about where the phrase comes from.

    What the studies show

    Predict how much faster AI makes an experienced developer, then see why the trials disagree, and label each claim you’ll hear by the evidence behind it.

    Step22.2

    Part 22
    Build, buy or generate
    Time
    10 min
    Last reviewed
    12 November 2026

    Collect the room’s predictions as numbers before the reveal, and write the average up. The lesson is the gap between belief and measurement. Don’t let it become “AI makes you slower”: that result is out of date, and METR says so on the page.

    Every business case for AI-assisted building rests on a speed-up. So before you see a single study, commit to a number.

    What one trial found – open after writing your numbers

    METR’s randomised trial (July 2025) gave 16 experienced developers 246 real issues from their own large, mature repositories, and randomly allowed or disallowed AI tools on each. With AI, “they take 19% longer”. Beforehand they expected AI to speed them up by 24%, and afterwards they still believed it had sped them up by 20%.

    Don’t quote the 19% as today’s fact. The page now opens with “These results are out of date.” METR ran a larger continuation from August 2025 (57 developers, more than 800 tasks), and reported in February 2026 that the point estimates now favour AI: tasks took 18% less time for returning developers and 4% less for new ones. Both confidence intervals cross zero. Between 30% and 50% of developers said they were holding back tasks they didn’t want to do without AI, and some declined to take part at all, so METR thinks its estimate is probably a lower bound. It calls the data “an unreliable signal” and is redesigning the study.

    The gap between belief and measurement is the finding to keep. In METR’s survey of 349 technical workers (May 2026), the median self-reported speed-up was 3x, far above any trial result in this step. METR’s own warning: “survey results are not necessarily grounded in reality”.

    Other trials point the other way

    Larger studies of other developers, on other work and with other tools, found gains. They measured different things, so the numbers don’t sit on one scale.

    • Field trials at three companies. Cui, Demirer, Jaffe, Musolff, Peng and Salz analysed three randomised experiments, run by the companies themselves, with 4,867 developers at Microsoft, Accenture and a Fortune 100 firm, using an autocomplete-era assistant. They found “a 26.08% increase (SE: 10.3%) in completed tasks”, and “less experienced developers had higher adoption rates and greater productivity gains”. We read the abstract only.
    • One enterprise task at Google. Paradis et al. (preprint, October 2024), 96 engineers: about 21% less time, “although our confidence interval is large”.
    • A rollout of coding agents. Murphy-Hill, Butler and Savelieva (preprint, July 2026) studied tens of thousands of engineers at Microsoft, their own employer, as coding agents arrived in early 2026. Adopters merged roughly 24% more pull requests, and “the lift persists across our four-month window”. The authors say themselves that a merged pull request isn’t the same as the value it delivers.

    Label the claim before you repeat it

    You will hear all of these in meetings. Sort each by the kind of evidence behind it, or mark it as one that doesn’t hold as stated.

    Our answers – open after placing all nine
    ClaimEvidenceSay it with this caveat
    An hour a daySelf-reportThe UK government’s trial (September 2025) found 56 minutes a day saved, from surveys. Its own telemetry showed 15.8% of suggested lines accepted, and only 39% of users said they committed suggested code. The report warns of optimism bias.
    26% more tasksControlled trialField trials with an autocomplete-era assistant, not agents. Less experienced developers gained most.
    19% slowerDoesn’t hold as statedTrue of 16 experts on mature code with early-2025 tools. METR marks it out of date.
    24% more pull requestsObservationalA proxy for output, measured by the employer, in a preprint.
    Three times fasterSelf-reportMETR’s survey: about 2% of those emailed responded, and METR says the results “plausibly suffer from significant selection bias”.
    Warnings and complexity rise and stay upObservationalOpen-source repository studies, preprints. A controlled experiment found no maintainability difference (see Going deeper).
    18% fasterDoesn’t hold as statedThe interval runs from 38% less time to 9% more, and METR calls the data unreliable. It may undercount the gain, too.
    Juniors scored lowerControlled trialShen and Tamkin (January 2026): 52 mostly junior engineers learning a library with a chat assistant scored 50% against 67%. Vendor-authored (Anthropic’s own researchers), and about a chat assistant rather than an agent. Step 14.2 has the detail.
    Less stable deliveryObservationalDORA 2025: a correlation in survey data, not a cause. Self-report is a fair answer too, because both measures come from survey answers.

    What this means for the architecture. The gains are counted where counting is easy: tasks, pull requests, lines accepted. The costs land later and somewhere else: review queues, stability and upkeep. When the curl project ended its bug bounty in January 2026 after a flood of AI-generated reports, its maintainer said “The current torrent of submissions put a high load on the curl security team” (The Register). A business case that counts only the first half is incomplete.

    Think deeper: METR could no longer run a clean trial, because the developers it most wanted wouldn’t work without AI. If the best way of measuring is closing, what will you accept as evidence in the next business case for AI-assisted building? Who in your organisation would collect it, and would they report a result the sponsor didn’t want?

    What can a business case honestly claim?

    The pattern

    Benefits realisation, and Goodhart’s law: a measure that becomes a target stops measuring. Thoughtworks’ Technology Radar (November 2026) keeps coding throughput as a productivity measure in its Caution ring, and says activity metrics such as the share of AI-generated code “may indicate adoption levels, they’re poor proxies for real productivity gains.”

    What is really being decided

    Which outcome the organisation will commit to measuring, and where: at the keyboard (speed, output) or at the service (stability, incidents, what it costs to run). DORA’s 2025 summary puts the choice bluntly: “AI doesn’t fix a team; it amplifies what’s already there.”

    The forces

    • Throughput against stability: more change, faster, with weaker controls downstream means more instability, by DORA’s account.
    • One person’s speed against everyone else’s review time: the curl case shows the cost moving to whoever has to check the output.
    • Juniors gain most, and may learn less: the field trials and the learning study pull in opposite directions for the same people.
    • Measurement against adoption: once everyone uses it, there is no comparison group left.
    • Self-report against telemetry: 56 minutes a day felt, 15.8% of suggestions accepted. Both are true, and neither is value.

    Left open

    • Which outcome would you measure a year from now that no vendor can influence?
    • If throughput rises and stability falls, whose budget absorbs it?
    • How will junior staff build the judgement to review code they didn’t write? Part 14, from step 14.1, asks the same question about architecture work.
    How to read a productivity study

    What was randomised? In a controlled trial, chance decides who or what gets AI, so other differences wash out. METR randomised issues; in Cui et al. the companies randomised developers’ access. Repository studies compare projects that chose to adopt with similar ones that didn’t (difference-in-differences). They are useful, and the adopters may differ in ways the matching misses.

    What was measured? Time on task, tasks completed, pull requests merged, lines accepted and minutes saved are different quantities. Only the first two are close to “faster”, and none of them is value delivered.

    Who was left out? METR’s 2026 study lost the developers keenest on AI and the tasks they most wanted to use it for. Selection can bias a result either way, so read who declined.

    Which tools, and when? Cui et al. studied autocomplete. METR’s 2025 trial used early-2025 tools. Agent-era studies are mostly observational so far. A result belongs to its tool generation.

    What is the interval? “About 21%, although our confidence interval is large” and “−18% (−38% to +9%)” are different kinds of claim from “26.08% (SE: 10.3%)”. Read the interval before the point.

    Who paid, and who wrote it? Employer studies of their own rollout and vendor-authored trials can be good work, and they are still not independent.

    Read more

    • Measuring the impact of early-2025 AI on experienced open-source developer productivity (METR, 2025)
    • The 2026 continuation (METR, February 2026)
    • Self-reported impact of early-2026 AI (METR survey, May 2026)
    • Three field experiments with software developers (Cui et al.)
    • AI coding assistant trial: findings report (UK government, 2025)
    Quality, upkeep and security: the evidence conflicts

    For every paper in this panel we read the abstract, not the body.

    Studies that find more debt.He, Miller, Agarwal, Kästner and Vasilescu (MSR ’26) compared open-source projects that adopted Cursor with matched controls: a “large, but transient” rise in velocity, and a “substantial and persistent increase” in static-analysis warnings and code complexity. Agarwal, He and Vasilescu (preprint, January 2026) found warnings up roughly 18% and cognitive complexity roughly 39% after projects adopted coding agents, with velocity gains large only where agents were the first AI tool. Xia and Miller (preprint, July 2026), across 182 repositories, found overall maintenance rates similar, but “agentic contributions require significantly higher rates of corrective maintenance and introduce more security weaknesses and dependency vulnerabilities.” Liu et al. (preprint) counted 484,366 issues introduced across 6,299 repositories, “code smells are by far the most common type, accounting for 89.3%”.

    The study that doesn’t. Borg et al. (preprint, a registered report) had 151 participants, about 95% professionals, evolve code that others had written with or without AI. They “did not detect systematic maintainability advantages or disadvantages”. That is a controlled task, not years in production, so the conflict is open.

    Security. In a user study with a 2022 model, Perry et al. (ACM CCS 2023) found AI users wrote “significantly less secure code” and were more likely to believe it secure. Spracklen et al. (USENIX Security 2025) found models inventing package names, “at least 5.2% for commercial models and 21.7% for open-source models”, which attackers can register. Sakib et al. (workshop paper, 2026) found 38.9% of 4,022 agent pull requests had at least one security smell, but humans introduced 67.6% of the genuine leaked secrets, and automated and human review missed 81.1% of those credentials.

    Mergeable is not the same as passing. In a METR study (March 2026), project maintainers wouldn’t have merged roughly half of the agent-written patches that passed a benchmark’s tests, and automated grader scores ran about 24 points above their merge decisions. Step 20.3 covers that study.

    What developers say. In the Stack Overflow Developer Survey 2025 (self-selected), 66% cited “AI solutions that are almost right, but not quite”, and 45.2% said debugging AI-generated code takes longer.

    Read more

    • Speed at the Cost of Quality (He et al., MSR ’26)
    • Measuring the Post-Merge Fate of Agentic Code (Xia and Miller, preprint)
    • Echoes of AI (Borg et al., preprint)
    • We Have a Package for You! (Spracklen et al., USENIX Security 2025)
    • Announcing the 2025 DORA report (Google Cloud)
  • I wrote my prediction before opening the trial result.
  • I sorted all nine claims, and can say which kind of evidence each rests on.
  • I can explain why neither “19% slower” nor “18% faster” holds as a present-tense fact.

    Previous step22.1 Why reuse came first Next step22.3 Rerun the decision

    Rerun the decision

    Take a Westmere renewal through the classic three-step analysis twice, before and after an agent built the core in an afternoon, and mark which criteria actually moved.

    Step22.3

    Part 22
    Build, buy or generate
    Time
    10 min
    Last reviewed
    12 November 2026

    Work in pairs: one argues for renewing, one for building, both from the same criteria. Four minutes to sort, three to decide, then open our reading. Watch for the room treating the prototype as the product. It is the most common slip.

    The UK NCSC’s CTO for Architecture describes a startup whose SaaS renewal quote came back at twice the price. Instead of renewing, “one of their engineering leads ‘vibe coded’ a replacement with the core functionality they needed within a couple of hours” (Chismon, March 2026). Here is the same thing at Westmere, invented, with the details a review board would ask for. Read it, then decide it twice.

    1 · Decide it as you would have in 2016

    Run the US OMB’s three-step analysis from step 22.1: prefer something you already have, then something you can buy, then a build. Forget the prototype for now.

    2 · Now an agent has built the core in an afternoon

    The first seven criteria are the OMB memo’s “Targeted Considerations”. We added two that come up in every review. For each, decide whether the prototype moves it towards building, leaves it where it was, or moves it the other way.

    3 · Decide it again

    The NCSC’s Dave Chismon expects building to spread along three lines: “how complex the service is”, “how important the service is” and “how risk averse the organisation is”. Use them to check your decision, not to make it.

    Optional: have an assistant argue for the build

    Send this prompt to any assistant, with the case pasted in place of its last line. Assistants differ, and so do runs. Everything in it is invented; don’t paste real contract or student data unless your organisation has approved it.

    Here is an invented case about a software renewal. First, make the strongest case you can for replacing the paid service with the prototype. Then, separately, list every cost, risk and obligation your case left out or played down, and say which of them you could not judge from the case. [paste the case]

    What this can’t show you: the assistant knows nothing about Westmere beyond the case, and it will argue whichever side you ask for. The value is in the second list. Compare it with your own.

    Our reading – open after deciding
    CriterionWhere we put itWhy
    Time to a first working versionTowards buildingThe clearest change. An afternoon against six weeks or a procurement.
    Resources required to later switch vendorsTowards buildingLeaving Marrowby is now cheaper, and Marrowby’s quote is now a negotiation.
    Total life-cycle cost of ownershipTowards building, partlyOnly the first-build part fell. Hosting, patching, support and accessibility fixes are all still to pay.
    PerformanceDoesn’t move140 events a year is a small load for any of the options.
    Security and privacy protectionsDoesn’t moveIf anything, it moves towards buying: student personal data, and a prototype with no university sign-in yet. Marrowby supplied a certification and a data processing agreement; a build needs its own.
    InteroperabilityDoesn’t moveThe sign-in and the records export are the hard parts, and the prototype has neither.
    Ability to share or reuseTowards reusingConfigured once, the CRM module could serve other faculties’ events too. A careers-only tool can’t.
    Availability of quality supportTowards buyingThe Careers Service has no developers, and the person who built it has another job.
    Who can explain the code in two yearsTowards buyingToday, one person, and she hasn’t read all of it.

    What we would decide. Don’t sign at 42,000 yet. Use the prototype twice: as a working list of what Careers really needs, and as the reason Marrowby should negotiate. Then compare the CRM module against a one-year renewal. Build only if someone funds an owner, as ADR-0012 requires, and the tool moves onto the university’s platform with sign-in and the export done. By then it isn’t an afternoon’s work.

    Groups reasonably differ on “go without”. Losing waiting lists and check-in may be acceptable to Careers, and saves 42,000 a year. Who gets to accept that loss is the real question.

    Now do the student records system in thirty seconds. It is critical to the business, hard to recreate, regulated, and holds data the whole university depends on. Nothing moves.

    What this means for the architecture. In this case the prototype changed the negotiation and the requirements more than it changed the decision. That is our reading of one invented case, but it matches the NCSC’s caution: the curve is shifting for “‘bespoke enough’ software”, and “this transition will take years rather than months.”

    Think deeper: Jason Lemkin’s team at SaaStr replaced a paid sponsor portal with an app built in “roughly a day and a half”, and he still wrote: “There’s no economic justification for building these apps based on software cost savings.” His reason was that the products on offer lacked features his business needed. When a team brings you a case to build, how will you tell a cost argument from a capability argument? Which should a review board accept, and on what evidence?

    What must stay bought?

    The pattern

    Core against context (Geoffrey Moore’s distinction between what differentiates you and what merely has to work), and the evolution from custom-built to product to commodity that Wardley mapping draws. Commodity goes to a supplier. Cheap code doesn’t change what is a commodity. It lowers the cost of building the bits between commodities.

    What is really being decided

    Where the line runs between what you would generate and what you would buy, and the line isn’t drawn by code. Chismon expects the SaaS services that survive to be those with “an inherent moat”: their services “have themselves become critical to a business, the service they provide is genuinely difficult to recreate, there are regulatory requirements they meet, or they simply have a critical mass of data across customers.” He expects infrastructure and platform services to be “less likely to be affected”, because generated applications need somewhere to run.

    The forces

    • Fit against shared upkeep: a tool built to your process fits better, and you alone maintain it.
    • Negotiating position: a credible rebuild changes a renewal even if you never build. Vendors will price that in too.
    • Data gravity: data that spans many customers, or that the whole organisation reads, stays where it is.
    • Assurance you inherit: a supplier hands you certifications, audit evidence and a processing agreement. A generated tool needs its own, and someone has to write them.
    • What gets left behind: “go without” is now a serious option, and the people who lose the feature rarely sit in the room that decides it.

    Left open

    • Which of your current renewals has no moat at all?
    • Would you tell a vendor you have a working prototype, and who decides that?
    • Who can accept a “go without” on behalf of the people who will lose the feature?
    The three-step analysis, read closely

    OMB’s memorandum M-16-21 calls it the “Three-Step Software Solutions Analysis”. Step one: “The alternatives analysis shall give preference to the use of an existing Federal software solution.” Step two, if none can “efficiently and effectively meet the needs of the agency”: look for “an appropriate commercially-available solution”. Step three, only if neither fits: “the agency may consider procuring custom-developed code”.

    Two details matter today. First, the memo already expects mixtures “throughout each step”, which is where most generated tools will land: a bought platform with a generated layer on top. Second, its criteria were never only about cost: “performance, total life-cycle cost of ownership, security and privacy protections, interoperability, ability to share or reuse, resources required to later switch vendors, and availability of quality support.” Only one of those mentions cost, and it says life-cycle.

    The NCSC’s Chismon names the option the memo lacks: organisations will “make different choices about buy vs build vs ‘go without’.” He also reminds us why SaaS won: running even a simple application meant patching, capacity and security, “But the real pain was maintenance.”

    Read more

    • M-16-21, Federal Source Code Policy (OMB, 2016, PDF)
    • Vibe check: AI may replace SaaS (but not for a while) (NCSC, March 2026)
    Is anyone really replacing SaaS?

    Observation and anecdote. The NCSC’s blog is a security agency’s reasoned view, part observation and part forecast. It reports “smaller, risk-tolerant startups vibe coding non-core SaaS replacements that do relatively simple things”, and “larger, more risk-averse organisations building tools that a single person or team uses, that might have once been just a feature in a SaaS.” It says plainly that it doesn’t predict organisations will vibe code a replacement for their CRM, and that today there “are risks that are likely far outside most organisations’ risk tolerances.” (You may see “intolerable risks” attributed to the NCSC. That wording is from its news release, not this blog.)

    A practitioner’s account. Lemkin (SaaStr, early 2026) describes replacing a paid sponsor portal, built by a colleague who isn’t an engineer. His rule is still “Buy everything you can off the shelf.” He is as blunt about upkeep, in the words that open step 22.5.

    A vendor’s survey. Retool (February 2026), which sells an app builder, surveyed 817 builders, including its own customers, in late 2025. 35% said they had replaced at least one SaaS tool with a custom build. Treat it as a vendor’s self-reported survey, with its own customers among those asked.

    A correction worth knowing. In 2024 Klarna’s CEO told analysts, “We just shut down Salesforce.” Later he wrote, “So no, we did not replace SaaS with an LLM”, and that Klarna had dropped a lot of its SaaS while building an internal stack to bring its data together (diginomica, March 2025, quoting his posts).

    What we couldn’t find. Independent data on SaaS spend, renewals or churn caused by building. If you see a confident percentage, ask whose survey it is and what exactly was asked.

    Read more

    • Vibe check: AI may replace SaaS (NCSC, 2026)
    • The 90/10 rule for AI agents (SaaStr)
    • 2026 Build vs. Buy report (Retool, vendor)
    • Klarna: no, we didn’t replace SaaS with an LLM (diginomica, 2025)
  • I decided the renewal before and after the prototype, and wrote down what decided it.
  • I sorted the nine criteria, and can say which moved and which didn’t.
  • I can name what makes a service hard to replace, and why none of it is about code.

    When generated code fails

    A tabletop on a reported incident where an agent deleted a production database in nine seconds. Find the controls and their owners, then see what “vibe coding” means and how strong the evidence for each safeguard is.

    Step22.4

    Part 22
    Build, buy or generate
    Time
    11 min
    Last reviewed
    12 November 2026

    Groups of three. Read the timeline aloud once, then give groups six minutes to name controls and owners before anyone opens the reveal. Keep the definitions of vibe coding short: the argument that matters is about oversight, not the word.

    In April 2026, by its founder’s account, a coding agent deleted a small company’s production database, and the backups stored with it, in one API call. In his words: “It took 9 seconds.”

    How well sourced this is. The account comes from the founder of PocketOS, in social media posts and emails, and from the comments of the infrastructure provider’s CEO, both as reported by The Register (27 April 2026). The AI Incident Database lists it as incident 1469. We didn’t read the original posts. The founder’s post is his own post-mortem, and we found no formal one from the provider. Treat every detail as reported, not established.

    1. A coding agent in an editor (Cursor, running an Anthropic model, according to the founder) is working on a task in the staging environment.
    2. It hits a credential mismatch and decides to fix it by deleting a storage volume.
    3. It goes looking for an API token, and finds one in an unrelated file.
    4. The token was created to add and remove custom domains, but it allowed any operation, including destructive ones. The founder says it wouldn’t have been stored if anyone had known how broad it was.
    5. The agent calls delete, with no confirmation, on an older API endpoint that lacked the provider’s delayed-delete safeguard.
    6. The production volume goes, and its backups with it, because, as the founder put it, “Railway stores volume-level backups in the same volume.”

    The data came back. The founder told The Register that the provider’s CEO helped restore it within an hour, on the Sunday evening. The provider says it keeps disaster backups as well as user backups, and has since patched that endpoint to delay deletes. Its CEO’s description of the design: “if you (or your agent) authenticate, and call delete, we will honor that request.”

    The tabletop

    Name every control that would have prevented this or limited the damage. For each, say who in your organisation would own it: a team or a role, not a tool. Look for at least five.

    Our list – open after naming at least five
    StepControlTypical owner
    1–2The agent runs in a sandbox that can’t reach production, or its credentialsWhoever configures the agent, against a platform standard
    3No secrets in files the agent can read: a vault, and secret scanning in the pipelineEngineering team, with the platform team
    4Tokens scoped to their purpose, and reviewed when createdPlatform or identity team
    5Destructive actions need a person’s approval, enforced outside the agentService owner; enforced by the platform, not by the prompt
    5Delayed or reversible deletes on every endpointThe provider. For you, a contract and due-diligence question
    6Backups kept apart from the data they protect, with restores testedOperations and the service owner

    Telling the agent “never delete production data” is the one model-level control. Our reading is that no instruction reliably stops an agent that has decided deleting is the fix, which is why the other five matter. Notice too what fixed this in the end: a person at the provider and, it appears, the provider’s own disaster backups.

    Now compare three other reported cases. Read how each is sourced: one is disputed by the company involved, and one is a security firm’s disclosure of an exposure, not a proven loss.

    In the three cases where an agent was reported to be involved (the tabletop case, the code-freeze case and the disputed outage), the companies’ announced fixes were conventional controls: separating development from production databases and a planning-only mode, delayed deletes, and mandatory peer review for production access. Our reading is that the argument in all three is about permissions and environments, not model quality.

    What “vibe coding” means

    The term is about 21 months old and already used loosely, so pin down which meaning someone has in mind.

    • The original. Andrej Karpathy, early February 2025, as quoted by Simon Willison: “where you fully give in to the vibes, embrace exponentials, and forget that the code even exists”, and “I don’t read the diffs anymore.” He added: “It’s not too bad for throwaway weekend projects”.
    • The strict meaning. Willison (March 2025): “building software with an LLM without reviewing the code it writes”. His own rule for everything else: “I won’t commit any code to my repository if I couldn’t explain exactly what it does to somebody else.”
    • The other end. Kent Beck (June 2025) contrasts it with augmented coding: “In vibe coding you don’t care about the code, just the behavior of the system.” By contrast, “In augmented coding you care about the code, its complexity, the tests, & their coverage.” Willison calls the disciplined version “vibe engineering” and later agentic engineering.
    • The line is blurring. By May 2026, Willison says he no longer reviews every line of agent-written code, even for production, and that the two have “started to blur for me already, which is quite upsetting.”
    • As a spectrum. The NCSC (June 2026): “Vibe coding isn’t binary. It exists on a spectrum”. It uses the term more loosely than Willison, for any agent-led building.

    Most professionals don’t work at the far right. In Huang et al.’s study (preprint, abstract read; 13 observed developers, 99 surveyed), experienced developers kept control of design and implementation. In the Stack Overflow survey (2025), 72.2% said “No” when asked whether vibe coding was part of their professional work.

    The safeguards, and how strong the evidence is

    No practice here has a controlled trial behind it that we found. The table says what kind of support each one has, as of 12 November 2026.

    PracticeSupportStrength
    Sandboxing and least privilegeThoughtworks’ Radar puts agent sandboxing at Adopt: “a sensible default for all agents”. The NCSC’s blog on its joint agentic AI guidance (May 2026): “give agents only the minimum access they need, for the shortest time required”. All three reported agent incidents turned on permissions or environmentsStrongest: agencies, practitioners and incidents agree
    Controls in rules and code, outside the modelThe NCSC’s Chismon asks how to use “known controls implemented in rules and code, rather than expecting an AI to limit another AI”An agency position, posed as a question still to answer
    Tests as the contractWillison: “Your job is to deliver code you have proven to work.” Mutation testing moved to Adopt on the Radar in November 2026Strong agreement they are needed. Measured evidence they aren’t enough (step 20.3)
    Small steps and real reviewThe Radar’s risk-tiered oversight (Trial). Less review goes with more upkeep (Xia and Miller, observational). Review missed 81.1% of leaked credentials (Sakib et al.)Moderate, observational. Review helps and misses things
    Harnesses and agent configurationA practitioner model (Böckeler). One preprint finds agent-first repositories without committed configuration gained more complexityEarly; the authors call it “hypothesis-generating”
    Specifications firstThe Radar placed spec-driven development at Assess (November 2025); Böckeler, who tried three of the tools, is scepticalWeak and contested
    Fitness functions, observability, provenanceNamed as countermeasures by practitioners and the NCSCA stated need; no measurement with agents found

    What this means for the architecture. The one safeguard that agencies, practitioners and the incidents all support is containment you can enforce without the model’s cooperation. It is also the one an architect owns, and step 20.4 designed it for an agent that acts on business systems. The rest of the list is still being worked out, by people who say so.

    Think deeper: Willison names the risk of reviewing less as code keeps turning out right: “normalization of deviance”. Each time it goes well, the next unreviewed change feels safer. Your review board approves the first generated tool with full scrutiny. What would stop the hundredth being waved through, and would anyone notice the day it should have been stopped?

    Who is accountable for code nobody read?

    The pattern

    Defence in depth and blast radius, with segregation of duties for production access (Amazon says it added mandatory peer review). You already apply all three to people. The change is applying them to a non-human actor that works at machine speed and has no reputation to lose. Willison again: “Claude Code does not have a professional reputation!”

    What is really being decided

    Whether you will accept code into production on the strength of the controls around it rather than a person’s review of it, and who signs for it when you do. Willison’s answer for now: “A computer can never be held accountable. That’s your job as the human in the loop.” The NCSC’s blog on its agentic AI guidance agrees: “A system may take an action, but humans remain accountable”. Neither says how that works when nobody read the code.

    The forces

    • Review coverage against pace: the NCSC says human review of all AI-written code is “creaking at the seams” for organisations that want to build fast.
    • Controls in the platform against instructions to the agent: one is enforced, the other is a request.
    • Approval against theatre: the Radar warns of “human-in-the-loop theater”, an approval step that checks nothing.
    • Convenience against blast radius: one token that can do anything saves a few minutes, once.
    • Provider defaults against your assumptions: “we will honor that request” is a design choice, and it is in someone’s terms of service.

    Left open

    • Who signs for a generated change nobody read, and what does the signature attest? Step 15.4 asks the same of documents.
    • Which actions in your estate should never be one API call away from an agent?
    • Do your contracts say what a provider does when an authorised agent calls delete?
    Tests, harnesses and fitness functions: how the practices work

    Tests that can fail. Willison’s test for a test: “That test should fail if you revert the implementation.” Mutation testing makes that systematic, by changing the code on purpose and checking a test notices. The Radar puts it at Adopt, “helping ensure generated tests don’t simply pass without catching logic changes”.

    Harnesses. Birgitta Böckeler (April 2026) splits the controls around a coding agent into guides, which anticipate the agent’s behaviour and aim to “steer it before it acts”, and sensors, which “observe after the agent acts and help it self-correct”, such as tests and linters whose messages tell the agent what to fix. Denisov-Blanch et al. (preprint, abstract read) looked at 441 repositories: agent-first ones without committed AI configuration showed “roughly twice the increase in cognitive complexity (+53% versus +27%)”. They call it “hypothesis-generating”.

    Specifications. Writing intent down first is widely advised, and Lemkin does it. Heavy spec tooling is another matter: the Radar warns of “lengthy spec files that are hard to review”, and Böckeler, after trying the tools, wrote “I’d rather review code than all these markdown files” and “I frequently saw the agent ultimately not follow all the instructions”.

    Fitness functions. An architect’s tool, from before generative AI: “an objective integrity assessment of some architectural characteristics” (Radar, November 2017). The Radar’s 2026 “codebase cognitive debt” entry names them as a countermeasure. Nobody has measured them with agents yet that we found.

    What is still unsolved

    Whether it can be made safe yet. The NCSC’s Chismon: “no one yet knows exactly what we need to introduce to ensure the ‘vibe coded future’ is a safer one.” The NCSC’s spectrum blog post: “But we’re not there yet. Calibrate your approach based on today’s reality, not tomorrow’s potential.”

    Verification at scale. The NCSC expects that “Over the next 5 years it will become increasingly common to see AI-written code in production systems that a human has never reviewed or even looked at.” Böckeler calls checking functional behaviour “the elephant in the room”, and asks: “If sensors never fire, is that a sign of high quality or inadequate detection mechanisms?”

    Comprehension debt. Addy Osmani (March 2026): “nothing in your current measurement system captures it”, and “Tests are necessary. They are not sufficient.” Margaret-Anne Storey (February 2026) describes a student team that “had accumulated cognitive debt faster than technical debt, and it paralyzed them”, and lists measuring it as an open research question. The Radar defines codebase cognitive debt as “the growing gap between a system’s implementation and a team’s shared understanding of how and why it works” (Caution, April 2026).

    Upkeep. Repository studies find more corrective work after agents arrive; a controlled experiment found no maintainability difference (step 22.2). All of it is recent and short.

    Ownership. The US Copyright Office (January 2025) concluded that AI outputs are protected only “where a human author has determined sufficient expressive elements”, and not by “the mere provision of prompts”. We read the Office’s announcement, not the report. Our reading: whether you own copyright in code nobody edited is open in the US. We checked no other jurisdiction. Who is liable for it, nobody we read has answered.

    Who runs what you generate?

    Write the operating ledger for something a team wants to generate instead of buy, restate the principle for today, then close the Part and the guide with a plan you can start on Monday.

    Step22.5

    Part 22
    Build, buy or generate
    Time
    14 min
    Last reviewed
    12 November 2026

    Ten minutes on the ledger in pairs, then the plan, then the discussion. Keep the last five minutes for the close: pair people up to read their plans aloud to each other, as at the end of Part 13, and finish there rather than with a summary from the front.

    Jason Lemkin, who runs SaaStr with a handful of people and many agents, put the cost of building plainly: “every app you build is an app you now have to maintain.” He also gave a number: “Each security update cycle takes us about a week to fully recover from.” His question for the next five years is who maintains ten apps and twenty agents: “Right now, the answer is us. That’s not sustainable.” (SaaStr, early 2026.)

    Write the operating ledger

    Use the Westmere careers tool from step 22.3, as if it were going ahead, or a tool from your own work described in general terms with nothing confidential. Fill in every row you can. Where you can’t, write who could, because the gaps are the result.

    Model answer for the careers tool – open after filling in your ledger

    Row 2 stops it. The prototype took an afternoon. The owner, under ADR-0012, takes a decision and a budget, and nobody has made either.

    The principle, restated

    Here is where the evidence leaves the principle, as of November 2026. This is our reading, not a standard, and it is the sentence we would put to a review board.

    Reuse, then buy, then build, for anything durable, shared, regulated or holding data people rely on. For a small tool one team uses, building it or going without can now beat buying, as long as it runs on the organisation’s paved road, has a named owner and has a planned exit. And “reuse” now has a second meaning: reuse the road, the pipeline, identity and hosting, even when the application is new.

    That keeps the order where its reasons still hold (step 22.1) and changes it only where the build was most of the cost. It also turns the hard question from “can we build it?” into “who runs it?”, which is the one cheap code didn’t answer.

    Think deeper: A tool starts disposable: one team, one term, no personal data. Eighteen months later three faculties use it, it holds student records, and its author has left. Nobody decided it should become durable. It just did. What would have to be true in your organisation for someone to notice the day it changed class, and who should that person be?

    You have finished Part 22

    You can now say which of the principle’s reasons cheap code changes and which it doesn’t; label a productivity claim by the evidence behind it; rerun a buy-or-build decision and show which criteria moved; run a tabletop on a generated-code failure and name the controls and their owners; and write the operating ledger that decides whether a generated tool should go live.

    Questions to discuss

    In a group session, share your answers, and park anything that needs a longer discussion for the end.

    • Which of your current renewals would nobody miss, and who would argue for keeping it anyway?
    • Where are people already building their own tools, and what need does that show you hadn’t met?
    • What would make you trust code that nobody has read? Is there anything?
    • Who should own the paved road for generated software here, and who pays for it?

    You have finished the guide

    Skills in depth · Parts 5 to 13Step 5.1Show whether a skill beats no skill, build ones that draft, check, route, cite and run scripts, connect them safely, chain them, and own them as a team.

    What stays true as the tools change

    Most product details in this guide will date. These ideas, in our reading, have held across every Part, and we expect them to outlast the tools:

    1. It predicts; it doesn’t know. Check claims against sources, not against how sure it sounds (step 3.5).
    2. It works from what it is given. Context, sources and permissions are design decisions, and the index is inside your trust boundary (step 4.5).
    3. Measure against doing without. With or without the skill, the tool or the agent, scored, not felt (step 5.3, and this Part).
    4. Enforce outside the model. Permissions, sandboxes and approvals hold when instructions don’t (steps 11.4 and 20.4).
    5. A named person decides, and answers for it. Models draft, check and act. People own the result (step 13.4).
    6. Date your evidence. Say what is measured, what is reported and what is your own reading, and check again next quarter.

    A last honest note. Much of the evidence in the later Parts is a preprint, a vendor’s report or a press account less than two years old, and we know of no study of whether working through a guide like this changes what teams build. Treat it as a well-sourced starting point, keep your own numbers, and expect to revise it.

    Export your notes: they hold your predictions, sorts, plans and ledgers from every Part you have done. They stay on your device unless you decide to share them.

    Disposable or durable: who decides when a tool changes class?

    The pattern

    Shadow IT and the paved road. Thoughtworks’ Radar puts “AI-accelerated shadow IT” in Caution (November 2026): software built outside traditional development “usually lacks testing, deployment pipelines and observability”, and its advice is “Be firm on security, and give useful tools a clear path to support.” Lilly Ryan, also of Thoughtworks, puts the cause first: “Shadow IT is often a lagging indicator of unmet organizational demand.” This is the inner-source and platform-engineering argument from step 13.5, applied to applications.

    What is really being decided

    Not whether people may build, because they already are. The decision is what triggers the move from disposable to durable, who watches for it, and what the road provides so that moving is cheaper than staying hidden. The alternative, which Ryan warns of, is ending up “reliant on automated processes that no one actually knows how to debug.”

    The forces

    • Freedom to build against the duty to run: the cheaper the build, the bigger the share of cost that sits in running.
    • The road’s friction against going around it: if the paved road is slower than a personal cloud account, people take the account. Ryan’s remedy is roads that “lower the friction of compliance”.
    • One author against continuity: a generated tool can have exactly one person who understands it.
    • Clear triggers against judgement: rules are easy to watch and easy to game; judgement doesn’t scale to hundreds of tools.
    • Retirement: a disposable tool that nobody retires becomes durable by default.

    Left open

    • What is your trigger list, and who watches for it?
    • Who funds the paved road: the platform team, or each team that uses it?
    • When a generated tool fails at 2 a.m., whose phone rings, and did they agree to that?
    A paved road for generated software

    The NCSC’s Chismon frames the open question as a platform one: “What platforms for hosting AI-generated services (and even human-generated ones) can we design to implement the controls above and protect the organisation and its data even if the code running is of poor quality?” He reports one large organisation already making sure “even the smallest project now has comparable test case coverage, automated security testing, and documentation, as they do for critical software they manually maintain.”

    Pieces that exist today, with the strength of support from step 22.4:

    • A sandbox for agents, away from production and its credentials, which the Radar now treats as the default for every agent.
    • Least privilege, briefly held. The NCSC’s blog on its joint agentic AI guidance adds a test for going live: “If you cannot understand, monitor or contain an agent’s actions, it is not ready for deployment”.
    • A pipeline with tests, dependency and secret scanning, and security checks that run on every change, whoever or whatever wrote it.
    • Hosting with backups kept apart from the data, with restores tested, and deletes that can be undone.
    • Monitoring and a register, so someone knows the tool exists, who owns it and whether it is up (step 20.5 does this for agents).

    What the builder still owns: tests for the behaviour users depend on, the ledger, and the decision to retire. None of these pieces has a controlled trial behind it for generated code. They are conventional controls, applied to a new kind of author.
